### B O O K   T H I R D.

### Explanation of the Reliefs of a singular Column, & of the Monuments of the Cathedral of Paris.

**CHAP. I.** General idea of the *Divinities* which comprise the subject of the third Book. How perplexing <note>original: "embarrassante"; the author finds it difficult to categorize these ancient gods</note> it is to arrange the *Gallic Divinities* each according to its rank. page * 1
**II.** Description of a beautiful Column found at *Cussy* <note>Cussy-la-Colonne in Burgundy, famous for its Roman-era funerary column</note>. * 4
**III.** Explanation of the first three Figures: *Minerva*, *Juno* & *Jupiter*. * 6
**IV.** Description of the fourth Figure; the difficulty of explaining it; it is *Hebe* according to some. It is more likely that it is *Andraste* <note>A Gallo-British victory goddess</note> or *Victory*. * 9
**V.** Portrait of *Pluto* with his true symbols: the Gauls made only one and the same Divinity of *Pluto* & *Teutates* or *Mercury* <note>The author is discussing the syncretism where Gallic and Roman gods were merged</note>. * 16
**VI.** The sixth Figure represents the *Venus* of the Underworld or *Libitina* <note>An ancient Roman goddess associated with funerals and burial</note>. Ceremonies observed in the sacrifices, where men served as victims. * 19
**VII.** The seventh Figure is *Hercules*: Victories of *Hercules* in the Gauls. The opinion of some Authors, that the Pillars of *Hercules* were located in the Gauls. Ancient Gallic Coin representing *Hercules*. Its explanation. * 20
**VIII.** *Hercules Magusanus*. Relief, Inscriptions & Medals of this God. *Hercules Magusanus* is the same as *Hercules of Deusone*. *Hercules* of *Strasbourg* called *Krutzman* <note>original: "Krutzman"; a local Germanic name for a hero or deity often identified with Hercules</note>. * 26
**IX.** A singular Altar of *Hercules Saxanus* <note>Hercules of the Rocks, often worshipped by soldiers and quarry workers</note> found in *Lorraine*: in what era it could have been erected. What *Hercules Saxanus* is. This God was honored as well in *Italy* as in the Gauls. * 32
**X.** The last Figure represents a human victim. To which Gods the Gauls offered these kinds of victims. Why they were bound. The poor success of those who took it upon themselves to represent the sacrifices of the Gauls from their own imagination. In what era the Gauls offered human victims. * 38
**XI.** Low-reliefs found in the Choir of the Cathedral of Paris <note>Refers to the 1711 discovery of the "Pillar of the Boatmen" under Notre-Dame</note>. The care taken to have them drawn faithfully. An account of this discovery. * 44
**XII.** The discovery of these Antiques makes a great stir. Some Scholars have them engraved differently from the original. These engravings produce several Dissertations in France & elsewhere. * 47
**XIII.** It does not appear that all these Monuments have yet been well explained. * 49

->*B O O K  T H R E E.*<-

->Explanation of the Reliefs of a remarkable Column, and of the Monuments<-
->of the Cathedral of Paris.<-

**CHAP. I.** General overview of the Divinities that are the subject of the third Book. How difficult a thing it is to arrange the Gallic Divinities each according to their rank. page * 1
**II.** *Description of a beautiful Column found at Cussy.* <note>Cussy-la-Colonne is a village in Burgundy famous for this Roman-Gallic monument.</note> * 4
**III.** *Explanation of the first three Figures: Minerva, Juno & Jupiter.* * 6
**IV.** *Description of the fourth Figure; the difficulty of explaining it: it is Hebe according to some. It is more likely that it is Andraste or Victory.* <note>Andraste was a War Goddess invoked by the British queen Boudica, often associated with Victory.</note> * 9
**V.** *Portrait of Pluto with his true symbols: the Gauls made only one and the same Divinity of Pluto and Teutates or Mercury.* * 16
**VI.** *The sixth Figure represents the Inferior Venus or Libythina <note>original: "Libythine," referring to the Roman goddess of funerals and burials</note>. Ceremonies observed in sacrifices, where men served as victims.* * 19
**VII.** *The seventh Figure is Hercules; Victories of Hercules in the Gauls. Opinion of some Authors, that the Pillars of Hercules were in the Gauls. Ancient Gallic Coinage representing Hercules. Its explanation.* * 20
**VIII.** *Hercules Magusanus <note>original: "Maguſan"</note>. Relief, Inscriptions & Medals of this God. Hercules Magusanus is the same as the Deusonian Hercules. The Hercules of Strasbourg called Krutzman.* * 26
**IX.** *Remarkable Altar of Hercules Saxanus <note>original: "Saxan"</note> found in Lorraine: in what time it could have been erected. What Hercules Saxanus is. This God was honored in Italy as well as in the Gauls.* * 32
**X.** *The last Figure represents a human victim. To which Gods the Gauls offered these kinds of victims. Why they were bound. The poor results of those who have attempted to represent the sacrifices of the Gauls from imagination. At what time the Gauls offered human victims.* * 38
**XI.** *Bas-reliefs found in the Choir of the Cathedral of Paris. The care taken to have them faithfully drawn. Account of this discovery.* <note>This refers to the 1711 discovery of the "Pillar of the Boatmen" (Pilier des Nautes) under the altar of Notre-Dame.</note> * 44
**XII.** *The discovery of these Antiquities causes a great stir. Some Scholars have them engraved differently from the original. These engravings produce several Dissertations in France and elsewhere.* * 47
**XIII.** *It does not appear that all these Monuments have yet been well explained.* * 49

# SUMMARY

XIV. *Explanation of the Inscription that occupies one face of the first stone. It has been claimed without cause that there were letters written* boustrophedon <note>original Greek: βουστροφηδον; meaning "as the ox turns," referring to ancient writing that alternates direction from right-to-left and left-to-right</note>. *What it means to write* boustrophedon. *The Gauls wrote in this manner for a long time. Several medals* <note>In the 18th century, "medals" often referred to ancient coins.</note> *prove it. Explanation of these medals.* \* 51

XV. *Explanation of two other faces of the same stone. True meaning of the word* Eurisés. *Grammatical observations on the diphthong* EI *and on the letters* S, T. *The Gauls carried arms while performing their religious duties. A circle carried in procession.* \* 60

XVI. *Druids represented on the fourth face of the first stone: by which signs they are recognizable. Explanations of the words* SENANI VEILO. *To what degree of esteem and veneration Mistletoe* <note>original: "le Gui"</note> *was held in the Gallic lands. Number of Druids represented.* \* 63

XVII. *General idea of the second stone. Selected features that provide a full understanding of the God Esus.* \* 68

XVIII. *The Gauls worshipped a Bull. Description of the* Tarvos Trigaranus <note>The "Bull with three Cranes," a famous deity depicted on the Pillar of the Boatmen.</note>. *Origin of these words. The ancient Celts swore by a Bronze Bull. They represented a Bull and three Cranes on their standards and on their shields. A curious detail reported by Artemidorus and applied to the* Tarvos Trigaranus. *Judgment that can be made concerning Gallic monuments laden with figures of bulls. An omen called* Tripudium Solistimum <note>A Roman term for a favorable omen observed when sacred chickens ate so greedily that food fell from their mouths.</note>. *The "Crane," a circular dance of the Ancients.* \* 70

XIX. *Castor and Pollux represented on the third stone. Journey of Castor and Pollux into the Gallic lands. Their birth. They did not initially have statues. They were served* <note>referring to ritual service or priesthood</note> *by women. Inscription of* Pollux Vincius. \* 80

XX. *Horned Gods of the Gauls. Etymologies of the word* Cernunnos; *Cult of this God. The Gauls took delight in hunting elk, fallow deer, stags, aurochs* <note>original: "Ures," the extinct wild ox of Europe</note>, *etc. Description of these hunts. Remarks on the symbols of Cernunnos. This God was to the Gauls what Alcis was to the Naharvali* <note>original: "Naharvales," an ancient Germanic tribe described by Tacitus as worshipping twin gods called the Alcis.</note> *of Germania.* \* 85

XXI. *Continuation of the same subject. Dog collars hanging from the horns of Cernunnos. German scholars believe that Cernunnos is the God Bacchus. An epigram by the Emperor Julian on the drink of the Celts* <note>Referring to a poem by Julian the Apostate mocking beer as "wine made of barley."</note>. *Mr. Eccard seems not to have grasped Julian's thought. Bacchus God of wine was not different from Bacchus God of Beer* <note>original: "Cervoise," a traditional barley beer.</note>. *If Cernunnos were Bacchus, it would rather be Bacchus surnamed Sabazius and "the Elder." Another opinion on the God Cernunnos: the authority that favors it.* \* 95

XXII. *Description of another Horned God of the Gauls.* \* 103

XXIII. *Explanation of the last face of the third stone. Deliberate precautions that the Druids took to receive the* Anguinum <note>original: "Oeuf Anguinum," the "Serpent's Egg," a legendary druidic talisman described by Pliny the Elder.</note> *Egg. System of the Egyptians, of Orpheus, and apparently of the Gauls regarding the creation of the world.* \* 105

# BOOK FOUR.

->Concerning Gallic Gods of the second class. Saturn, Vulcan, Volianus, Bacchus, Telesphorus, Circius, Cybele, Proserpine, Ardoina, the Oracle of the Isle of Sein, Nehalennia, Isis, Onuava, the Mother Goddesses, Deified Cities, etc.<-

**CHAP. I.** What is to be understood by the Gallic Gods of the second class. page 1

**II.** Saturn. Human victims offered to Saturn in the Gallic lands, all of whom were of the age of puberty. The Druids held that Saturn was imprisoned in one of the islands near England. 3

**III.** The cult of Vulcan in the Gallic lands. 5

**IV.** Concerning the God Volianus. Diverse opinions on this God. According to some, he is Belenus <note>A major Celtic sun god, often compared to Apollo.</note>; according to others, he is Noah, etc. Refutation of these opinions. Apollo and the Sun were two different deities in civil worship. It is more likely that Volianus was Vulcan. 8

**V.** Bacchus. The antiquity of the cult of Bacchus in the Gallic lands. Women who served in one of his Temples. Their extraordinary customs. Temples of Bacchus in Aquitaine. 19

**VI.** The horns of Bacchus. In the Gallic lands, this God was represented as an old man. Epigram by the Emperor Julian on the drink of the Gauls <note>This likely refers to Julian the Apostate's poem mocking beer as a "wine made from grain" rather than grapes.</note>. Epigram by Ausonius on the Bacchus of the Gauls. 22

**VII.** Different explanations of an ancient Gallic Medal <note>In this period, "medal" was commonly used to refer to ancient coins.</note>. Concerning the God Telesphorus. 25

**VIII.** Of the two following Figures, one appears to be Apollo. They have a similar type of hat. Could it be the Hymen's <note>Hymen was the Greek god of marriage ceremonies.</note> hat of flowers? Acclamations at weddings; their origin: a true portrait of Hymen. These two Figures have somewhat the air and features of Hymen. 27

**IX.** Deified winds, especially Circius <note>A violent local wind of the Narbonnese region of Gaul.</note>. 30

**X.** Cybele. A Gallic coin representing a Ceremony in honor of Cybele. Description of this Ceremony in the Gallic lands and in Germany. A similar ceremony practiced in Egypt. Discovery of two Figures of Cybele in Paris. 32

**XI.** Ceres and Proserpine. The Cabiri <note>A group of enigmatic underworld deities worshipped in mystery cults.</note> and their mysteries. 40

**XII.** Ardoina <note>Arduinna, the tutelary goddess of the Ardennes Forest.</note> or Diana. The Gauls consecrated entire Forests to one of their Gods and made them bear his name. The Ardennes were consecrated to Diana. A fine relief representing five Gallic Deities. The duration of the cult of Diana in the Gallic lands. Diana honored in Marseille. 43

**XIII.** Concerning the Oracle of the Isle of Sein. The Maidens who served the Oracle. Their morals and customs. The Deity of the Oracle was the Moon. Why the Gauls chose Maidens to serve the Oracle. In this, they agreed with other Nations. The Moon honored in the Gallic lands. This Deity was later called Bensozia, Herodias, Nocticula, Domina, etc., or Diana. A singular figure of Bensozia. Isis was sometimes represented in nearly the same way. A troop of women who went

*by night through the air. Description of Empusa <note>A shape-shifting female demon or spirit from Greek mythology, sometimes associated with Hecate</note>; a Divinity often malevolent; sometimes benevolent.* 51

XIV. *A number of Islands on the coasts of Gaul & Britain inhabited only by Druids & Druidesses. Some were deserted; but all were consecrated to certain Divinities. The opinion of the Druids who inhabited these Islands regarding storms & tempests.* 67

XV. *Clarifications on the name of the Virgins of the Isle of Sein. A true reading of a passage by Mela <note>Pomponius Mela, a Roman geographer who described the nine virgin priestesses on the Isle of Sein who could control the weather and transform into animals</note>.* 70

XVI. *Relief found at Narbonne. The opinions of Scholars. Conjectures of the Author.* 76

XVII. *Discovery in Zeeland & at Nîmes of the Goddess Nehalennia. Description of the bas-reliefs representing her.* 78

XVIII. *What two Divinities are those to whom two Inscriptions are consecrated: how these Inscriptions should be read.* 82

XIX. *Nehalennia. The Divinity of the Oracle of the Isle of Sein was the same as Nehalennia. Various etymologies of the word Nehalennia. Nehalennia was the new Moon. Depictions that the Ancients left of Statues of the Moon. The Gauls & Germans held the new Moon in singular honor. Parallel between Nehalennia & the Oracle of the Isle of Sein. Essential difference between the Vestals and the Virgins of Gaul.* 88

XX. *Diana-Moon found in Lorraine; conjectures on her cult. Opinions of the Ancients on the cause of Eclipses.* 104

XXI. *Onuava or Celestial Venus. Celestial Venus taken for Medusa & for the Sun. Derceto, Dagon, the Syrian Goddess, Atargatis, Salambas, Oannes, Oën, &c. all Monsters or Divinities who had something of the fish <note>These are ancient Near Eastern deities often depicted with fish tails, representing fertility or the sea</note>. The Onuava of Gaul is this same Monster or Divinity. Apotheosis of Serpents <note>The elevation of snakes to divine status</note> accepted in several countries. What the wings on the head of a Divinity signify. Onuava, according to Bochart <note>Samuel Bochart, a 17th-century biblical scholar known for his work on geography and animals in the Bible</note>, is the Onka or the Minerva of the Phoenicians: He is refuted. The Venus of Paphos came from Phoenicia. Celestial Venus adored almost everywhere. The cult of this Divinity consisted above all in the abstinence from fish. Diseases & penance of those who ate it. Infamous consecration that Women made in honor of Celestial Venus. Priests of this Divinity: their manners & their character. Why the body of Onuava is much larger in proportion than its head.* 110

XXII. *Isis. It has been claimed that Isis was neither known nor adored in Gaul. Inscriptions which prove the contrary. The Isis of Saint-Germain-des-Prés. Observations on the language of the Celts. Etymologies of the words Senones & Parisii. In the first centuries of Christianity, idols were either set up or buried within Churches without distinction.* 131

XXIII. *Concerning the Mayor Goddesses, Mothers, Matrons, Ladies, &c. in general. Description of the reliefs representing them. True sense of the name they bear <note>Commonly known to modern archaeology as the "Matres" or "Matronae," often depicted as a trio of seated women holding fruits or children</note>.* 147

XXIV. *Various opinions on the Divinities called Mayors, Mothers, &c.; they were the Fates. They presided over childbirth. Different titles with which they were honored. Birth-beds consecrated to the Fates. True meaning of the term Augustus <note>In this context, used as a title of divinity or sacredness (e.g., "The August Mothers")</note>. Lucina <note>The Roman goddess of childbirth</note> represented in the same manner as the Fates. Opinion of the Ancients that the Fates sometimes showed themselves. Other ideas held regarding these Divinities. The devotion people had for them soon surpassed that which they had for the greatest Divinities.* 153

XXV. *Continuation of the same subject. Extract of a letter from an Antiquarian on two Inscriptions—*

Gaulish traditions. The Mothers <note>original: *Maires, Meres*</note>, etc. are the same Divinities as the Suleviae <note>A group of Celtic goddesses often associated with the Matrons and springs</note> and the Sylphs <note>In folklore, these were elemental spirits of the air</note>. Rural Divinities of both sexes. The intimacies that both had with the men and women of this world. People took pride in claiming their origin from this species of Divinities. ## BOOK FIVE.

->Of Funerals, Tombs, Mausoleums, Urns, Sepulchral<-
->Inscriptions, etc., of the Gauls.<-

<margin>CHAP. I.</margin> Funerals were part of the Religion of Nations. Immortality of the soul. The dwelling place of Souls. Benevolent and malevolent Souls. Sacrifices, libations, meals, etc., performed for the dead: for what motives. 211

<margin>II.</margin> Funerals of the Gauls; their Tombs. The feelings of the Druids and the Gauls on the death of prominent persons, and of those who served as Victims to the Gods. 214

<margin>III.</margin> Several Authors have claimed that the Gauls believed in Metempsychosis <note>The transmigration of souls, or reincarnation</note>. Their error. On what it is founded. The Gauls incontestably held to the immortality of the soul. They said that the soul was eternal. Pythagoras held the same language. The true sense of this term. 218

<margin>IV.</margin> The Infernal Gods <note>Gods of the underworld</note> of the Gauls were Venus, Mars, and Mercury. Reasons for this choice. 228

<margin>V.</margin> Of Sepulchers consecrated "under the adze" <note>original: *sub Ascia*. This was a common Roman funerary formula, usually depicted as a tool on a tombstone, whose exact meaning is still debated by historians</note>. Different opinions on the meaning of this formula. 236

<margin>VI.</margin> The Adze <note>original: *l'Ascia*</note> of the sepulchers was truly a Hoe or Mattock. The Gauls had several kinds. A marble Cippus <note>A small, square pillar used as a landmark or tombstone</note> consecrated "under the adze." This consecration had a great connection to that of the foundations of Cities. 242

<margin>VII.</margin> Description of a truly Gaulish Tomb. Figures of Women found in this Tomb and in others. Different explanations regarding these Figures. 264

<margin>VIII.</margin> Tombs representing the different clothing of Gaulish men and women. Bas-reliefs of Dishes found at the foundations of two houses. Description of a Tomb found at Bourges. [...to consult] the Writers of all centuries, and to study all the monuments which have escaped the ravages of time. Thus, by gathering the smallest details, and even the slightest traces of a Religion whose knowledge was becoming increasingly obscure, more difficult every day, and seemed to flee and distance itself from us, we strive to remedy the dryness of sources that refuse to flow, and to compensate for the deficiency or silence of Authors.

All the reflections that make up this Work justify these truths; but those forming this third Book place them in a clearer light. Indeed, they offer to the <gloss>eyes of</gloss> Scholars the precious treasures of two discoveries which good fortune—shall I say of the Gauls or the French—has brought about in our day in two Provinces quite distant from one another; and they trace the efforts required to shed light upon Reliefs <note>Bas-reliefs; stone carvings where the figures project slightly from the background</note> which, having preserved no mark to identify them, were beginning to fall into indifference, and were passing from indifference into oblivion and neglect. However, these insights, however useful they may be, have in particular only kept us for a long time in embarrassment <note>In this historical context, "embarrassment" (embarras) refers to intellectual perplexity or the difficulty of categorizing new information within an existing system</note>; for whatever new and surprising object they offer, the Divinities represented are always by their nature or number among those who form the base and foundation of the Religion of the Gauls, and on that footing they should, according to our system, have had a place in the second Book; or finally, they are Divinities of the second class, that is to say, of a second order, who only concerned the heart of the Religion through the publicity and establishment of a cult—

...[that] which was simultaneously added and subordinate to the first: and in this case, they would have had to be relegated to the fourth Book. But neither option could be carried out without causing all these Divinities to lose those graces and that certain *indescribable something* <note>original: "je ne sai quoi"</note> which they derive from the grouping that Antiquity gave them.

It is true that after having them each engraved separately and according to the rank they were to hold, one could have also represented them all together, as they are in the original; but this divided the reader’s mind too much, and caused him to lose much time in consulting the whole Figure and relating it to the reflections he was reading. Not to mention that we ourselves, speaking of these Divinities in so many disparate places, could not have easily indicated all the connections they have with all those who formed a single body with them.

To avoid all these inconveniences, a middle ground <term>temperament|a compromise or balancing of different considerations</term> was chosen that would reconcile everything: we have made a single body of all these Divinities, to place it as if in the middle of the Gaulish Divinities of the first and second class, so that according to the different tastes of Antiquarians <note>scholars of ancient history and artifacts</note>, some might relegate each to its own class, and others might see them all joined together. After all, this was the only course we could take; for most of these Divinities are of too singular a nature to deserve being confused with the others.

This approach, so simple in appearance—though the idea only came to us after trying several others—frees us from a new embarrassment. The Gauls are not like the Greeks and Romans. The first glance

Even regarding the Divinities whose classification the Gauls agreed upon with the Greeks and Romans, the former gave them a rank very different from that which they held among the latter. In treating the Religion of the Gauls, one could not avoid arranging their Divinities according to the order of the Gauls themselves, on pain of violating the order of <term>Celtic Theology|the religious systems and beliefs of the ancient Celtic peoples, specifically the Gauls</term>. However, in following this order, one could not fail to shock those who, solely prejudiced in favor of the Greeks and Romans, believe that the taste of these peoples should serve as a rule for all Nations. They do not realize that the Greeks and Romans, whom they boast of so much and give to us as models, were the first not only to alter but even to overturn, so to speak, the Religion of the earliest times, turning its simplicity into chaos and confusion.

### ON THE GAULS. Book III.

[The task] of announcing it was reserved for the enlightenment and good taste of a person who knows the value of Antiquities.

<margin>
Supplement, volume 2, page 224.

The Monument in question consists of a Column, which the Author of *Antiquity* <note>The author is likely Bernard de Montfaucon, referring to his multi-volume work *L’antiquité expliquée et représentée en figures*.</note> divides into four almost equal parts; the bottom part, which serves as a sub-basement, has eight faces, of which four smaller ones are in a curved line, and four larger ones form an arc that recedes into the structure. The second part, which can be viewed as the pedestal of the Column, is a perfect octagon. Each face of this octagon is decorated with a Figure, which is often no longer recognizable. Above this sort of pedestal rises a round Column, the lower half of which is adorned with wide bands that, by crossing each other, form lozenges <term>lozenges: diamond-shaped decorative patterns</term> each filled with a floret; the upper half of the Column, which makes up the fourth part of the total, is entirely covered in scales. The manner in which the Column ends leads one to judge that something is missing, which time has caused to fall and which has been lost. There is indeed a stone decorated with sculptures in the Cemetery of Cussy <note>Cussy-la-Colonne in Burgundy, France, famous for its Roman column.</note>, which is said to have served as the capital <term>capital: the crowning member of a column</term> for the Column; but this is merely a local tradition, says Mr. de Mautour <note>Philibert-Bernard de Mautour (1654–1737), a noted French antiquarian.</note>, which is without foundation, because the style in which this stone is worked has no relation to the rest of the work.

<margin>
See what I have said regarding the Mercuries of Framont, book 2, page 339.
</margin>
One may notice in passing that the Gauls, when erecting Columns, observed several different orders at once, and made them from several pieces that could each have formed a whole on their own. It is true that by grafting them one upon another, they nonetheless composed a single whole through proportions and reciprocal relationship, which smoothed over the entire contrast.

It is surprising that this Monument has been preserved intact for so many centuries and that it has been able to resist the damage of the weather in this way, without suffering any other damage than that of the capital <term>capital: the decorative top part of a column</term> or some other similar ornament that rested upon the upper part of its shaft. Thus, all lovers of Antiquity owe a great debt to those who have owned the meadow where it stands until now, for not having destroyed it, whether to make use of the materials or to clear the land it occupied.

## CHAPTER III.

### *Explanation of the first three Figures of the Column.*
### *Minerva, Juno & Jupiter.*

The Figures in the niches of the perfect octagon are mostly without symbols <note>In classical art, "symbols" or "attributes" refer to identifying objects, like Jupiter's thunderbolt or Minerva's owl.</note> and are consequently very difficult to recognize. They are all in very good taste; their appearance draws partly on the Roman style and partly on the Gallic. This mixture, which is infinitely pleasing to the eyes of all connoisseurs, is an enigma that one can hardly solve.

The first Figure is a Minerva in the Gallic style: the helmet she wears is adorned with a plume <term>plume: originally "aigrette," a tuft of feathers or ornaments on a helmet</term>; she is leaning against a tree trunk, dressed in a sleeveless tunic, and wears over it a large peplum <term>peplum: a traditional long, draped garment worn by women in ancient Greece and Rome</term>, with which she covers her body. Ganymede, whom Jupiter had carried off by an Eagle to make him his <term>Cupbearer: a high-ranking official who serves drinks to a monarch or deity</term> <note>original: "Echanſon"</note>; he is often found engraved on ancient artifacts, performing this duty for the Eagle of Jupiter himself. But the figure here is a true Woman, as the curls of her hair, her breast, and her clothing make it impossible to mistake her. We must therefore search the Mythology of the Ancients for a Woman whose life circumstances might relate to this relief: now, according to some Antiquarians, there is no one whom this fits better than Hebe, Goddess of Youth. Although I do not share their sentiment, here is the argument used to clarify and support that view.

Hebe was the daughter of Jupiter and Juno according to some, and according to others the daughter of Juno alone; she was conceived in a most singular manner. Juno was sterile and passionately desired to have children: she consulted Apollo, the God of Medicine, hoping he might have some secret to end her sterility. Apollo invited her to a feast where he served wild lettuce; Juno had barely tasted it when she felt herself pregnant. When she reached her term, she gave birth to a very beautiful daughter. Jupiter was so pleased with her that he named her Goddess of Youth and chose her to pour the <term>Ambrosia: the food or drink of the Greek gods, often depicted as conferring longevity or immortality</term> <note>original: "ambroiſie"</note> at his table. However, during a fall she took while performing her duties, the disarray of her clothes caused the assembly of the Gods to laugh; Jupiter consequently stripped her of her office and gave it to Ganymede. Later, Hebe married Hercules when he was admitted to heaven and counted among the Gods.

Jupiter, perhaps *Hebe*, Goddess of Youth: the helmet with which she is crowned does not absolutely weaken this opinion; the hairstyles of the Gods and Goddesses of Antiquity were subject to as many variations as the whims of the craftsmen or the tastes of those who commissioned them. It is the same with the symbols of the Gods and their manner of representation: one finds *Pallas* <note>The Roman name for Athena, Goddess of Wisdom and War.</note> with *Cupids*, and *Venus* armed with pikes, etc. All of these things create contrasts for which it is impossible to give any reason other than the one I have mentioned.

This Figure, if it were truly an *Hebe*, would confirm what I have already said: that the *Gauls*, upon receiving the *Gods* of the *Romans*, exercised some reservation. They only admitted them into their *Fasti* <term>Fasti: the records or official calendars of religious festivals and legal days in Ancient Rome</term> by representing them somewhat differently from their conquerors. But what is more singular is that they clung to ancient dogmas rather than those that were current at the time they blended their own *Fables* <note>The author uses "fables" here to mean mythology or sacred stories.</note> with those of the *Romans*. Thus, when the *Romans* subjugated the *Gauls*, the mythological history of *Hebe* honored with the dignity of *Cupbearer* to *Jupiter* had fallen into disuse; *Ganymede* had long since been substituted in her place and had erased her memory. One does not even find any *Monument* where *Hebe* is represented pouring ambrosia into the cup of *Jupiter*: a strong indicator that perhaps no people ever thought to preserve that memory. Notwithstanding this, in the view I am presenting, the *Gauls* set aside *Ganymede*, his abduction, and his employment, and instead revived *Hebe*, giving her pla- <meta>catchword: pla-</meta>

<margin>Callimachus, Hymn to Jove, verse 47. Apollonius of Rhodes.</margin>
...I have taken regarding this Figure; the first concerns the proximity of Jupiter and the young Jupiter. Now, it is established that Adraste <note>Adrasteia, a nymph in Greek mythology who, along with her sister Ida, was charged by Rhea with protecting and nursing the infant Zeus (Jupiter) to hide him from his father, Cronus.</note> had been charged with raising Jupiter from his most tender infancy, when he was still in swaddling clothes; and at that time, she carried him everywhere in a golden cradle. (a) Fable even asserts that Adraste had given Jupiter a small globe to roll about, to serve as a toy. (b) These circumstances easily explain the youthfulness with which Jupiter is represented here.

<margin>Caesar, Gallic Wars, Book 1, near the end.</margin>
The other reason is taken from the very essence of the Religion of the Gauls, and constitutes one of its principal characteristics. We are dealing here with a famous sacrifice, where a man must serve as the victim. This man was undoubtedly an illustrious Captive, as the bas-reliefs <note>Low-relief sculptures where the figures lead slightly out from the background.</note> bear witness. The respect shown for the birth of persons of the highest rank did not exempt them from such a rigorous punishment; it only delayed it; and they did not proceed to the execution until the auguries <term>augury: a ritual of divination where the behavior of birds or other natural signs was interpreted as the will of the gods</term> had spoken. All of this is drawn from Caesar, who says that Procillus <note>Caius Valerius Procillus, a Gallic nobleman and trusted friend of Julius Caesar, who was captured by the Germanic leader Ariovistus.</note>, having been captured by the Germans, only escaped death because the Lots, which had been consulted up to three times, had been favorable to him: though even this had not yet put him out of danger. This being established, it appears here that Adraste shows through the Auguries that it is necessary to immolate the victim, about whom they had been consulted. This explanation does not negate the first, because the Ancients themselves taught us that the representation of their mysteries was capable of multiple meanings.

### CHAPTER V.

->*True portrait of Pluto & his symbols. The Gauls made but one and the same Divinity of Pluto and of Teutates or Mercury.*<-

A naked young man occupies the fifth rank: he wears upon his head a skin that one might take for the hide of a Lion, which descends from both sides and crosses over his chest: he leans his whole body to one side upon his staff; he crosses his legs, and is in the posture of a man either fatigued, or awaiting the outcome of some great event; at his feet is a dog looking up at him.

Seeing this Figure all alone, and independently of another which we shall soon describe, one would take this young man for Hercules: the skin with which he is headdressed in the manner of Hercules would authorize this explanation; but it cannot hold here: a true Hercules <note>Hercules was a Greco-Roman hero-god known for his strength and his signature lion-skin cloak; the author argues that because a more traditional Hercules appears later in the series, this figure must be someone else.</note> who follows later destroys this idea, and does not permit us to believe that in all these niches <note>recessed architectural spaces used to display statues</note> there is a repetition of characters. Moreover, the Lion’s hide, even assuming it to be one, is in itself ambiguous; since other Gods besides Hercules have it as an ornament or symbol. Furthermore, this skin is by no means that of a Lion: it is neither wide enough nor long enough to be such; its small volume betrays it.

I have seen no one until now who has undertaken to offer a judgment on this Figure: I myself would not dare to put forward anything, had chance not fortunately led me

A custom that the Ordinances of our Kings ordinarily waive with this clause: *notwithstanding the cry of Haro* <note>The *Clameur de Haro* is an ancient legal protest used in Normandy and the Channel Islands; the speaker calls for immediate justice against a grievance.</note>. The Anonymous author will permit us to assert, *notwithstanding the cry of Haro*, that *Ar* never signified God in the language of the Celts: it is *Di* which signified God, as *Divona* bears witness; for this word, according to the testimony of Ausonius <note>Decimus Magnus Ausonius (c. 310–395 AD), a Roman poet from Bordeaux.</note>, meant *Divine Fountain* <note>original: "Fontaine Divine"</note>. *Arus* appears rather to have the meaning of the *Ars* or *Hars* of the Armoricans <note>People of Armorica, modern-day Brittany.</note> of today, which signifies a boundary in the literal sense, and in the figurative sense an obstacle, *everything that holds back, prevents, or stops; Maen Hars or ars, a stone that serves as a boundary.*

According to this etymology, this reverse of a Medal represents the belief of the Segusii <note>A Gaulish tribe located in the region of modern-day Forez, near Lyon.</note> concerning the columns of Hercules; the Celts believed in general that these Columns were in the Gauls, and the Segusii took pride in having them in their country, as if Hercules had stopped there, and had there put an end to his labors.

<margin>Tacitus, *On the Manners of the Germans*, ch. 3.</margin>
Whatever may be the case regarding these popular rumors, it is nonetheless certain that the cult of Hercules was very much in vogue in the Gauls before the arrival of Caesar. This truth is confirmed by that quantity of Cities, Ports, and Villages which were built or consecrated to Hercules, and which incorporated the name of this God into their own. Pillars of Hercules <note>original: "Herculis Columnæ"</note>; ( a ) Stony Fields or Hercules’ Field <note>original: "Campi Lapidei seu Herculeus Campus"</note> ( b ); Port of Hercules <note>original: "Portus Herculis"</note>; ( c ) and several others ( d ) which ancient Historians and Geographers mention.

We certainly possess several Monuments to Hercules, both in Inscriptions and in bas-reliefs <note>Low-relief sculptures carved into stone.</note>, dating from the reduction of the Gauls under the Roman yoke: but most of them say nothing that is not based on the general idea that all nations held of this God. Thus, we shall be very careful to speak here only of the most singular ones; not wishing to unnecessarily swell this Work, nor to go against the plan we have proposed for ourselves: to speak only of what is purely of Gaulish invention.

Nor do we intend to recall here Ogmius <note>A Gaulish deity associated with eloquence and strength, famously described by Lucian as an elderly Hercules leading men by chains attached from his tongue to their ears.</note>, or the alleged Gaulish Hercules of Lucian, on whose word all Writers in general and in particular have been somewhat misled <note>original: "pris un peu le change"</note>.

### CHAPTER VIII.

*Hercules Magusanus <note>A regional deity of the Batavi (a Germanic tribe in the Rhine delta), often identified with the Roman Hercules.</note>. Relief of Hercules surnamed Magusanus. Inscription in honor of this God, & of another Gaulish Divinity. <margin>Keysler p. 200. <note>Johann Georg Keysler (1689–1743), a German scholar famous for his work on Northern European antiquities.</note></margin>
The most remarkable Hercules that I know of from Antiquity is the one found in 1514 on the seashore at Westcapelle, a town in Zeeland, on the Island of Walcheren. Its appearance is entirely barbaric <note>In this context, "barbaric" refers to a non-Classical, local style that appeared crude to 18th-century scholars accustomed to Greco-Roman aesthetics.</note>, at least regarding the symbols that accompany it. The drapery, which covers only the back of his body, forms a kind of veil over his head that descends all the way to the ground; having been brought from the left shoulder over the arm, it covers him and creates many folds. Hercules holds a dolphin in his right hand, and in his left a large forked staff: at his right side is a square altar, fairly well <gloss>well-made</gloss> wrought, from which rise flames that have the full shape of artichoke leaves; at his left is represented an unknown fish which resembles a squilla <note>A type of marine crustacean, such as a mantis shrimp.</note>. Along with this Monument was found this Inscription.

<margin>Ibid. p. 201. <note>original: "Ibidem," meaning "In the same place"</note></margin>
The meaning of the Inscription is that M. Primius or Primillus, as it is believed it should be read, has willingly fulfilled the vow he made to Hercules Macusanus. There are several Medals <note><term>Medals</term> refers here to ancient coins or commemorative tokens</note> of Postumus <note>Marcus Cassianius Latinius Postumus, ruler of the breakaway Gallic Empire in the 3rd century AD</note>, which have for a legend *To Hercules Macusanus*; others read *Magusanus*; but it is noted in the Monuments of Antiquity that C and G are used interchangeably, especially before vowels, where the difference in the pronunciation of these consonants was almost imperceptible. These Medals are not, however, as interesting to us as a marble provided by Mr. Keysler with its Inscription. It is at the entrance of the beautiful Library of the Reverend Jesuit Fathers of Brussels.

In Mr. Keysler's work the Inscription is so jumbled and inaccurate that, being unable to understand anything, I was obliged to have recourse to the original. The Reverend Father du Solier, a Jesuit, did me the favor of sending an exact copy on paper the same size as the field of the stone containing the Inscription; by this I saw that the stone is eighteen inches high by fourteen wide, besides the pediment and the base. In Mr. Keysler's version almost all the letters are leaning and thin; on the contrary, on the marble they are quite straight, well-formed, and truly Roman.

There are several Medals <note>In 18th-century scholarship, "medals" (médailles) usually referred to ancient coins.</note> of Postumus <note>The emperor of the "Gallic Empire" from 260–269 AD.</note> which bear the legend *To Hercules Macusanus*; others read *Magusanus*; but it is noted in the Monuments of Antiquity that 'C' and 'G' are used indifferently, especially before vowels, where the difference in the pronunciation of these consonants was almost imperceptible. <margin>The same, p. 201.</margin> However, these Medals are not as interesting to us as a marble stone provided by Mr. Keysler <note>Johann Georg Keysler (1693–1743), a German scholar and traveler known for his antiquarian writings.</note> with its Inscription. It is located at the entrance of the beautiful Library of the Reverend Jesuit Fathers of Brussels.

In Mr. Keysler’s work, the Inscription is so scrambled and unfaithful that, being unable to understand anything of it, I was obliged to have recourse to the original. The Reverend Father du Solier, a Jesuit, did me the favor of sending me an exact copy on a paper of the same size as the field of the stone containing the Inscription; by this I saw that the stone is eighteen inches high by fourteen wide, besides the pediment and the base. In Mr. Keysler’s rendering, almost all the letters are slanted and starved <note>The term "affamées" (starved) here describes letters that are thin, weak, or poorly formed in the engraving.</note>: on the contrary, on the marble they are quite straight, well-formed, and truly Roman.

It is precisely this weapon or fork that our *Hercules Macusan* holds. Thus this term, far from being a topical name <note>A name derived from a specific place or "topos"</note>, serves rather to characterize and depict the Divinity who carries it.

These truths might well lead us to something more real and more solid than Fable: if I am permitted to set out my conjectures here, I will have no difficulty in admitting that this forked weapon, and the fish that accompany this Barbarian God, give rise to the thought that *Hercules Macusan* owes his birth to some native of the country, a Lord of the region, who reigned at *Duiz* <note>Modern Deutz, across the Rhine from Cologne</note>, and who had made himself so famous—either by defending the banks of the *Rhine*, or by making raids on this side and that of this River, and by making himself master of its course—that after his death his subjects or compatriots, to preserve his memory, had placed him among the number of the Gods. This fits perfectly with *Postumus* <note>Marcus Cassianius Latinius Postumus, leader of the breakaway Gallic Empire in the 3rd century AD</note>, who was fond of having *Hercules Macusan* engraved on the reverse of his Medals <note>In this period, "medals" usually refers to ancient coins</note>.

For this Prince was *Gallic* by birth, and adored by all the *Gauls*; he always had weapons in his hand, as much to defend the *Gaulish lands* from the incursions of the Barbarians, as to resist the Emperor *Gallienus*, who wanted to make him relinquish the *Purple* <note>The "Purple" signifies the imperial rank and power, referring to the dye used for an emperor's robes</note>, which he had [assumed]...

The Hercules of Strasbourg differs from Roman versions of Hercules only by a certain indefinable quality <note>original: "je ne fai quoi"</note> that is truly Gallic, which one cannot fail to recognize, and which is felt in his expression, his face, his posture, his club full of large knots, and in the way the lion’s skin wraps around his arm. The original is a bronze statue that remained in a chapel of the Strasbourg Cathedral dedicated to Saint Michael until 1525, when it fell into the hands of a private citizen of the city. He sold it for a sum of money to a French Lord. This Lord had it carried to Paris, from where it was transferred to Issy, into a garden belonging to Mr. Vanhoelen, the Treasurer of France.

I will finish what concerns Hercules Magusan <note>A deity worshipped by the Batavi and other Germanic-Gallic tribes, often merged with the Roman Hercules but retaining local attributes</note> by saying that it appears this God was invoked for all kinds of sea voyages. His forked staff, serving as a trident, the dolphin he holds in his right hand, another sea fish at his feet, and finally his association with Nehalennia <note>A Gallo-Roman goddess of fertility and seafaring, often depicted with a dog or a basket of fruit</note> make this point evident.

# RELIGION

Inscriptions dedicated to *Hercules Saxanus* are more frequent in *Gaul* than in *Italy*. 3°. It is found that all these inscriptions were made by people who followed the profession of arms <note>That is, soldiers or officers of the Roman legions.</note>: and thus the cult in question likely owes its birth to some exploit of war.

I am well aware that one might respond that the Romans always had their soldiers camp during times of peace, and that they employed them in public works: and thus the Italian inscription may have been made by soldiers who worked for the service and by order of the Republic at the Rocks of Tivoli <note>Tivoli, ancient Tibur, was famous for its travertine quarries used to build Rome's monuments.</note>. But one may oppose this with the same foundation using the Quarries of Norroy <note>Located in Lorraine, France, these were major Roman limestone quarries used for military and civil construction.</note>, which, in a similar scenario, should not yield to the Rocks of Tivoli. Nothing, therefore, prevents us from believing that the cult of *Hercules Saxanus* is truly Gallic in origin: and here is what it can be attributed to.

It was a constant opinion among the Greeks and the Romans that the rain of stones that Jupiter caused to fall so opportunely in favor of Hercules—at the time when this Hero, for lack of weapons, ran the risk of being captured or killed by his enemies—occurred in the *Gauls* <note>The author refers to the myth of Hercules at the Plain of Crau (near Arles), where Jupiter/Zeus sent a rain of stones to help him defeat the Ligurians.</note>. Such miraculous help got Hercules out of trouble and enabled him to achieve a complete victory. This Fable was engraved in the minds of all soldiers. Their profession was exposed to the same dangers: an unforeseen attack, an ambush into which they fell, a mountain pass where they were overwhelmed, false marches, and other sudden and unexpected cases where their loss was certain, brought back to their memory the stones that had saved Hercules, and led them to address themselves to

Hercules, when invoked in these dire straits, was called *Saxanus* <note>The name *Saxanus* is derived from the Latin *saxum*, meaning rock or stone, linking the god to the rocky terrain or the "rain of stones" myth mentioned previously.</note>; and people were grateful to him for their salvation, from wherever it might come.

These reflections reveal roughly the motives held by the authors of the inscriptions addressed to the God *Saxanus*. In particular, I would believe that the first was made on the occasion of some great peril in which Publius Talpidius Clemens found himself in some corner of *Germania* <note>The Roman name for the regions east of the Rhine, often a site of intense military conflict.</note>. The mace <term>mace: a heavy, blunt-headed club used as a weapon</term> which is on one of the faces of the altar was certainly for the use of the Germans. Its design is singular; the handle is entirely wrapped with cords or bands, which served to provide a grip and prevented it from slipping: it was short but heavy. This one in particular may be considered an offering or a consecration, in gratitude for the good fortune of having avoided falling into the hands of the Germans, and perhaps for having triumphed over them.

### CHAPTER X.

*The last Figure represents a human victim: to which Gods the Gauls offered these kinds of victims. Why they were bound. The failure of those who attempted to represent the sacrifices of the Gauls from their own imagination. Until what time the Gauls offered human victims.*

The eighth Figure concludes this long sequence of Gods and Goddesses, which we have just deciphered as best we could. It is the saddest of all the spectacles that antiquity can mention, and that it has passed down to us. A man in the twilight of his life, dressed in a kind of sleeveless tunic that only reaches his knees, standing upright, hands tied in front, his head bowed as if deploring his misfortune, turning to the side as much as he can to hide from himself the horror of his execution, his left foot resting on a tree trunk—apparently an oak <note>The oak was sacred to the Druids; their name itself is thought to be derived from the Greek word for oak, *drus*.</note>—waits in this posture for a Druid <term>Druid: a high-ranking member of the priestly and learned class in ancient Celtic societies</term> or a Druidess to come from behind to strike him with a fatal blow, in order to make their observations on the way he falls dead, how the blood spurts, and the nature of the wound he received.

I do not see in all of Antiquity a monument rarer than this one, nor one that instructs us better on the Religion of the Gauls. We previously knew only three Gods: *Taranis* <note>original: "Taranis"; the Gallic god of thunder, often associated with the Roman Jupiter.</note>, *Esus* <note>original: "Esus"; a deity often depicted as a woodcutter, associated with strength and sometimes war.</note>, and *Teutates* <note>original: "Teutates"; a protector of the tribe, often identified by Romans as Mercury or Mars.</note>, of whom

...the Gauls purchased divine favor with the blood of human victims: here are five others revealed to us all at once by this Monument—Minerva, Juno, Andate <note>Andate, also known as Andraste, was a goddess of victory worshipped in Roman-era Britain and Gaul.</note> or Victory, Venus Infera <note>The "Lower Venus," likely a reference to a goddess associated with the underworld or the earth.</note>, and Hercules. If they believed that all the deities they recognized shared in this nature equally, then it is beyond doubt that they honored it equally in each of them. The Druids <term>Druid: a high-ranking member of the priestly and learned class in ancient Celtic societies</term> were consistent; their dogmas were self-supporting, and nothing has yet come to light that destroys or even weakens this view. However, as new discoveries daily provide fresh insights, we await stronger evidence before presenting as certain truth what we currently only venture to propose as an opinion.

Isaac, who should be considered the true model for this practice, was bound by his father. (a) Ovid, Virgil, Servius, and others provide countless similar authorities. Indeed, I found a great many medals written from right to left, among which the six I present here are very remarkable.

However, I was taking steps to examine for myself the Inscription of the Cathedral of Paris <note>This refers to the Pillar of the Boatmen, a monumental Roman-Gallic column dedicated to Jupiter by the guild of sailors in the 1st century AD, discovered under the choir of Notre-Dame in 1710</note>, as well as the reliefs accompanying it, both to consult them and to ensure the accuracy of the engravings that had been made of them. But what was my surprise when, at first glance, I saw that the two letters—which were claimed to be engraved from right to left [an assertion promoted as a discovery that had escaped the most famous Antiquarians <term>Antiquarian: a scholar or collector of ancient artifacts and records, the predecessor to the modern archaeologist</term>]—were written in the usual way, from left to right. This experience opened my eyes and made me more cautious. At first, I even felt some annoyance at having fallen into the trap, and at being unable to provide as proof of the ancient manner of writing of the...

It was then that the name *Diaule* <note>original: *Diaule*; from the Greek *diaulos*, meaning a double pipe or a double-course race</note> was transferred to the second type of race, which was part of the Olympic Games; because the athletes imitated in the stadium those returns, or backwards movements, that were made when playing the pastoral flute. These reflections show with how much reason Pausanias <note>A 2nd-century AD Greek traveler and geographer</note> compares the manner of writing of the ancient Greeks and Gauls to the race called *Diaule*, since the same order was observed throughout. The legends of the six Coins that I am going to present are engraved <term>boustrophedon <note>original: βουστροφηδὸν; literally "as the ox turns," referring to writing lines alternately from left-to-right and right-to-left, like a plow in a field</note></term>; one sees there the justification and the completion of the proofs I have given in so many places of two truths, which I established from the beginning of this Work; namely, that the language the Gauls spoke, and the characters they used, were Greek from the most ancient times. I have placed these two truths in a level of clarity that strikes the minds of those who are not prejudiced. These Coins still bear witness that the manner of writing <term>boustrophedon</term> was common to the Gauls, not only in the most remote times, but also in later centuries; unlike the Greeks, who had ceased writing in this way so long ago that the one and only Monument of that Nation that survives written <term>boustrophedon</term> precedes the time of Simonides <note>Simonides of Ceos, a Greek poet credited with refining the Greek alphabet around the 5th century BC</note>. (a) <note>original Latin: *Omnia sanantem appellantes suo vocabulo.*</note> "Calling it 'the all-healer' in their own tongue."
Many people believe that these Latin words from Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, author of *Natural History*.</note> should be understood as referring to the sixth day of the Moon; I share their opinion. In fact, the word for mistletoe (*viscum*) cannot grammatically agree with the word for healing (*sanantem*). Notwithstanding this, one finds Authors who apply this passage to the Mistletoe. As I do not wish to quarrel with anyone, and since the matter is indifferent in itself, I believed I could take these terms in the sense of the latter here.

(b) <note>original Latin: *Quale solet sylvis brumali frigore viscum / Fronde virere nova, quod non sua seminat arbos, / Et croceo fœtu teretes circumdare ramos. / Talis erat species auri frondentis opaca / Ilice, &c.*</note>
"Just as in the woods during the winter cold, the mistletoe is accustomed to bloom with new leaves—which the tree itself did not sow—and to encircle the smooth branches with its yellow fruit: such was the appearance of the gold leafing on the dark oak, etc."

The Inscription naturally leads one to believe that the Druids had used this plant to honor the dedication of the Altar that the Parisian Boatmen <term>Nautes Parisiens; a guild of merchant sailors in Roman Lutetia (Paris) who commissioned the famous Pillar of the Boatmen</term> consecrated to Jupiter; and that the sculpture represented some mysterious ceremony of which time has denied us the knowledge. Now Esus, as the source of all the wonders that Mistletoe performed, and the only God the Druids had formerly recognized, was the immediate object of the worship they gave to this plant.

Whatever the case may be, it is noted that our Druids form a group arranged in a different direction from those on the other two faces. The Parisian Boatmen seem to turn to the left, whereas the Druids turn to the right. One can see what I said about these different ceremonies in the last two chapters of the first Book. It is difficult to determine the number of Druids who composed this group. It is certain there were more than three, but that is all one can say. Mr. Baudelot <note>Nicolas Baudelot de Dairval (1648–1722), a French antiquarian and scholar of ancient medals and inscriptions.</note> believed he saw six there; it may indeed be that the craftsman engraved six; this number was sacred in the Religion of the Gauls; and the portals of some Temples I have mentioned provide examples where Druids were sometimes represented by six: but that concludes nothing for this case. And one will always be entitled to ask Mr. Baudelot to produce some other person besides himself who has seen six Druids on the face of the stone where he believed he saw them.

## CHAPTER XVII.

->*General idea of the second stone. Selected features providing full knowledge of the God Esus.*<-

The second stone represents four Gods, some of whom are as well-known and common as others are rare and little-known. Vulcan and Jupiter are the first: the last two are Esus and the <term>Bull with Three Cranes; known in Latin as Tarvos Trigaranus, a mysterious Gaulish deity often depicted with three birds perched on its back</term>. Each of these Gods occupies an entire face of the Stone, and this Stone is the only one for which both halves could be found <note>The Pillar of the Boatmen was discovered in 1710 under the choir of Notre-Dame de Paris, broken into several blocks; the author notes that the fragments for this specific block were successfully reunited.</note>. It would be either to distrust the Reader or to succumb to the temptation of indulging in useless remarks to pause here on Vulcan and Jupiter; since, besides the fact that I speak elsewhere of these two Divinities, the Monuments do not represent them any differently than the Romans represented them, and there is no one who could be ignorant of what the Romans thought of these Gods. I could also dispense with speaking of Esus, since I have already utilized everything that the most laborious criticism could provide me in terms of records to make this Divinity known. But the universal ignorance and oblivion in which Esus has been buried until now lead me to believe that it will not be out of place to provide here a summary of what I have said elsewhere at greater length, while adding whatever new information comes to me on such an interesting subject.

Esus was not initially the name of a specific God; it was an indefinite term that meant *God*.

Suetonius and Hesychius <note>original: "Suetone & Hesychius"; Suetonius was a Roman historian and Hesychius of Alexandria was a Greek grammarian.</note> tell us that he <note>Referring to the god Esus.</note> was Etruscan in origin: but the possession the Gauls have always held in using his name proves that he was no less Gaulish than Etruscan—that is to say, that it was a truly Greek term, as it would be easy to prove against the authors I have just cited. By this word, our ancestors understood a Being above the senses, who could neither be enclosed within the walls of Temples, nor represented under any tangible figure. By digging deeper into this thought and tracing back to the origin of things, one arrives at the system of the unity of a single God, which we find to have been the first belief of the Gauls, and of which traces were preserved among them long after Jesus Christ. I have shown through strong arguments that Esus was the unknown God of the Athenians, the nameless God of the Samaritans, and the ineffable God of the Jews. Better known to the Druids than to the common Gaulish people, it was to him that these **Philosophers** <term>Philosophers: early modern historians often referred to the Druids as philosophers to emphasize their roles as the learned intellectual and scientific class of Celtic society.</term> referred all the sacrifices they offered; and what is remarkable is that to contemplate him with less distraction and to study him with more profit, they attached his memory to the presence of **Oaks**, and often made it an essential point of **Religion** to spend their entire lives in forests entirely planted with these trees. The veneration they had for **Mistletoe**, which sometimes grows on the **Oak**, could not have been greater: thus they brought extraordinary care and ceremonies to gathering it. On our **Monument** <note>The Pillar of the Boatmen, discovered in 1710.</note>, Esus gathers or cuts it himself: this is to signify that the Druid who gathered it was to be regarded only as the instrument whom Esus used for

The origin of the oath they swore upon this Bull was a custom introduced since Antiquity: placing one's hands upon a sacrificed Bull and calling the Gods to witness the commitments being made. This is clearly expressed in Aeschylus: seven Princes, he says, encamped before Thebes, after having sacrificed a Bull upon a shield, held their hands over the victim and called upon Mars, Bellona, and Fear <note>In Greek mythology, Phobos (Fear) was often personified alongside the gods of war.</note> to swear they would overthrow Thebes from top to bottom; or if they could not achieve this, to put its entire territory to fire and blood. ($a$) Mr. Boileau <note>Nicolas Boileau-Despréaux (1636–1711), a famous French poet and critic.</note>, in his translation of *Longinus* <note>Referring to Boileau's 1674 translation of the Greek treatise *On the Sublime*.</note>, translated this passage and gave it much more force in our language than it possesses in the original:

### OF THE GAULS. BOOK III.

For the Cranes, he substituted two Crows. Now, to justify why the two Crows of Artemidorus <note>Artemidorus of Ephesus (c. 100 BCE) was a Greek geographer; his descriptions of Gaul were often cited by later writers like Strabo.</note> are likely the three Cranes from the Monument of the Cathedral of Paris <note>This refers to the Pillar of the Boatmen, a Roman-Gallic monument discovered beneath the choir of Notre-Dame de Paris in 1710, which depicts a bull with three cranes perched on its back, labeled "TARVOS TRIGARANVS."</note>, one need only look at the location where the Cranes are placed: it is a lake and a marsh from which reeds, brushwood, and trees arise, in the middle of which the Bull is entangled, equipped with three Cranes. There, the Bull bears the name "Three-Cranes," which is exactly the name of the lake where all the wonders of Artemidorus’ tale occurred—though according to him, it was named "Two-Crows."

Add to this that *Lake of the Two-Crows* and *Bull with Three Cranes* are compound phrases made of the names of certain birds that a poorly informed foreign historian might easily have confused, substituting one for the other.

Furthermore, one senses a certain analogy between the Gauls' use of the *Bull with Three Cranes* according to Plutarch <note>Plutarch (c. 46 – 119 CE) was a prolific Greek biographer and essayist.</note>, and their use of the *Lake of the Two-Crows* as reported by Artemidorus. Both were intended to resolve disputes that arose. I even suspect, from Artemidorus' account, that the litigants of whom he speaks began their legal proceedings with an oath, and only resorted to the ordeal <term>ordeal: a divine trial or judicial test used to determine the truth in a legal dispute</term> of the Crows—or rather, the Cranes—when the path of the oath had yielded no result.

I would not deny that the title or epithet of the Bull worshipped in the lake might have passed to the lake itself; history provides a thousand such examples. However, it is probable that the Bull alone first bore this name and eventually shared it with the lake, which served as the stage where the credulity and simplicity of the Gauls were exploited.

K ij
*

He has substituted two Crows for the Cranes. Now, to justify that the two Crows of Artemidorus <note>Artemidorus of Ephesus (c. 100 BCE) was a Greek geographer whose descriptions of Gaul were preserved by later writers like Strabo.</note> are likely the three Cranes from the Monument of the Cathedral of Paris, one only has to look at the location where the Cranes are placed: it is a lake and a marsh from which reeds, brushwood, and trees rise, in the midst of which is the Bull, entangled and adorned with three Cranes. The Bull there bears the name of **Three-Cranes** <note>original: "Trois-Gruës", which translates the Gaulish epithet "Trigaranus" found on the pillar.</note>, which is precisely the name of the lake where all the wonders of Artemidorus's tale took place—though he claimed it was named **Two-Crows**.

Add to this that *Lake of Two-Crows* and *Bull of Three-Cranes* are terms composed of the names of certain birds that an ill-informed foreign historian must have confused, substituting one for the other.

On the other hand, one senses a certain analogy between the use the Gauls made of the *Bull of Three-Cranes* according to Plutarch <note>Plutarch was a Greek-Roman biographer and philosopher who wrote extensively on ancient customs and symbols.</note>, and the use they made of the *Lake of Two-Crows*, as reported by Artemidorus. Both were intended to settle the disputes that arose. I even suspect, based on Artemidorus's account, that the litigants he mentions began the formalities of their lawsuits with an oath, and only resorted to the trial of the Crows—or rather, the Cranes—when the path of the oath had produced no result.

I would not want to deny that the surname or epithet of the Bull worshipped in the lake might have passed to the lake itself; history provides a thousand examples of this. However, it is probable that the Bull alone first bore this name, and that he eventually communicated it to the lake, which was the theater where the credulity and simplicity of the Gauls were exploited.

<summary>The author argues that the "Two Crows" in Artemidorus's account are a mistaken identification of the "Three Cranes" (Trigaranus) associated with the Gallic Bull-god. He suggests that these birds were part of a ritualized judicial ordeal used by the Gauls to resolve legal disputes when oaths failed.</summary>

This means, according to Monsieur Dacier <note>André Dacier (1651–1722) was a prominent French classical scholar known for his translations of Plutarch and other ancient authors.</note>, that Theseus, who led the dance, expanded and contracted the circle to imitate the twists and turns of the labyrinth; just as when cranes fly in a flock, there is always one leading the others, who follow in a circular formation.

The authors who prompted this digression are convinced that the way the three cranes are arranged on the relief we are explaining corresponds to the "Crane Dance" <note>In Greek, this dance is known as the *Geranos* (Crane), traditionally said to have been performed by Theseus on the island of Delos.</note>. One might also add, if one wishes, that the Bull on the monument represents the Minotaur of the labyrinth.

That the Gauls had their dances just as other peoples did is an indisputable fact; but that they performed the "Crane Dance" is impossible to prove as long as one seeks evidence other than the *Tarvos Trigaranus* <note>original: "Tarvos Trigaranus" is a Gaulish-Latin name meaning "Bull with three cranes." # RELIGION

What distinguishes the Cernunnos of the Cathedral of Paris <note>This refers to the Pillar of the Boatmen, a Roman-era monumental column found under Notre-Dame de Paris in 1710.</note> from others most significantly is that he has large satyr-like ears and devices that appear to be rings passed through his horns. The one belonging to M. de Chezelles also has this remarkable feature: he wears a crown in the shape of a diadem and holds an animal's head in his right hand, which to the eye seems to be that of a young kid <note>A young goat.</note> whose horns have not yet grown.

The name Cernunnos has only been known since the discovery of the stone bearing this figure. Following this discovery, several learned individuals took pride in enriching the public with their reflections and research. As we follow different paths and move entirely away from the opinions of all those who have written on this subject, we shall content ourselves here with simply and ingenuously stating our own; leaving for examination in a specific chapter the views of certain German scholars, who congratulate themselves a bit too much on what they have proposed.

<margin>Boxhorn <note>Marcus Zuerius van Boxhorn (1612–1653), a Dutch scholar and linguist who studied the origins of European languages.</note></margin> Cernunnos is an ancient Celtic word composed of two others from the same language; the first is *Cern*, meaning horn, and the second is *ynn* or *onn*, which signifies a spear. Greek, which I have stated was originally the same language as Celtic, has two similar words, namely *keras* <note>original Greek: κέρας</note> (horn) and *hynis*, *hynnes*, or *hynne* <note>original Greek: ὕνις, ὕννης, or ὕννη</note>, which in Latin is *vomer* <note>plowshare</note> and in English a <term>plowshare</term> <note>original French: "ſoc de charruë"</note>—the sharp iron that serves to open and split the earth during plowing, and which among the ancients took the form of a spearhead, as can be seen in the works of Spon <note>Jacob Spon, a 17th-century pioneer of archaeology.</note> and in *Antiquity Explained* <note>original French: "l'Antiquité expliquée," a landmark multi-volume work by Bernard de Montfaucon.</note>. # OF THE GAULS. Book III.

...the *hynnis* <note>original Greek: ὗννις</note> of the Greeks determines the sense in which one must take the *ynn* or *unn* of the Celts; that is to say, one should understand these words to mean only the iron tip of the spear; or if one wishes to encompass the entire spear, it should only be insofar as its point wounds, splits, and makes an opening wherever it strikes. This serves admirably to make known the nature of the God Cernunnos, and the object of the worship offered to him.

Indeed, although one finds nowhere the specific use the Gauls made of this Divinity, it is presumed with good reason that they invoked him primarily during the exercise of the hunt, which for them was so frequent, so noble, and so perilous; always consisting of hunting down Aurochs <note>original: *Ures*, extinct wild cattle</note>, Elk, Red Deer, Fallow Deer, etc., with which the vast forests of Gaul were filled. One also notes that the horns with which Cernunnos is represented are those of Fallow Deer, Red Deer, and Elk, whose strikes are very dangerous.

<margin>Strabo, Book 4</margin>
To ensure a more successful hunt, the Gauls made use of arrows poisoned with the sap of a fruit resembling a Corinthian capital <note>original Greek: παραπλήσιον κιονοκράνῳ κορινθιουργεῖ — "resembling a Corinthian capital"</note>, (a) which grew on a tree that resembled a fig tree. They also rubbed their darts with hellebore, and a herb they called *Belenion*, of which we have already spoken enough. They derived two considerable advantages from this poison: for besides the fact that no harm ever came back to them from it, they secured their prey and had the pleasure of finding its flesh much more tender and delicate. By this, we see that the Gauls did not limit themselves to the worship of a single female Divinity to preside over their hunts. They distinguished between hunting for pleasure and perilous hunting, which demanded both strength and skill. They honored Diana for the first kind of hunt and reserved Cernunnos for the other, thus maintaining the natural suitability <note>original: "convenances"</note> that exists between the nature of these two types of hunting.

<margin>Tacitus, *On the Customs of the Germans* <note>Known as the *Germania*, written c. 98 AD</note>.</margin>

According to this, the *Alces* or *Alcis* of the Naharvali was the Cernunnos of the Gauls, whom they invoked when hunting wild beasts to be guaranteed protection from their claws, horns, teeth, or tusks. # CHAPTER XXII.

## *Another Horned God of the Gauls.*

THE species of Divinity that I present here has too much in common with Cernunnos for me to be able to resolve to place it elsewhere.

<margin>Gautier, *History of Nîmes*.</margin>
A beautiful head of white marble, which is seen in Nîmes, represents a young man of perfect beauty; his hair is curled like the wool of a fleece; he has a very hairy forehead; finally, on the front of the head, a little above the forehead, there emerges a horn, which is taken for that of a Ram.

This Figure has passed until now for being the head of <term>Jupiter Ammon<note>A syncretic deity combining the Greek king of gods with the Egyptian ram-headed god Amun, typically depicted with two curling ram's horns.</note></term> or Hammon; especially as this God was depicted with ram's horns. This opinion is among those that are current only because no knowledgeable person has taken the trouble to challenge them. Also, if one digs and examines this one even a little, one sees immediately that it cannot be sustained. Jupiter Hammon has always been represented with two horns curled almost horizontally, which grew right against his ears, like a ram's. One sees the opposite here; for besides there being only one horn, which is anything but curled, it is only a little curved—

This is at best only a conjecture; but this conjecture relates to the figures engraved on this stone. To be convinced of this, one must recall what I have said elsewhere: that there was in Gaul a type of *egg* that the Druids had made very popular. They said that it was formed from the saliva or slime of snakes, and from the foam that came out of their bodies when they gathered together in summer; that they intertwined and all formed a ball. When the egg was formed, the snakes raised it into the air and supported it there by the force of their hissing; the Druids, who were attentive to what was happening, watched for the moment it was about to fall, and received it in a <term>sagum <note>A coarse, square woolen cloak worn by the Gauls and Roman soldiers.</note></term> before it touched the ground. This precaution was necessary, less to prevent the egg from breaking than to preserve all the virtues <note>In the language of the time, "virtues" refers to the magical or medicinal powers believed to be contained within the object.</note> it contained. The Druid who had received it immediately took flight, mounted on a very swift horse, to escape the pursuit of the snakes, which never failed to chase after him until they reached a river that blocked their passage.

If I may simply state my opinion, I will frankly admit there is reason to suspect that Pliny only reported the outward appearances with which the Druids shrouded the mystery of the serpent’s egg. Now, as I have said elsewhere, these Philosophers <note>The author refers to the Druids as "Philosophers," a common view among 18th-century scholars who saw them as keepers of ancient wisdom.</note> never explained themselves except through riddles; thus, it is likely that this egg, and the marvelous nature of its production, related to some fundamental doctrine that Pliny had not grasped. If, however, in that author’s time, the entire mystery of the egg in question consisted solely of these outward shows, it must still be presumed that the Druids of that era had changed significantly and had fallen far from the heights of their predecessors. It is true that one cannot say precisely how the later Druids deviated from the earlier ones. Nevertheless, there is reason to believe that the doctrine of the latter was based roughly on that of the Phoenicians and Egyptians, which I will describe in a few words.

From the mouth of Cneph <note>Kneph or Khnum, an Egyptian creator deity often depicted as a ram-headed god or associated with the cosmic egg.</note>, they said, came forth an egg, from which hatched the God Phta <note>Ptah, the craftsman god of Memphis.</note>, who is the Vulcan <note>The Roman god of fire and smithing, equated here with the Greek Hephaestus and Egyptian Ptah.</note> of the Greeks: and this egg was the world, to whose Divinity a Sheep was consecrated in memory of the milk which had served as drink for the first men of the world.

Athenagoras <note>A 2nd-century Christian apologist who wrote to the Roman emperors defending his faith.</note> in his *Apology for the Christian Religion*, reporting the sentiment of Orpheus on creation, says that this poet-philosopher made water the principle of all things; that from water, mud was formed; (a) that from water and mud was born a Dragon which had the head of a Lion; that this animal, between the head and the body, bore engraved the image of the God called Hercules or Chronus <note>Chronos, the personification of Time in pre-Socratic philosophy and later Orphic mysteries.</note>; that this Hercules had fathered an EGG of extraordinary size; (b) that this Egg being quite full, he who had fathered it had split it in two, and had decreed that the upper part should be Heaven, and the lower part Earth. Plutarch enters into the system of Orpheus, adding that the Theology of the Ancients attributed to this Egg the priority of time and the germ of all creatures. (c)

It appears that all these different hypotheses were but one in the beginning, and that their diversity only came from the flaw attached to falsehood, which cannot sustain itself in its principles. But

Could one truly believe that this mythical history of the creation of the world is based on the true history of creation set forth by Moses in Genesis? A single word from this holy Legislator, misunderstood, gave rise to this monstrous collection of extravagances. The Spirit of God, says Moses, was carried over the waters. (a) The Hebrew term <note>The Hebrew verb is *rachaph*.</note> which is translated by *was carried* <note>original: "ferebatur"</note> signifies, according to some, the action of a bird moving its wings, for example, when it wishes to encourage its young to fly. Others maintain that in Syriac it signifies to hatch or brood over eggs, and that Moses used it to indicate that the Holy Spirit gave heat, movement, form, and life to all things.
