This is the foundation of this Egg, the principle of all things according to the Egyptians, according to Orpheus, and apparently according to the Gauls. The idea of incubation, of wings, of flight, etc., gave rise to the imagining of an egg existing prior to any hen or bird whatsoever. (b) What finally succeeds in persuading us that this entire Fable is forged from the truth contained in Scripture is this Mud, this Image of God, which is spoken of in both places; it is also the Egg emerging from the Mouth of Cneph <note>Kneph, an Egyptian creator deity.</note>, which is nothing other than the Universe created by the efficacy of the all-powerful word of God. Finally, Cneph dividing the Egg into two parts, which form one the Earth and the other the Heaven, is an obvious falsification of the doctrine contained in this Verse of Scripture: God said let there be...

...Gauls <note>The text begins mid-sentence, likely continuing from a point discussing the tendency of the ancient inhabitants of Gaul to deviate from common practices.</note>, to almost always deviate from the ordinary paths. By Gods of the first Class, Mythology understands the principal Gods, the superior Gods, or the Gods of the great nations—that is to say, those who were recognized, or believed to be recognized, by all nations. Their number was fixed at twelve, and they composed the supreme Council of Jupiter; this led them to be called the *Consentes* Gods <term>Consentes <note>From the Latin *Dii Consentes*, meaning "the Gods who are together" or "the Agreeing Gods." They were the twelve major deities of the Roman pantheon.</note></term>; here they are, all included in two verses by Ennius <note>Quintus Ennius (c. 239–169 BC) was a Roman poet often considered the father of Roman literature.</note>.

> *Juno, Vesta, Minerva, Ceres, Diana, Venus, Mars;*
> *Mercury, Jupiter, Neptune, Vulcan, Apollo.* <note>original: "Juno, Vesta, Minerva, Ceres, Diana, Venus, Mars; Mercurius, Jovis, Neptunus, Vulcanus, Apollo."</note>

The rest of the Gods were therefore in the second class; they were qualified as Gods of the lesser nations, because they were often honored only by a certain people, or within a single Province or City, or some even smaller location.

In the Religion of the Gauls <note>The Celtic peoples inhabiting the region of Gaul, which covers modern-day France, Belgium, and parts of Germany and Italy.</note>, it is not quite the same thing. By Gods of the first class, one understands those whose worship had been established first, and which served as the foundation of the entire Religion; it is of these Gods only that we have spoken in the preceding Books.

On the contrary, the Gods of the second class were those whom the Gauls had introduced or invented later, modeled after the Divinities of other nations. Their worship had only been introduced secondarily at first; but it had imperceptibly gained the upper hand, to the point of standing on equal footing with that of the Great Gods, and even eclipsing it, or causing it to be forgotten.

After this clarification, one should not be at all surprised to find in the second class of Gaulish Gods—

...having received. In a word, the disorder of the human heart and spirit, clever at blinding itself, never lacked pretexts to color the excesses that reason fought against.

<margin>Book 34, Chapter 17.</margin>
Based on these principles, the skill of the Gauls in working metals and creating curious and useful works where the help of fire was necessary, provided them with a pressing reason to take Vulcan <note>Vulcan was the Roman god of fire, metalworking, and the forge.</note> as one of their Gods—perhaps to credit him with the glory of the invention. For Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, a Roman author and naturalist.</note> remarks that they were the first to find the art of tinning <term>tinning (étamer): the process of coating a metal surface with a thin layer of tin to prevent corrosion or mimic silver</term> copper vessels so neatly that they could hardly be distinguished from silver vessels; and that they had brought the perfection of this art so far as to plate horse harnesses and chariot hitches with silver (a).

<margin>*Images*, Book 1, *The Hunters*.</margin>
It is also of this Gallic art and this invention that Philostratus <note>A Greek scholar of the Roman imperial period.</note> speaks when he says that the Barbarians who lived by the ocean <note>Ancient Mediterranean authors often referred to the Gauls and Britons as "Barbarians of the Ocean."</note> very delicately coated copper, fresh and red from the fire, with gold, silver, and other colors, so that everything became a single solid body—a mixture of excellent enamels.

The Gauls, therefore, recognized the divinity of Vulcan and gave him a place among their other Gods. The monuments that represent him and which have survived to us are rare. The only complete figure we have of him is on one of the four faces of an Altar found in the Church of Notre-Dame...

Then they also began to boil silver onto them in a similar way, especially for horse ornaments and the yokes of draft animals.

The only thing to note before finishing this chapter is that the worship of Vulcan was very ancient in the Gauls; since more than two hundred years before Jesus Christ, the Gauls, having declared war on the Romans to repair the losses they had previously suffered in two different wars, their King Viridomarus made a vow to consecrate all the enemies' weapons to Vulcan. But the success did not match his zeal or his piety. Viridomarus was defeated and killed by the very hand of Consul Marcellus; his army was routed, and the Gallic weapons were carried in triumph to the City of Rome and hung in the Temple of Jupiter Feretrius <note>Jupiter Feretrius was an ancient Roman manifestation of the god to whom "spolia opima" (the armor of an enemy king killed in single combat) were dedicated.</note> (a).

Based on these principles, the skill of the Gauls in working metals and creating curious and useful works where the help of fire was necessary, had been a pressing motive for them to take Vulcan as one of their Gods: perhaps to attribute to him the glory of the invention; for Pliny <note>Gaius Plinius Secundus, a Roman author and naturalist.</note> remarks that they were the first to find the art of tinning <term>tinning: the process of coating a metal surface, like copper, with a thin layer of tin to prevent corrosion or for decoration</term> copper vessels so neatly that one could hardly discern them from silver vessels; and that they had carried the perfection of this art so far as to varnish with silver the harnesses of horses and the hitches of chariots *(a)*.

<margin>Philostratus, *Imagines*, Book 1, "The Hunt."</margin>
It is also of this Gallic art and this invention that Philostratus speaks, when he says that the barbarians who inhabited the ocean delicately coated copper, coming red-hot from the fire, with gold, silver, and other colors, so that the whole formed but a single solid body and a mixture of excellent enamels.

The Gauls, therefore, recognized the divinity of Vulcan and gave him a place among their other Gods. The monuments representing him that have come down to us are rare. The only complete figure we have of him is on one of the four faces of an Altar found in the Church of Notre-Dame

The only thing that must be noted before finishing this chapter is that the worship of Vulcan was very ancient in the Gauls; since more than two hundred years before Jesus Christ, the Gauls having declared war on the Romans to repair the losses they had previously suffered in two different wars, their King Viridomarus made a vow to consecrate all the weapons of the enemy to Vulcan. If we can thus consider *Volianus*, *Belenus*, and *Apollo* as the same Divinity, it is natural to believe that he was one of those who were formerly the object of worship for the Gauls, just like *Jupiter* and *Mercury* whom they worshipped under the names of *Taramis* and *Teutates*.

The *Nannetes* people—neighbors of *Vannes* toward the mouth of the *Loire*, and part of the alliance that formed to oppose *Caesar*, as stated in the third Book of his *Commentaries*—might have recognized *Apollo* or the Sun, under the name of *Belenus* or *Volianus*, as their tutelary Divinity.

There would still be another opinion, which would not lack foundation, to establish that *Volianus* was the same as *Janus* or *Noah* under his name: if one has recourse to the *Hebrew Language*, one will find regarding the etymology of *Volianus* that this name is composed of *ol* or *vol* taken from the verb *Bala* <note>original Hebrew: בָּלָה (*balah*), meaning to wear out or grow old</note>, which means old or to grow old, being joined with the Hebrew name *Jana*, which comes from *jain* <note>original Hebrew: יַיִן (*yayin*), meaning wine; the author connects this to the biblical story of Noah planting a vineyard</note>, that is to say, to plant the vine: one would conclude that the old *Jana* or *Janus* is none other than the Patriarch *Noah*, to whom was given the surname *Janus the Elder* or *Vol Janus*, because of his extreme old age, which surpassed 그hat of the men who remained after the flood.

...allotted Asia, Japheth Europe, and Ham <note>In traditional biblical genealogy, the sons of Noah (Shem, Ham, and Japheth) were believed to be the ancestors of the three "races" of the world as known to early modern Europeans.</note> Africa; one must not interpret this in such a precise manner as to suggest that descendants of Noah’s sons are never found outside the boundaries of their specific allotment. For it is certain that several sons of Japheth and Ham lived in Asia; and it is almost beyond doubt that the first families of Shem, Ham, and Japheth, who were settled there before the construction of the **Tower of Babel**, did not leave that vast country: they only later divided into various colonies, which spread into Africa and Europe as they multiplied. Consequently, the dispersion of nations that occurred after the confusion at Babel was carried out only gradually, and over a long span of time. Nothing, therefore, is more misunderstood than these long sea voyages that some imagine the first men of the world undertook. Even their descendants only advanced into countries that were not yet populated by moving gradually across the land; and they perhaps only thought of, or grew bold enough to board, ships after the whole world was already inhabited.

In Armorica <note>The ancient name for the northwestern region of France, primarily Brittany.</note> [this word] means *pit* or *furnace*; and *Can* signifies sparkling, brilliant, or fire-white; it is the *candens* <note>Latin for "shining" or "glowing."</note> of the Latins. ## CHAPTER V.

*Bacchus. The antiquity of the cult of this God in the Gallic lands. Women who served one of his Temples: their extraordinary customs. Temples of Bacchus in Aquitaine.*

Bacchus <note>The Roman god of wine, ritual madness, and ecstasy, equivalent to the Greek Dionysus.</note> was particularly revered in the Gallic lands; and what we are about to say persuades us that the cult of this God was established there before the Romans had made its conquest.

<margin>Strabo, Book 4, on Gaul. See Casaubon's <note>Isaac Casaubon (1559–1614) was a renowned classical scholar who produced definitive editions of ancient texts.</note> commentary on this passage.</margin>
In a small Island situated at the mouth of the Loire, and which is one of the Samnite islands <note>While the Samnites are famous as an Italian people, Strabo uses this name to refer to a Gallic tribe (likely the Namnetes) living near the Loire estuary.</note> included in Little Brittany <note>A historical name for the region of Brittany (Armorica) in Northwest France.</note>, there was a temple of Bacchus, where the Gallic women alone consecrated themselves to the service of this God. Men never set foot on the Island; so that these women, never being distracted by their sight, were solely occupied with the care of the mysteries with which they were charged; only once every year did they come to see their husbands, in order to have children.

What these women observed most particularly was that they never failed each year to remove and replace themselves, on the same day, and before the sun had set, the roof of the temple they served: and as they worked on it, they celebrated the Orgies <note>In the ancient world, "Orgies" referred to the secret, ecstatic religious rites of Bacchus, not necessarily the modern definition of the word.</note>, and all those violent actions which were proper to the Bacchantes <note>The female followers of Bacchus, famous in mythology for their ritualistic frenzy.</note>; it was rare that one among them did not let her burden fall: then all her companions believed it an act of Religion to tear her into pieces, what[ever...] <note>The text cuts off here, as the sentence continues on the following page.</note>

# OF THE GAULS. BOOK IV.

In the Gauls, he [Bacchus] was almost never represented except as an old man, and with horns. It is regarding this figure—so rare and so extraordinary elsewhere—that it was recently claimed that the Emperor Julian <note>Julian the Apostate (r. 361–363 AD), a Roman Emperor who spent significant time in Gaul and wrote about its culture.</note> had written an epigram; but I have shown that Julian had in view only the quality of the beverage drunk in the Gauls, which was nothing but beer.

To be convinced of this truth, one has only to read the epigram in question without prejudice; here it is:

> Who are you? Where do you come from, Bacchus? By the true Bacchus, I do not know you at all: I know no Bacchus but the son of Jupiter; he exhales a scent of nectar, whereas you smell like a goat. My word, the Celts, for lack of grapes, have made you from I-know-not-what ears of grain. That alone should make you take the name of Demetrius <note>A pun referencing Demeter, the goddess of agriculture and grain.</note>, or that of "Born of Wheat" or "Born of Barley," rather than that of Bacchus or Bromius <note>Bromius is a common epithet for Bacchus; the Emperor Julian is punning on the Greek word *bromos*, meaning oats.</note>.

<margin>See Mr. Huet, *Demonstratio Evangelica*, p. 117.</margin>

This epigram could not have in our language the graces it possesses in the Greek; because all the mystery and all the wit consist of wordplay that presents a double meaning to the mind, which they do not have in English. This statue was called <term>Myobarbe</term> <note>From the Greek *mys* (mouse) and *barba* (beard).</note>; because this God was represented with a long and pointed beard, that is to say, one that ended in a cone like the body of a rat. # CHAPTER VII

### *Different explanations of an ancient Gaulish Medal [Coin].*

### *On Telesphorus.*

<image-desc>A detailed engraving showing both the obverse and reverse of an ancient Gaulish coin. The obverse on the left shows a profile head wearing a helmet, facing right, with a partially visible legend "SECV...". The reverse on the right depicts the standing figure of Hercules leaning on his club, with a smaller figure to his right. The inscription "ARUS" appears vertically between Hercules and his club. The lion's skin is draped over his left arm.</image-desc>

I had already provided the reverse of the Medal <note>In 18th-century archaeology, "medal" often referred to any ancient coin.</note> that I now present here in its entirety. This coin is ancient, and Antiquarians date it to the times before Caesar. The head represents the Province of the Segusiavi <note>The Segusiavi were a Celtic people located in the region of modern-day Forez, near Lyon.</note> in the form of a small bust wearing a helmet, with the legend *Secusia*. On the reverse, one sees Hercules leaning on one side upon his club, and on the other upon a small figure. Between Hercules and this figure, the lion's skin hangs from Hercules's left arm; likewise, between Hercules and his club, one reads the inscription ARUS.

Everyone agrees that the word *Arus* must apply to the small figure. I have already stated that *Arus* appeared to come from the Celtic *ars* or *hars*, which signifies a *boundary* or *obstacle*, and that *Arus* was merely a Latinized version of *ars*. This opinion is supported by the attitude of Hercules, who is visibly resting and seems to have no desire to proceed further. On this account, the land of the Segusiavi must have been considered by our ancestors as the place where Hercules put an end to his labors and his exploits, and where he planted the famous columns <note>Referring to the "Columns of Hercules," usually associated with the Strait of Gibraltar, but here localized to Gaulish myth.</note> that bore his...

Following the example of Dom Montfaucon <note>Bernard de Montfaucon (1655–1741) was a Benedictine monk and a founding figure of modern archaeology.</note>, we do not separate these two figures, which possess an entirely similar head ornament; although they may be very different in their essence. One can only speak here by guessing; and it would be reckless to claim to bind everyone to the system one might establish. The symbols are neither numerous enough nor characteristic enough to be able to assert that it is one Divinity rather than another. All I can say is that, assuming the first figure does not represent Apollo, and that these two figures are those of the same Divinity, it seems they could be taken for those of **Hymenaeus**.

No one is unaware that **Hymen**, or **Hymenaeus**, was the mythical Divinity whom the Pagans believed presided over marriages. People spoke differently of his birth: those who gave him **Cupid** for a brother made him the son of **Bacchus** and **Venus**; but others held that **Terpsichore** <note>The Muse of dance and choral song.</note> was his mother, that he had married early, that he had disappeared in the nuptial bed, and that the searches made to find him had given rise to the custom of making acclamations during weddings and of frequently repeating his name. Many other reasons were also alleged 
<margin>Aeneid, Book 1, line 655.</margin> 
for this custom: but **Servius** <note>Maurus Servius Honoratus (late 4th century AD), a Roman grammarian famous for his detailed commentary on Virgil’s "Aeneid."</note> maintains that they were all false; and that the only true one was that an Athenian called **Hymenaeus**, in the midst of a cruel war, had protected some girls from the violence that might have been done to them: and that in memory of this generosity, newlyweds invoked Hymenaeus during the wedding festivities and often had his name on their lips.

Aulus Gellius believes that the name Circius had been given to it because of the whirlwinds it formed in the air, and the things it rolled, tossed, and carried away. In later times, this word was used to denote the North: *The island of Britain, situated almost at the extreme limit of the world toward the North and the West* <note>Original Latin: "Britannia insula in extremo ferme orbis limite Circium occidentemque versus"</note>, etc. I must not forget that Circius also bore the name Caurus; *Caurus, when it blows more violently than the North Wind through the Gauls* <note>Original Latin: "Caurus Aquiloni cum vehementior Gallias perflat"</note>, says Ampelius in a small work that Saumaise <note>Claude Saumaise (1588–1653), a renowned French classical scholar.</note> had printed in 1657 at the end of Florus’s *History*.

The wind Circius greatly inconvenienced the Port of Mourgues <note>Modern Monaco; the name "Mourgues" is the Provençal form of "Monaco."</note>, and made access very difficult for ships, according to the report of Lucan.

->Gaulish coin representing a ceremony in honor of Cybele. Description of this ceremony in Gaul and in Germany. Similar ceremony practiced in Egypt. Discovery of two figures of Cybele in Paris.<-

Cybele is a very well-known Goddess, which is why I shall refrain from speaking of her birth and her adventures; which are, moreover, quite disputed by the very Authors who speak of or report them. We have several monuments found in France that bear witness—some to the love this Divinity conceived for Attis, a young shepherd of Phrygia, whom she made a eunuch because he had been unfaithful to her; others to the mural crown <note>A crown shaped like city walls and towers, representing Cybele's role as a protector of cities.</note> that she wore because she was the Earth, who is the support and nurse of Cities; and finally others to the *Taurobolia* <term>Taurobolium: A ritual sacrifice of a bull where the initiate was "baptized" in the animal's blood to achieve spiritual rebirth.</term> that were offered to her, one of the greatest and most mysterious sacrifices of all Antiquity. The Acts of Saint Symphorian, a Martyr of the second century, inform us that on the days consecrated to Berecynthia, her statue was carried through the streets in a sort of coach or chariot <term>carpenta</term> <note>A two-wheeled carriage, often covered, used in Roman times for women and for transporting sacred objects.</note> pulled by oxen.

And that the people in great numbers preceded the Chariot, singing and dancing; *singing and dancing before this idol* <note>original: "cantantes atque saltantes ante hoc simulacrum"</note>. This superstition, moreover, was general throughout the Gauls, not only regarding Cybele, but also regarding all the Gods indiscriminately; the peasants especially took it to heart, and they put it into practice because they believed it effective, and that it restored or procured fertility for their lands.

To show more honor to their idols, they covered them with large white veils, which fluttered at the will of the wind (b).

> *The image sits with the face of a woman, enclosed in silver:* <note>original: "Mulieris oris, clausus argento sedet"</note>

We see here that the most distinguished people of Rome followed the chariot barefoot; the statue of the Goddess was made of blackish stone, represented sitting on a silver seat. We also know that people flocked from all sides, from both the city and the countryside; and the ceremony was performed outside the walls near the St. Sebastian gate, where the Almo flows into the Tiber.

<margin>Acts of St. Symphorian</margin>
There is no mention in the *Acts of St. Symphorian* or in the writings of Gregory of Tours <note>A 6th-century historian and bishop who wrote about the history of the Gauls.</note> of the ceremony of the washing of the statue of Berecynthia as practiced in Autun; however, this silence does not prevent us from believing that it took place there. Autun was the capital of the Hedui <note>A powerful Celtic tribe in Gaul.</note>, who were always allies of the Romans, who even called them their brothers before they had conquered the Gauls. Furthermore, aside from this silence, everything else was practiced as it was in Rome, which is apparent from what Gregory of Tours says: that they led the chariot of the statue into the countryside while singing and dancing; (*a*) and everyone flocked to this festival. (*b*)

I conclude these details regarding the worship of Cybele by observing that a remote people of Germany particularly honored this Divinity, and the most important part of her cult consisted of carrying figures of boars. These figures served those who carried them in place of offensive and defensive weapons, protecting them from all danger, even in the midst of the fire and carnage of the enemy.

The following figure represents a beautiful head of Cybele, which was found around the year 1684 in the garden of Mr. Berrier near St. Eustache in Paris: it was two <term>toises<gloss>An old French unit of length, roughly equal to 6.4 feet or 1.9 meters.</gloss></term> deep in a ruined tower; it is made of bronze and is a little larger than life-sized. From the bottom of the neck to the top of the tower, it is twenty-two and a half inches high, two feet nine inches in circumference, and one foot three inches across the widest part of the face. She has a hexagonal tower on her head; the eyes had been removed, perhaps because they were made of silver, as were most of those in the ancient statues of the Divinities. The tower has six angles, marking the taste of the Gauls, who in later centuries gave several angles to their buildings without taking away the roundness that had always been the foundation of all their structures.

Scholars initially believed this could be the tutelary <note>A guardian or patron deity of a specific place.</note> Goddess of the city of Paris during the times of paganism, and that this figure was that of Isis, either because of the tower upon her head, or because this Goddess was greatly honored in Paris.

The fame of the cult of Isis in the city of Paris is not a legitimate foundation for believing that the Figure of which we speak ever represented Isis. It is not disputed that Isis was often taken for Cybele, and Cybele for Isis: but one is convinced that those who had a Goddess represented with a crown of towers on her head almost never intended to represent Isis, but only Cybele. <note>In ancient iconography, the "mural crown"—a crown shaped like city walls and towers—is the defining attribute of Cybele, representing her role as a protectress of cities.</note>

The original of the Cybele that follows is in the <term>cabinet<gloss>A private collection or "cabinet of curiosities" where an antiquarian would store and display artifacts.</gloss></term> of Mr. de Mautour; <note>Philibert-Bernard de Mouchet, sieur de Mautour (1654–1737), a French scholar and member of the Academy of Inscriptions.</note> it is made of bronze, and was found at the foot of Montmartre; it represents in miniature the same face as the Cybele of which we have just spoken. The tower with which the head of the Divinity is crowned, although composed of faces and protruding angles, is in the same style as the previous one. These antiques are incontestably from the time when the Gauls fashioned themselves after the Romans, and preserved only some trace of their own Religion.

Of all the things upon which the Ancients have most varied, one can boldly assert that there is hardly any on which History is more muddled than on the Cabiri. <note>The Cabiri (or Kabiroi) were a group of enigmatic deities whose identity and number changed depending on the source; they were often associated with protection at sea and fertility.</note> I have no intention of undertaking to display here all that Antiquity has left us in writing, nor to report the judgment of the Scholars of our day. If one is to judge the honors that the Gauls rendered to Diana by the fact that they consecrated this forest to her, worshipped her, and had it bear her name, it must be admitted that these honors must have been very great. They would, in some way, correspond to the immense extent of the country that this forest contained; for even if the cult of Diana had been confined to the Ardennes alone, and restricted to the people bordering this forest, this Divinity would have been honored by a very large portion of the peoples of the Gauls. It is true that the Ardennes currently occupy a territory of only thirty-five to forty <term>leagues</term> <note>An old unit of distance, usually about 3 miles or 4.8 kilometers.</note>; but in Caesar's time, they had a much greater extent. On one side, they crossed the entire Archbishopric of Trier and went almost as far as the Rhine; on the other sides, they extended as far as Reims and the <term>Tournaisis</term> <note>The region surrounding the city of Tournai.</note> in Flanders. Nevertheless, it is certain that Diana was recognized throughout all the Gauls, as evidenced by the monuments and inscriptions of this Divinity that remain to us.

One can judge the antiquity of the cult of Diana in these countries by the age of her name; for there is no doubt that from the Celtic name *Arduinna*, which is that of Diana, came the name of the forest that the Romans called *Arduenna*. Now, it is well-established that this forest bore the name *Arduenna* long before the Romans were masters of the Gauls.

<margin>Gruter, page 39, inscription 8. <note>Jan Gruter (1560–1627) was a scholar who compiled a famous collection of ancient Roman inscriptions, which served as a primary source for historians of this period.</note></margin>
In the vast forest of Ardennes, there were several marshy places where the waters gathered and formed deep pools. It was in these lakes that the Gauls honored Diana before they had the custom of representing the Gods in tangible forms. The reason why our ancestors gave Diana the name **Arduina** <note>The author is identifying the Roman Diana with the local Celtic goddess Arduinna, the tutelary deity of the Ardennes forest.</note> was undoubtedly because this Divinity was thought either to take pleasure in making her home in the water or in taking the pleasures of bathing there. It is also with this in view that the Romans called Diana Queen of the Waves, Nymph, and the Glory of the Marshy Woods <note>original Latin: *Regina Undarum, Nympha, decus nemorum*</note>. I further believe that the Gauls practiced this in particular because, making Diana and the Moon one and the same Divinity, and knowing that the Moon greatly influences the rising and falling of the waters, they wished to honor the part she played in this phenomenon.

As for ***Arduena***, it is a word that also comes from the article *ar* and from *Duen*, meaning black or dark, and is said particularly of thick and dark forests; thus the <term>Lower Bretons</term> <note>People from the western part of Brittany who spoke the Breton language, a Celtic tongue related to the ancient Gallic speech.</note>, instead of saying *ar coët Duen*, which means "the Black Forest," they say simply *ar Duen*. The Greek word *to plunge* <note>original Greek: δύιν (*dyin*)</note> corresponds closely enough to the Celtic word, for it means to dive or to slip away as if to hide oneself.

While the Gauls were free, they gave their Gods no other names than those their ancestors had given them. But as soon as they were forced to undergo the Roman yoke, the Latin language having become familiar to them, they related their religion to that of the victors; and

### OF THE GAULS. Book IV.

...that Mr. Quartinius, a Gaul from the city or territory of Reims, settled in the Sabine region <note>A mountainous area in central Italy, north of Rome.</note>; where, continuing to offer his ancestral Gods the worship in which he had been trained and raised, he led the Sabines to accept these foreign Gods and to adore them.

The figure representing Ardoina <note>Arduinna, the Celtic goddess of the Ardennes Forest, usually equated with the Roman Diana.</note> on this marble is a woman in a short tunic, with a quiver on her shoulder.

From this, it is easy to conclude that the Gauls thought of Diana as the Greeks and Romans did: that this Goddess’s sole occupation was hunting; that she had always remained a virgin like her sister Minerva; and that her resolve for this came from the fact that when her mother Latona gave birth to twins, Diana, having been born first, served as her midwife. Seeing the sharp pains her mother suffered while giving birth to Apollo, she conceived such an aversion to marriage that she petitioned Jupiter for his consent to remain forever a Virgin.

<margin>*Gregory of Tours, History, book 8, chapter 14, column 387.*</margin>
The Ministers of Diana in the Gauls were men. In the decline of Paganism, the Gauls celebrated the mysteries of this Divinity with excessive songs and all the debaucheries produced by love and wine. This, at least, is what they practiced at the end of the sixth century, on a mountain in the Ardennes located in Luxembourg, four small leagues from Ivoy, (a) on the borders of the Archbishopric of Trier. But Saint Vulphilaicus <term>Lom- <note>Likely "Lombard"; Saint Vulphilaicus (also known as Saint Walfroy) was a 6th-century stylite monk of Lombard origin who famously destroyed a giant statue of Diana in the Ardennes.</note></term>

We could say many curious things about the honors that the *Phocaeans* <note>Greek settlers from Phocaea who founded Marseille around 600 BCE.</note> of *Marseille* rendered to *Diana*; how they brought a *Statue* from *Ephesus* <note>The Great Temple of Artemis/Diana at Ephesus was one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World.</note> on their ships, through the leadership of *Aristarche*, <note>Original: "Aristarque." But as this *Diana* is that of *Ephesus*, and as she has nothing in common with the tastes, mysteries, and customs of the *Gauls*, we shall refrain from speaking of her further; <margin>*Athenaeus, book 4.*</margin> especially since the *Ancients* regarded the *Marseillais* as a people entirely distinct from the *Gauls*.

I shall therefore finish what I have to say regarding *Diana* by observing that as late as the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries, *Gaulish women*—or *French*, if you prefer—enrolled in some sort of *Society*, and believed in the minds of others, and perhaps even in their own, that they traveled throughout the night on horseback through the air with *Diana*, *Goddess* of the *Pagans*, whom they also <margin>*Manuscript Statutes of the Church of Couserans.* <note>Original: "Conseranensis." ### OF THE GAULS. BOOK IV.

G iii

observations of the Moon, as well as the Druids. This is why I noted, when speaking of the reliefs <note>The author refers to bas-relief stone carvings often found on ancient ruins.</note> that still remain on the gate of an ancient Gallic Temple, that besides six Druids who consult the Moon, there is a Druidess who, alongside them, draws up the plan for the supposed predictions with which she deceived the people, and who delves into a mystery of magic that I will develop later.

The name *Sena* <note>The ancient name for the Isle of Sein.</note> which the Priestesses of the Oracle bore, and which they had communicated to the Isle of Sain, means six in Latin <note>original: "signifie six en Latin." The author is likely connecting *Sena* to the Latin *seni* (six each) or *senary* counts.</note>. This meaning has a rather natural connection, not only with the sixth day of the *Moon*, which was entirely consecrated by the Druids; but also with the number of women they might have been. For although Mela <note>Pomponius Mela, a 1st-century Roman geographer.</note> counts nine of them, it is perhaps by error and a lack of being well-informed. But even if he were not mistaken, the number of nine Druidesses might refer only to the time in which he wrote, and not to that of the institution of the Oracle—a time at which these girls might have been only six, to honor, as I said, the sixth day of the Moon. Indeed, there are only six Druids represented on the gate of the Temple of Montmorillon <note>A famous archaeological site in western France where 17th and 18th-century scholars believed they had found a Druidic temple.</note>. If, therefore, in the century of Mela, the number of these Druidesses had been raised to nine, what happened in that regard was perhaps what happened to the Roman Vestals <note>The Vestal Virgins, priestesses of Vesta in ancient Rome.</note>; they were at first only four, they soon rose to six, and then <margin>Epistle to Valentinian</margin> up to seven, if one takes literally these words of St. Ambrose: *scarcely seven Vestals are chosen* <note>original: "vix septem capiuntur Vestales."</note>.

Similarly, in the beginnings of the Oracle of Delphi, one was satisfied with a single Pythia <note>The priestess who delivered the oracles of Apollo.</note>: she was sufficient at that time for those who came to consult Apollo...

But besides these general reasons, there were others taken from the particular tastes of the Gauls. These peoples, as well as the Germans, regarded the state of being a young girl as possessing a certain indefinable holiness, which disposed them to be more fit for divine communications: (*a*) to the point that they treated some of them not only as Goddesses, but actually considered them real Goddesses during their lifetime. This is also why they sometimes entrusted them with the administration of Justice and the government of the Republic. (*b*) This practice still occurred in Germany long after Jesus Christ. (*c*)

<meta>This page continues the author’s argument from page 57, which ended with a discussion of Saint Hilary and the transition from pagan worship to Christian practice at Mount Helanus. The author is proving that the deity worshipped there, as well as on the Isle of Sein, was the Moon.</meta>

...was not the Moon. The word *Helanus*, as Gaulish as it might have been, was also no less Greek, and meant Moon or splendor; since <term>ἑλάνη</term> <note>original: *helánē* (ἑλάνη). In ancient Greek, this refers to a torch or bright light, which the author here links etymologically to the moon and the name of the mountain.</note> means the same thing. Now, it appears that there was a great connection between what occurred on the **Isle of Sein** and on Mount ***Helanus***. For first, both places were deserted, and one had to travel there specifically. 2nd. The Lake at the foot of Mount ***Helanus*** corresponds to the sea that bathed the shores of the **Isle of Sein**. 3rd. Finally, the "commanded" storms, triggered equally in both places, clearly justify, it seems, that one and the same Divinity was their author; for to put it simply, the Pagans divided among each God their duties, attributes, and jurisdiction; and in the portrait they have left us of each, one does not see one deity encroaching much upon the rights of another. Thus, finding that the **Gauls** honored the **Moon** on Mount ***Helanus***, and that they attributed to this deified celestial body a despotic authority to stir up storms, it is beyond doubt that the Divinity of the **Isle of Sein** is also the Moon; since, among several other similarities, she disposed of storms at her will.

If, after what I have just said, one were not yet fully persuaded that the Divinity of the Oracle of the **Isle of Sein** was the **Moon**, here are three authorities against which it would be difficult to stand; for the authors from whom we draw them all lived in centuries where the same superstitions in use on the **Isle of Sein** in the time of **Mela** <note>Pomponius Mela, a Roman geographer of the 1st century AD, famous for describing the druidesses of the Isle of Sein who could control the weather.</note> were still in force. They even have this advantage over **Mela**: they reveal mysteries to us that he was not in a position to penetrate.

Capitularies <note>Collection of royal ordinances or laws, particularly those of the Frankish kings.</note> of our Kings, in the Councils of France and elsewhere. And everywhere one observes that these superstitions can be traced without interruption back to the century of Mela <note>Pomponius Mela, a Roman geographer of the 1st century AD who wrote about the Druids.</note>; they still persist in the minds of the common people, who hold that there are nocturnal assemblies, which they call the Sabbath, where everything takes place much as in the descriptions I have just copied.

The Druidesses were thus true Witches: despite this, they were in such great fashion that all women, even those of high rank, prided themselves on being among them. Among the latter are counted Basine, wife of the King of Thuringia; the mother of the Tyrant Magnentius <note>A 4th-century commander who usurped the Roman imperial throne.</note>; and several others whom Historians do not fail to mention.

<margin>*Hist. Fra. l. 5. col. 216. edit. nov.* <note>New edition of the History of the Franks, likely by Gregory of Tours.</note></margin>
Gregory of Tours speaks of these women under the name of Pythian priestesses or Pythonesses <note>In antiquity, women possessed by a spirit of divination; the author links this to medieval witchcraft.</note>. ## CHAPTER XV.

### Clarifications on the name of the Virgins of the Isle of Sein.
### The true reading of Mela.

---

<margin>Book 3, ch. 6.</margin>
Mela <note>Pomponius Mela, a Roman geographer of the 1st century AD whose work provides some of the earliest descriptions of the Gaulish coast.</note>, who has provided us with the foundation for everything we have said regarding the Virgins of the Isle of Sein, calls these maidens *Gallicenes*. (*a*) Scholars and interpreters have split this single word into two, claiming that one must read it as "the Gauls call [them] six"; <note>original: "Galli senas vocant"</note> and it was this that initially led us to believe that the name borne by these priestesses was *Sena*, from which the name of the Island was derived; and that this word, in its Latin origin—if indeed it had one—marked the number six, to which the number of Virgins might have been fixed.

Others derive the name *Gallicena* from *Gallus* <note>meaning a Gaul</note>, and from *cano* or *cecini* <note>meaning to sing or to prophesy</note>; they believe that this word signifies Gaulish women who predicted the future by means of the oracles they delivered; as if the text had *Gallicinas* <note>Gaulish singers or prophetesses</note>, just as one says *Fidicinas* <note>lute-players</note>, *Lyricinas* <note>lyre-players</note>, etc.

For my own part, I also believed for some time that one should simply read *Gallicanas* <note>Gaulish women</note> instead of *Gallicenes*. This reading, where there is only a single letter to change, is supported by a passage from Vopiscus <note>Flavius Vopiscus, a historian credited as one of the authors of the *Augustan History*, a collection of Roman imperial biographies.</note>, who calls our Druidesses *Gallicanas* to distinguish the Druidesses of the Gauls from those of England and Germany:
<margin>In the Life of Aurelian, ch. 44.</margin>

...to know if the Empire would remain in his family. (a) It has been seen at all times and in all types of languages that usage always tends to shorten the terms and expressions used to explain our thoughts; especially regarding things that are frequently in the mouths of an entire Nation. The Latin word *Vestalis* [Vestal], which usage finally consecrated to mean a Vestal Virgin, was originally an adjective that could not carry a fixed and positive meaning on its own, and consequently served only to indicate that the thing expressed by the noun to which it was applied was consecrated to the service of Vesta; thus one said, before and after Cicero, *Ara Vestalis* <note>Vestal Altar</note>, *festa Vestalia* <note>Vestal festivals</note>, *foci Vestales* <note>Vestal hearths</note>, and *Virgines Vestales* <note>Vestal Virgins</note>. But as, of all that was consecrated to the worship of Vesta, the Virgins charged with the sacred and perpetual fire not only held the first rank, but were also the only ones distinguished and respected in Rome and throughout the Empire; usage finally prevailed and became so well established that the idea of a Priestess of Vesta was attached to this single term.

I applied the same reasoning regarding the Druidesses of the Gauls: before Mela, and in subsequent centuries, the entire Pagan world <note>original: "Gentilité," referring to the non-Christian peoples of antiquity</note> was obsessed with omens and predictions. ->*Relief found at Narbonne. Opinions of Scholars.*<-

Dom Bernard de Montfaucon <note>Bernard de Montfaucon (1655–1741) was a Benedictine monk and a founding father of modern archaeology and paleography.</note> has placed among the Spirits <term>Genies|In ancient Roman religion, a 'Genius' was the individual instance of a divine nature that is present in every person, place, or thing.</term> and Household Gods <term>Lares|Guardian deities in ancient Roman religion believed to protect the household and domestic activities.</term>, the figures of which he provides in his *Supplement to Antiquity*, a Monument that was found at Narbonne; but without wishing to assert that it effectively represents a Household God or a Spirit. on the Religion of the Gauls, it would take an Oedipus <note>In Greek mythology, Oedipus was the only one capable of solving the riddle of the Sphinx; here the author uses him as a metaphor for a master of solving complex puzzles.</note> to explain this plate. I will, however, risk a few words on it; but first, I will allow myself to make a sincere confession: that I would not dare offer what I am about to say as irrefutable; and thus, without adopting or rejecting the sentiments of others, I am merely proposing my conjectures, which I shall attempt to support with the authority of the Ancients.

I believe, then, that the Woman engraved on the stone tablet is the Moon, upon which the Gauls, and the Druids in particular, based and regulated all their predictions and their auguries <term>Augury|The practice of interpreting omens, often from the flight of birds or celestial events, to predict the future.</term>. The foundation of my conjecture is the action of the man holding this tablet, who seems to be warning everyone to fix their eyes upon it and to consult it: which appears to me to have some relation to the Druids we have already seen, who are occupied only with Moons and lunar cycles, as has been shown. Even the branch that this woman holds in her hand, laden with leaves and fruit, could well be a symbol of the
<margin>In the *Phaenomena* <note>original: "Φαινομέ-", referring to the *Phaenomena* by Aratus, a didactic poem about astronomy.</note>, see p. 20.</margin>
Moon; for according to Aratus <note>A Greek didactic poet (c. 315–240 BC) whose work on astronomy and meteorology was highly influential in the ancient world.</note>, the Ancients held that plants and pastures drew their sap and their substance from the influences of the Moon.

But who is this naked man? The path is slippery <note>A French idiom meaning the subject is difficult or hazardous to navigate.</note>, and the question is embarrassing: however, I shall have no difficulty in confessing that I believe it is a Druid, who plays the same role in this relief as the six Druids on the portal of the Temple of Montmorillon <note>A reference to a Romanesque site in France which the author believes depicts ancient Druidical figures.</note>; that is to say, he contemplates the Moon, studies it, and meditates upon the deceptions <note>original: "prestiges," here referring to magical illusions or tricks used to dazzle the public.</note> with which those of his sect dazzled the public. His nudity seems to insinuate that he traveled through the air in the wake of the Moon, just as the Drui-

To which one may add that since the Druidesses received all their secrets from the Druids who trained them, the Druids were no less eager to exercise over the atmosphere the same command they had imparted to their pupils.

## CHAPTER XVII.

### *Discovery in Zeeland and at Nîmes of the Goddess Nehalennia. Descriptions of the bas-reliefs representing her.*

Nehalennia is a Goddess whom the Gauls formerly worshipped. Her name was unknown until about the middle of the seventeenth century. I would say the same of the cult rendered to her, were it not for the reasons I have to believe that she is the same Divinity whose Oracles were consulted on the Isle of Sein <note>An island off the coast of Brittany, famous in antiquity for a college of nine virgin priestesses said to possess magical powers.</note>, and whom I have shown to be certainly the Moon. Before presenting my reasons, I shall follow the order kept by Wrée <note>Olivier de Wree (1596–1652), a Flemish historian and lawyer.</note> and Mr. Keysler <note>Johann Georg Keyssler (1693–1743), a German scholar who wrote extensively on ancient Celtic and Germanic religions.</note> in the description they [give...]

On the fifth day of January in the year 1647, an east wind blew with such violence upon a point formed by Zeeland <note>A coastal province of the Netherlands composed of islands and peninsulas.</note>, which extends into the Ocean, and pushed the sea waves so strongly toward the opposite side, that the shores were left dry and exposed. People flocked there from all directions and saw ruins that the sea had previously covered: altars, vases, urns, <term>medals</term> <note>Likely referring to ancient coins, which were often called medals in early modern antiquarian texts.</note>, <term>fibulae</term> <note>original: "agraphes"—ancient brooches or pins used to fasten garments.</note>, and other items, almost all in the Roman style. Statues of *Jupiter* and *Neptune* were also found there, and above all a great many reliefs of the Goddess *Nehalennia*, along with inscriptions bearing her name, except for a single one which did not. Since most of these images are very similar, we provide only a small number in which some difference can be observed, contenting ourselves with describing them all without obligating ourselves to report the inscriptions, from which no further enlightenment could be drawn. Furthermore, the stones or altars on which *Nehalennia* is represented are sometimes three, sometimes four feet high, by about two and a half feet wide; the grain of the stone is coarse and crumbly.

In the first image, *Nehalennia* is seated, holding in her lap a basket full of apples and other fruits; at her right side is a dog, and at her left a basket filled with fruit like the first. The borders are also adorned with several kinds of fruit.

The second figure represents *Nehalennia* standing upright; the dog is again at her right; and at her left is a ship's prow <note>The forward part of a vessel, signifying her role as a protector of seafarers.</note>, upon which *Nehalennia* rests her foot.

<note>Original Latin: DEAE NEHAE / ERIATTIUS JUCUN / DI PRO SE ET SUIS / V. S. L. M. The final abbreviation stands for "Votum Solvit Libens Merito," a standard Roman formula for fulfilling a religious promise.</note>

That is to say, Eriattius, son of Jucundus, has willingly and out of gratitude fulfilled the vow he made to the Goddess Neha, for himself and for his family. Reinefius <note>Thomas Reinesius (1587–1667), a German scholar who specialized in ancient inscriptions.</note> does not doubt that Neha is the same as Nehalennia. Indeed, Gruter says that the Goddess mentioned on this marble is represented there with two <term>horns of plenty<note>Also known as cornucopiae, these are symbols of abundance and nourishment, typically depicted as large goat horns overflowing with fruit and grain.</note></term> at her sides: a detail that leads me to agree with the sentiment of Reinefius; for Nehalennia is everywhere accompanied by baskets of fruit, and sometimes by two horns of plenty, and in some places by baskets of fruit and horns of plenty all at once.

Reinefius even goes so far as to believe that one should read *Nehalenniae* in the inscription instead of *Nehae*; and that the letters missing to complete the word have been eaten away or erased by the ravages of time. However, Reinefius is clearly mistaken; he failed to notice that the sculptor took pride in not including more letters or syllables in the first line of the inscription than are present. The last word of the second line is proof of this truth: the worker moved one syllable of it to the third,

This proves that nothing has been eroded or erased in the Inscription; for if they had intended to engrave the full word *Nehalenniae* <note>original: "Nehalenniae," the dative form of the name Nehalennia used in Latin dedications.</note> instead of *Nehae*, almost everything that Reinefius <note>Thomas Reinesius (1587–1667) was a German scholar known for his work on ancient inscriptions.</note> believes to be erased in the first line would have been pushed down to the second.

What I have just said does not prevent *Neha* from being understood as *Nehalennia*: several reasons work together to persuade us of this. 1st. The fruits, which decorated the reliefs of both one and the other. 2nd. *Neha* is merely an abbreviated or shortened name for that of *Nehalennia*. Now, it is not surprising that a name as common as *Nehalennia* must have been—as I shall demonstrate—would have been gradually shortened, especially in a region as vast as the Gauls <note>In this period, "The Gauls" (les Gaules) referred to the broad territories inhabited by Celtic tribes, spanning modern France, Belgium, and parts of neighboring countries.</note>. 3rd. *Neha* contains at least half of the true meaning of the name *Nehalennia*. 4th. Finally, the small difference between *Neha* and *Nehalennia* justifies the variation in dialects that Caesar <note>Gaius Julius Caesar (100–44 BC), who described the diverse languages and customs of the Gallic tribes in his writings.</note> and later authors asserted were in use throughout the Gauls. Add to this the location where the Inscription was found: it was at Deutz <note>original: "Deutsch," referring to the district of Deutz in modern-day Cologne.</note>, across from Cologne, beyond the Rhine.

The proximity to rivers further strengthens my opinion. *Neha* or *Nehalennia* was certainly the Moon, or at least the new Moon: the Gauls conflated the Moon with Diana <note>The Roman goddess of the hunt and the moon; the author suggests the Gauls viewed their local goddess and the Roman Diana as the same figure.</note>, and made them into a single Divinity: they took pride not only in building the Temples they erected to the Moon and to Diana adjacent to rivers and marshes; but also in giving Diana a Celtic name, which signified a "water abyss."

### CONCERNING THE GAULS. BOOK IV.

The goddess whom I believe to be Nehalennia <note>Nehalennia was a goddess of ancient Germanic or Celtic origin, often depicted with symbols of fertility and seafaring; her cult was centered in the region of modern-day Zeeland, Netherlands.</note> is engraved on a marble slab, which I mentioned is in the Library of the Jesuit Fathers in Brussels. Mr. Keysler <note>Johann Georg Keyßler (1689–1743) was a German traveler and antiquarian known for his documentation of European antiquities.</note> presented it so unfaithfully that, based on the suspicion I had, I wrote to Brussels to ask skilled individuals to compare the copy with the original, and to note the differences for me. The Armoricans <note>The Armoricans were the ancient Celtic people inhabiting the northwestern coast of France, in the region now known as Brittany.</note> of today still say *Nevez* instead of the French *Nouveau* [New], and their consonant V, much like that of the Celts, is merely a strong aspiration <note>An "aspiration" is a breathy sound, similar to the English "h".</note>.

I said at first to suppose that the first letter of the name of the Deity in question was an N, and not an H. Indeed, in later centuries—to which alone this Inscription must be dated—these two letters were often confused and taken for one another, because both the H and the N were formed using a horizontal or nearly horizontal line to link the two parallel and perpendicular strokes in these letters: which rendered them so similar that they could only be distinguished by context. Our ancient Coins and our old Charters provide several proofs of this truth. More can be found in the *Diplomatics* of Dom Mabillon <note>Jean Mabillon (1632–1707) was a Benedictine monk and scholar who founded the sciences of palaeography (the study of old handwriting) and diplomatics (the study of historical documents).</note>, and in the same author's *Benedictine Annals*, especially on page 481 of the first volume.

That the letter F was substituted for an E is a proposition that Antiquaries <note>A term for historical scholars who studied ancient artifacts and inscriptions.</note> will have no difficulty accepting: they are well aware of the innumerable errors that crept into Inscriptions through the ignorance and blunders of engravers. The error supposed here would be one of the least significant; since the similarity of the E with the F made such a mistake frequent, and in a way, familiar and pardonable. One can even prove by Festus <note>Sextus Pompeius Festus (2nd century AD) was a Roman grammarian whose work is a major source for ancient Latin and Roman customs.</note> and other authors that the Ancients sometimes intentionally used an F instead of an E; for one finds in the...

At the time the Inscription was made, Duiz was only a Fort that the Romans had built beyond the Rhine to keep the Barbarians of Germany in check. Now, a Fort could not have had enough Temples or Divinities to lead to a confusion of their names and relationships; which might have happened if the *Hafua* of the Brussels Inscription were different from the *Neha* we have from Gruter.

These are the reasons I have for suspecting that one must read *Neva* or *Neha* in the Brussels Inscription, and not *Hafua*; from which I draw a new argument against those who claim that one must read *Nehalenniae* <note>Nehalennia was a goddess of the North Sea, often depicted with a dog and a basket of fruit, whose altars were frequently recovered from the waters near Zeeland.</note> in Gruter’s Inscription, instead of *Nehae*.

*Nehalennia. The Divinity of the Oracle of the Isle of Sein was the same as Nehalennia. Various etymologies of the word Nehalennia. It was the New Moon. When one comes to compare the two Divinities—that is to say, Nehalennia and the one from the Oracle of the Isle of Sein <note>The Île de Sein is a small island off the coast of Brittany, France, which ancient sources described as the home of powerful priestesses known as the Gallizenae.</note>—one finds features so similar that there is no risk in saying they were one and the same Divinity.

I have shown that the Divinity of Sein was unquestionably the Moon. Here are the reasons that demonstrate the same thing regarding Nehalennia.

Although the origins I have just given for Nehalennia do not present the slightest difficulty; it will not be out of place to join some others to the first ones, which help to dispel the darkness in which this Divinity is shrouded. The third syllable of the word Nehalennia could also come from the Celtic *Llen*, which means veil; to signify that at the time of the new Moon, the greater part of her light is covered by a veil, which hides her from the sight of mortals. This conjecture is supported by the manner in which the Gauls represented Nehalennia; for they gave her garments that hid her entirely, except for the face. So that in their minds, when the Moon was new, there was properly only the face of the Divinity that could be discovered, and that was perceptible to our eyes.

<margin>Maunoir <note>Julien Maunoir (1606–1683) was a Jesuit priest and linguist known for his work on the Breton language.</note>.</margin>
Here is yet another etymology of Nehalennia, which does not seem to me to be dismissed: *Len* is a Celtic word which means pond or pool. The Gauls honored the Moon in ponds; and the Druidesses <note>Female priests or seers among the Celtic peoples who often lived in communities on islands or near sacred water.</note> who served her Temples usually stationed themselves on ponds or on the water's edge; they made their observations there, rendered their Oracles, and put into practice the magical illusions that were within their province. But this worship of the new Moon, which we see having lasted into such late centuries; would one truly believe that it was hardly less ancient within the Nation than the Nation itself? What leads us to presume this is that we see it observed at all times in the East, from where the Celts had undoubtedly brought it. We even see in Scripture that the Eastern peoples attached some kind of virtue to the figure of the Crescent, which led them to wear it as a preservative <note>In this context, a "preservative" refers to a protective amulet or talisman.</note>, and that they attached it to the animals they wished to protect. It is through this channel that the custom of wearing Crescents on the neck or on the head—hanging over the forehead—was imperceptibly introduced; <margin>See Calmet, *Commentary on Isaiah*, ch. 3, v. 18 & ch. 65, v. 11.</margin> it eventually passed to the Romans, who made it one of the finest ornaments of their shoes. <note>The Roman *lunula* was a crescent-shaped ornament worn on the shoes of senators.</note>

### ON THE GAULS. BOOK IV.

<margin>Lipsius, *On Vesta and the Vestals*, synthesis chapter 13, volume 2, page 759. <note>original Latin: "Lips. de Vesta & Vestal. synt. c. 13. t. 2. p. 759." This refers to a work by Justus Lipsius, a famous 16th-century humanist scholar.</note></margin>
The perpetual virginity, which they professed, obliges me to point out here that it is without foundation that Lipsius has asserted that there were Vestals <note>Priestesses of the Roman goddess Vesta, sworn to celibacy and tasked with maintaining the sacred hearth fire.</note> only in Rome, and that all those elsewhere were mere shadows of Vestals; who approached neither the distinction, nor the splendor, nor the merit of the Roman women. One might overlook this paradox in this Author, if he had said only that Rome alone possessed a **College** <term>College: In this historical context, a "college" refers to a formal religious society or organized body of priestesses rather than an educational institution.</term> of girls consecrated to Vesta, and destined by their profession to maintain the sacred fire: although it would be very easy to destroy this sentiment by several authorities and Inscriptions. But as the meaning of Lipsius’s proposition seems to exclude every other College of girls than that of the Vestals: as if outside of Rome there had been no assemblies, nor societies of girls, who were committed forever to the service of some Divinity, with the obligation to always keep their virginity; it is appropriate to say that this view is contrary to the truth: and without entering into a great detail of proofs, it suffices to remark in passing that the Romans thought quite differently from Lipsius, at least regarding the Gallic virgins: since the latter having wanted to challenge the Law which was the foundation of their institution, in order to conform to the Vestals of Rome: they <note>The Romans.</note> regarded this change as a step that tarnished their glory; and they believed they had acquired great honor for having put the virgins of Gaul in a state to infinitely surpass the Roman Vestals.

## CHAPTER XX.

### Diana-Moon found in Lorraine; conjectures on her cult. The view of the Ancients on the origin of Lunar Eclipses.

<margin>In 1718.</margin>
The Diana-Moon <note>A syncretic deity combining the Roman goddess Diana with lunar attributes, often associated with the Greek Selene.</note> which was found five or six years ago on the mountain of Faucogney in Lorraine, near the Parish of St. Martin, is like an appendix to Nehalennia <note>A goddess of Germanic or Celtic origin, usually associated with seafaring and abundance, whose altars were frequently discovered in the Low Countries.</note>. It is for this reason that I place her here intentionally, because this is her true rank. The figure is of coarse workmanship; one notices some red traces on the face, which lead us to believe that the entire face once had full layers of this color. She has a crescent moon upon her head; her clothes are modest, but one cannot provide a full description of them; because besides the fact that they are quite unique, the figure is only a bust; which, being able to represent only the head, shoulders, and chest of the Divinity, thereby robs us of the knowledge of the entire figure and the shape that the rest of her garments took. The original is sixteen inches in height by almost as much in width. This Figure was not alone; she was accompanied by several others which represented pigs and other animals. They were in poor taste, and similar in every way to those which were found at Framont and at Zurich, along with two statues of Mercury.

I have only a few things to say about this Figure; because whether it served the two different uses that I am going to propose, or whether it was restricted...

I do not fear to say it: of all the mysteries of the Religion of the Gauls, where the Figure of the Moon appears to have been employed with the most certainty, they are those of **Mithras**. Indeed, in almost all <term>Mithraic tablets<note>These are ancient stone reliefs depicting the god Mithras, typically shown sacrificing a bull (the tauroctony), a central image in the Mithraic mysteries which spread throughout the Roman Empire.</note></term>, a bust of the Moon similar to this one, and aligned with that of the Sun, holds the highest rank alongside that star; undoubtedly because the Moon has always been regarded as one of the two great luminaires of the sky. The figures of animals found with the Moon represented the planets and constellations, as I have already stated several times.

To avoid any misunderstanding <note>original: "prendre le change," an idiom meaning to be misled or to follow a false trail.</note>, one must take great care not to consider the Moon in this specific instance as the "soul" or primary focus of the ceremony and mystery being celebrated: the Sun was the Divinity to whom all honors were directed. According to the custom of the Persians and that of the Romans, who modeled themselves after the former, Mithras was the Sun. The Gauls only partially followed in the footsteps of the Persians and Romans; especially since they substituted **Mercury** for **Mithras**, and identified him among themselves as the Sun. Mercury could not, therefore, fail to be represented in the Temple where the Figures found on the mountain of **Faucogney** <note>A commune in the Haute-Saône department in eastern France, known for Gallo-Roman archaeological remains.</note> were located: and if his statue was not among those discovered, it is undoubtedly because it was hidden elsewhere. ## RELIGION

A number of statues of <term>Mercury</term> <note>Mercury was the Roman god of commerce and travel, whom Julius Caesar identified as the most popular god among the Gauls.</note> have been found, accompanied by several figures of animals similar to those at Faucogney. On that occasion, I demonstrated the metamorphosis that the <term>Gauls</term> had performed, transforming <term>Mercury</term> into <term>Mithras</term> <note>Mithras was a sun god of Persian origin. The author is suggesting the Gauls blended their local traditions with these foreign mystery cults.</note>.

Although the sentiment I just proposed regarding the Moon of Faucogney seems entirely true to me and does not present the slightest difficulty, I have another thought regarding this monument that could also be true. I see no disadvantage in it being just as valid as the first. All the great masters who have delved into <term>Ancient Theology</term> know well that it is filled with such contrasts, which often reach the point of contradiction.

This thought is that this Moon could very well be that <term>Diana</term>, <term>Herodias</term>, <term>Bensozia</term>, or <term>Nocticula</term> <note>Names used in historical and folkloric texts to describe a "Queen of the Night" or a leader of nocturnal spirits, often associated with the "Wild Hunt."</note>—the sovereign presiding over the night—of whom I spoke in relation to the <term>Oracle of the Isle of Sein</term> <note>A small island off the coast of Brittany, famous in antiquity for an oracle served by nine priestesses said to possess magical powers.</note>. It is true that this figure is quite different from the other; however, this difference implies no contradiction. The <term>Gauls</term> could have had several versions of <term>Herodias</term>, some more modest than others; Egypt, Rome, and Greece provide an infinite number of such examples.

Moreover, everything here concurs to establish this sentiment: first, there is the Moon, and even the new Moon, judging by the crescent she wears on her head. Of all the periods of time that composed the <term>Gallic</term> months, years, and centuries, none approached the sanctity of the new moon in the minds of our ancestors, nor was any more central to their social and religious life. In this case, the animals which—

Marcel, following the example of several others, confuses two deities here; he wrongly joins Apollo and the Sun into one and the same God, even though their worship rendered them quite distinct, as I have shown elsewhere.

The relief of Clermont is, in my view, one of the most interesting pieces regarding the religion of the Gauls. This is because, whether it was made before or after the reduction <note>The "reduction" refers to the Roman conquest of Gaul.</note> of the Gauls, it reveals to us the primary Gods of the Nation and serves as a demonstration that the Gauls did not borrow their religion from any other people whatsoever.

Under the molding and the entablature of an ancient Temple of the Gauls, which can still be seen in its entirety at Montmorillon in Poitou, there are several extraordinary heads. Two of these approach, or at least share something with, the relief of Clermont. This was my reason for joining them to <term>Onuava</term> <note>A Gaulish goddess, sometimes associated with the earth or celestial waters; her identity was a subject of much debate among early antiquarians.</note> and representing them with her in the same Plate.

It is neither Medusa, nor Belenus, nor the Sun that is the subject of this antique. It is a true figure of the **Celestial Venus**, such as the majority of Eastern peoples represented and adored. One only has to cast an eye upon it and follow my reasoning to be convinced of this.

The woman's head, which is the principal part of the relief and holds the primary position, represents a Divinity whose remaining body was that of a fish. Indeed, one sees here a human head without a neck, attached to the body of a fish. This body, which faces forward and is horizontally arranged—and consequently fades into the heart and center of the relief—does not fail to appear; for its scales would make it noticeable to even the least observant eyes. All that remains to be observed in this regard is that the fish's body is not in proportion with the head attached to it; its size exceeds that of the head. This is a mystery that I shall clarify in what follows.

The Serpents arranged in garlands around the face I have just described are the symbol of another famous Divinity of the Phoenicians, Egyptians, Babylonians, and other peoples. And Pliny, confirming this, says that she is the Derceto of the Greeks. (a) <note>original Latin: "Ibi prodigiosa Atargatis, Graecis autem Derceto dicta colitur" (There the wondrous Atargatis, called Derceto by the Greeks, is worshipped).</note>

<margin>Book 8, ch. 8.</margin>
Athenaeus speaks of Atergatis, and says that a Queen of Syria named Gatis loved fish with such passion that she forbade her subjects from eating it, except for herself, Gatis—"without Gatis" <note>original Greek: "ἄτερ Γάτις" (*ater Gatis*), a pun suggesting the queen's name was derived from the Greek word for 'without' or 'except'.</note>; and it was from this exception, which her subjects always had in their mouths, that she was later called Atergatis.

But this is a baseless etymology with no foundation; for the word comes from *Dag* <note>Hebrew for "fish."</note> and *Adir* <note>Hebrew for "magnificent" or "glorious."</note>; that is to say, Atergatis is the magnificent fish *par excellence*. It is in this sense that the Philistines spoke of the Ark of the Lord when they learned it had arrived at the Hebrew camp: <margin>1 Samuel 4:8</margin> *Who will deliver us from the hand of these magnificent Gods?*

<margin>In Schedius, *On the German Gods*, p. 127.</margin>
The Babylonians, who also honored this Goddess, called her Salambas because she made her home in the sea, which the Greeks call *salos* <note>original Greek: "σάλος" meaning the tossing or surge of the sea.</note>. *Athenaeus* <note>Athenaeus of Naucratis was a Greek rhetorician and grammarian who recorded various historical anecdotes.</note> speaks of *Atergatis*, and says that a Queen of *Syria* named *Gatis* loved fish with such a passion that she forbade her subjects from eating it, except for herself, *Gatis*, *ater Gatis* <note>original: "ἄτερ Γάτις", meaning "without Gatis" or "except Gatis"</note>; and that it is from this exception, which her subjects always had in their mouths, that she was since called *Atergatis*.

This superstition eventually spread to *Greece*, and then to *Rome*. In *Epirus*, there was a grove surrounded by walls and consecrated to *Apollo*; within it, a great number of serpents were seen, which were believed to be descendants of the Serpent *Python* that *Apollo* had killed. A virgin was entrusted with feeding them. There were similar dragons in a grove dedicated to *Juno of Argos*, near *Lavinium*; on certain days, girls were brought into this grove blindfolded, carrying a mixture of water and flour for the serpents: it is said that these animals would not touch what was offered to them if the girls were not chaste. Everyone knows that the Romans, after a great plague, sent to fetch the Serpent worshipped at *Epidaurus*: the animal came of its own accord onto their ship and chose its home on an island in the *Tiber*, where it received divine honors from the Roman people, who regarded it as a God of health. I conclude this subject by saying that *Egypt* was always, as it were, the stage where the Serpent was held in the greatest veneration; it appeared in nearly all their mysteries, and they represented it in several different ways, as can be seen in the surviving monuments, and above all in the *Isiac Table*. <note>The Isiac Table (Tabula Isiaca) is a famous bronze tablet featuring Egyptian iconography, widely studied by early modern scholars of religion.</note>

learns that some gates of the City of Thebes bore the name of *Onkaian* <note>original: Ὀγκαῖας</note>; which implies that the Goddess **Onka** was worshipped in Thebes, and that these gates were consecrated to her.

One cannot deny that the conjecture or opinion of **Bochart** <note>Samuel Bochart (1599–1667) was a prominent French scholar who attempted to prove that many Greek and Gallic myths originated from Phoenician culture.</note> is compelling, especially when one considers the idea held of **Onuava**, that she had shown men the arts and sciences: which is precisely what the Gauls attributed to **Minerva**. On the other hand, it is certain that Minerva bore the name of **Belisana** in the Gauls, under which name alone it seems she was recognized and revered. Furthermore, there is no vestige in Antiquity that suggests in the slightest the metamorphosis of Minerva into a fish, nor that this Goddess ever adorned herself with the remains or symbols of that animal, nor finally that she had any relation to the sea and rivers. I believe, therefore, that we must seek another Divinity to whom all this applies.

It appears more likely that **Onuava** was, as I have said, **Venus**—not the vulgar and public one, but the **Celestial**, who alone was known in the East; the other is of the Greek fashion: for to put it in two words, there were two Venuses, one ancient, daughter of the heavens and without a mother, called **Celestial**; the second younger, daughter of Jupiter and Dione, who bore the name of **public**. <meta>This page continues the investigation into the iconography of the goddess Venus (associated with the Gaulish Onuava), specifically explaining why her head appears disproportionately small compared to the large fish-body depicted in the relief sculpture mentioned on the previous page.</meta>

# RELIGION #

> Bearing the snake-footed Typhon upon winged shoulders, 
> And he thrust his fires into the scaly fish.
<note>original: "Anguipedem alatis humeris Typhona ferentem, / Inseruitque suos squamosis piscibus ignes." These lines describe the giant Typhon and the gods' transformation into fish to escape him.</note>

Now, as this retreat of Venus into the body of a fish is the foundation of the Myth <note>The author uses "Fable" in the classical sense of a mythological narrative.</note> which led her to be given not only a fish’s body, but the very body of the fish in which she sought refuge, it is evident that the entire body of the fish had to have a circumference and a capacity much greater than the Goddess in order to contain her. Thus, the fish-body of the Goddess had to be incomparably larger than her human (or divine, if one prefers) head. In short, everything that was fish-like in the Goddess had to have a size that exceeded the usual proportions between a body and a head. What confirms all of this is that, on our relief sculpture, it seems that in representing Venus with a fish's body, the intention was to set before the eyes the very moment when this Divinity—emerging from the fish to fly back into the heavens—had precisely only her head outside, while the rest of her body remained within the fish.

They had a language that was their own: and it is not at all probable that they would give the cities and peoples names drawn from a language other than the one they spoke. There is only one thing that one cannot grant to *M. de M.*: he pushes his principle too far, though it cannot be contested; and he draws from it a consequence that would be difficult for him to justify. He does not want one to have recourse to the Greek language to explain Celtic words, the true understanding of which time has stolen from us. His claim would be good and well-founded if the language of our ancestors had nothing in common with the Greek language.

However, the language of the Celts was, in its origin, the same as that of the ancient Greeks; both appear to have been the one that *Cadmus* <note>In Greek mythology, Cadmus was the Phoenician prince who introduced the alphabet to the Greeks; here, the author suggests a shared primordial language.</note> had...
