[substi]tute for the words that do not come to them, words from their own country; or they use French words that do not quite capture their thoughts, without however straying far from the true meaning of the term they seek. They believe, moreover, that they have handled the matter well because they use a word dressed in the French fashion, or because they use a French word, even though at its heart the word does not quite express what they wish to say. <note>The author is comparing the linguistic habits of the ancient Gauls to people of his own time, suggesting that both groups often misuse or adapt words when they cannot find the exact term in a second language.</note>

From this we must infer that since the Gauls, with all these words we have just listed, intended only to express the word for *Mother* in Latin, one should not quibble over terms that do not perfectly signify this; since, after all, they hardly differ from that meaning.

One might also reasonably suggest that the corruption that has crept into these words comes from the lack of skill of the Engravers and Sculptors; for experience teaches us only too well that most of the errors observed on the Monuments of Antiquity come from the gross ignorance of those in that trade.

Another reason that persuades us that our forefathers <note>Original: "nos Peres." Here referring to the ancient inhabitants of France/Gaul.</note> meant nothing by all these words but the name of Mother is that these Inscriptions contain only prayers for the prosperity of Houses and Families, as we have already noted. Consequently, it follows that the Divinities to whom they addressed their prayers were meant to act as Mothers toward these families and Houses.

## CHAPTER XXIV.

*Diverse opinions on the Divinities called Maires, Mothers, etc. They were the Fates. They presided over childbirth. Different titles with which they were honored. Childbed couches consecrated to the Fates. True meaning of the term Augustus. Lucina represented in the same manner as the Fates. Opinion of the Ancients that the Fates sometimes made themselves seen. Idea one had of these Divinities. The devotion one had for them soon surpassed that which one had for the greatest Divinities.*

Everything we have said until now is only to prepare the Reader, and lead him to a full knowledge of the Divinities who are the object of these researches. Thus it was only the smallest part of the difficulty that we had to clear up: the principal matter consists in guessing what these goddesses *Maires*, *Mothers*, *Matrons*, or *Ladies* truly are. <note>In this period of French, "Maires" was an archaic spelling or regional variant of "Mères" (Mothers).</note>

Chorier <note>Nicolas Chorier (1612–1692), a French historian of the Dauphiné region.</note> and Fabretti <note>Raffaele Fabretti (1618–1700), a famous Italian antiquarian and collector of inscriptions.</note> following him, believe that these types of Divinities were of those called Country and Rustic. nument reported by Gruter, <note>Jan Gruter (1560–1627) was a Dutch philologist and collector of ancient inscriptions.</note> *Sacred to the Suleviae and the Field-Goddesses*. <note>original Latin: *Sulevis & Campestribus Sacrum*</note> Monument consecrated to the Suleve and Country Goddesses.

I will make no difficulty in admitting that the Divinities of whom I treat were truly *country and rustic*, based on the opinion held that they made their home in the countryside. I even maintain that the Suleviae and the Field-Goddesses were the same Divinities as the Maires, Mothers, etc. But to infer from this that they were at first known only in the country, from where their cult had passed to the Cities and Provinces, is certainly not sustainable. Moreover, for any explanation, to limit oneself to saying that the Maires, Mothers, etc., were *country* Divinities is to seek to create an illusion with empty words, which do not advance us much and leave us far behind what we seek.

Keyler <note>Johann Georg Keysler (1693–1743), a German scholar who wrote extensively on Celtic and Northern European antiquities.</note> specifically wrote a Dissertation on the Maires: he claims that they were Druidesses, some of whom were regarded as Divinities during their lifetime, and all as being filled with eminent light regarding the future. This, according to him, had prompted the Celts from that time onward to place their fields and cities under their protection, and to leave them there after their death. He supports his sentiment on the terms of Caesar, who <margin>*Book 1.*</margin> calls the Druidesses of the army of Ariovistus <term>Matres-familias<gloss>Mothers of the household or Matriarchs</gloss></term>; and notes that the Greek <margin>*Plutarch in Caesar. Clement of Alexandria, Stromata, book 1.*</margin> Authors give these women the name of *sacred*. (*a*)

### OF THE GAULS. BOOK IV.

It might be objected that the two Inscriptions I have just utilized to prove that the *Maires* <term>Maires: a variant of *Mères* (Mothers), referring to the *Matronae* or mother-goddesses worshipped in Roman Gaul.</term>, etc., were called Ladies, have elsewhere been applied to Druidesses. In fact, they can apply equally to Druidesses and to the *Maires*. In the system of those who hold that the *Maires* were truly deified Druidesses, these two applications carry no contradiction. It is not quite the same in our view: one must choose; yet that is not easy to do, because we are almost inevitably ignorant of the intention of those who commissioned these Inscriptions. To resolve this difficulty, it seems there would be a middle ground to take; that is to give one or the other of these Inscriptions to the Druidesses, and reserve the other for the *Maires*. If one wishes for no such division, one would be more justified in relating them all to the Divinities of whom we are speaking.

Furthermore, I cannot accept the opinion of those who believe that the Women who are represented alone on reliefs, which are unearthed from time to time, are Mothers or Matrons, etc., even though they have their clothing and symbols. These Mothers were certainly the Fates <term>Parcae: the three sisters of destiny in Roman mythology.</term>, inseparable sisters, forever inseparable. Indeed, all the Monuments that represent them always offer them as three; the Authors who treat them do not separate them, and the Inscriptions dedicated to them always speak of them in the plural. It appears rather that these women thus detached, and who have the attire of Matrons, are Lucina <term>Lucina: the Roman goddess of childbirth, whose name implies "bringing to light."</term>, with whom the Mothers agreed in almost everything: Lucina was nothing other than the Moon, according to Porphyry <term>Porphyry: a 3rd-century Neoplatonist philosopher known for his "On Images."</term>, of whom I have reported a—

<page-num>172</page-num>
<header>THE RELIGION</header>

...placed in the first class of Divinities. For through the chaos one must pierce to carry one's sight that far, one sees clearly that the Fates <note>The *Parcae*, or three goddesses of destiny.</note> or Mothers were, among our ancestors, only second-order Deities, who did not form part of the fundamental Religion of the Country. Thus, although they perhaps believed, along with the Greeks and Romans, that Jupiter and the other superior Gods were obliged to consult the Fates before deciding anything—even what was within their own Jurisdiction—so as not to compromise their authority, they nevertheless regarded them as a species of local, domestic deities <note>original: "divinitez bourgeoises"; the author implies they were common, civic, or household spirits rather than major national gods.</note> who did not stand on equal footing with Teutates, Hesus, Taranis, and the other Gods of the Nation. It is true that their cult became very famous in later times, and was the most widely practiced, as the Monuments remaining to us bear witness; but to tell the truth, I believe all the glory of it was due to the Druidesses. These individuals, both maidens and wives, were held in extraordinary regard, and everyone consulted them about the future. The Fates were the source of all their predictions, since it was only upon their decrees that the Druidesses rendered their answers; the Druidesses therefore could not fail to promote the Fates and to lend authority to their cult.

## OF THE GAULS. BOOK IV.

Of these corrections, the first—which consists of reading *our* <note>original: "nostram" or "nostra"</note> or *ours* instead of *yours* <note>original: "vestra"</note>—is clearly necessary. By means of the second, I read *that* <note>original: "que"</note> instead of *who* <note>original: "qui"</note>. I admit that this latter change is a matter of indifference, because the Gauls honored the <term>Divinities</term> in question under both sexes; or to put it better, they believed there were both males and females among them, as I shall soon demonstrate. I will say nothing of the letter following *Doninda*, nor of the word ending the fourth line; there is nothing there that should cause any delay. I will only add that I could justify the corrections I have made with an infinite number of examples drawn from Antiquity, were I not wishing to spare the refined Reader the distaste they would feel at the sight of so many <term>barbarisms</term> <note>referring to the poor Latin grammar often found in provincial inscriptions</note>, contradictions, and constructions that go beyond being merely flawed.

To come to the question proposed—namely, whether the *Sulfes* of the newly unearthed Inscription are the *Sylphs* of the *Count of Gabalis* <note>A famous 1670 satirical novel by Abbé de Villars about elemental spirits</note>—I respond that if by *Sylphs* one means the wives or daughters of the *Sylphs*, whom the Author of the book calls *Sylphids*, there is no room for hesitation. The reason I have for restricting the *Sulfes* to the *Sylphids* rather than the *Sylphs* is that the *Sulfes* are certainly the *Sulevae* of that Inscription first provided by <term>Fabretti</term> <note>Raphaël Fabretti (1620–1700), a noted Italian antiquarian</note>.

<header>CONCERNING THE GAULS. BOOK IV.</header>

The antiquity of these deities does not invalidate this opinion. Gaul swarms with inscriptions and reliefs, all bearing the hallmark of the Nation; the few found elsewhere suggest they are merely overflows that help us recognize their source. The Gauls erected chapels in the countryside to these phantom deities, which bore the name *Cancelli* <note>Latin for "lattices" or "railings," likely referring to small, enclosed shrines or screened areas.</note>; they would travel there with candles, make offerings, and sacrifice a sow; they pronounced magic words over bread, herbs, or charms <term>ligatures: magical knots or bindings intended to cast a spell</term> to enchant them, and hid these things in a tree or at crossroads with two, three, or four exits. By these means, they claimed not only to protect their livestock from all contagion and even death but also believed they could bring about the loss of their enemies' herds. There were many other superstitions they practiced, but it would be too long to detail them: they can be seen in the writings of Saint Faustinus, in Saint Eligius <note>Saint Eligius (c. 588–660), Bishop of Noyon, who famously preached against the survival of pagan customs.</note>, in the Councils of Gaul, in the Capitularies <note>Decrees or laws issued by Frankish kings, particularly Charlemagne and his successors.</note> of our Kings, and finally in the ancient Penitentials <note>Books containing rules for penance, often listing specific pagan sins to be confessed.</note> or Church Rituals.

<margin>Count of Gabalis, p. 61. <note>A reference to "The Count of Gabalis," a 1670 satirical novel by Henri de Montfaucon de Villars, which popularized the idea of elemental spirits like Sylphs.</note></margin>

The term *Suis* <note>Latin for "to his/her own" or "to their own."</note> from the first inscription marks the alliance that the Gauls believed they contracted with the *Suleviae* or *Sylphs* <note>original: "Suleves ou Sylphides." Suleviae were local Celtic goddesses; Sylphs were elemental air spirits in 17th-century occultism.</note>; and the words that follow, *who attend to our cares* <note>original Latin: "quæ curam nostram agunt"</note>, allow us to judge the love and gratitude of these "invisible mistresses," and with what ardor they sought to please the charitable philosophers of the earth who applied themselves to immortalizing them. These are the very words of the *Count of Gabalis*. I do not take it upon myself to prove that the Gauls, in allying with the Sylphs, had motives as elevated as...

On this basis, I derive *Moras Moratis* from *Mora* <note>original: Μωρὰ</note>, which in the decline of the Greek language <note>The author refers to the transition from Classical to Medieval or Byzantine Greek.</note> signified a Fairy or a Sorceress: terms that express the very nature of the imaginary deities in question. Furthermore, as they believed that male *Sylphs* <note>Elemental spirits of the air, often described in early modern occultism and folklore as supernatural beings inhabiting the atmosphere.</note> and female *Sylphs* married amongst themselves and had truly *Sylph* children who continued and multiplied the species, they also convinced themselves that the children born from the embraces of a *Sylph* and a terrestrial man were themselves terrestrial and took after the nature of their father. And so, these descendants—following their bloodline as far as it might extend and wherever it flowed—far from keeping their birth secret or being ashamed of such an ambiguous origin, took pride not only in having a *Sylph* for a mother, but they even made a parade of the *Sylph* brothers and sisters that this *Sylph* mother gave them from her marriage to a *Sylph*. This entire doctrine is contained *as a whole* <note>original: "in globo"</note> in the very inscription I am explaining, as well as in the one from Luxembourg. If one wishes to see an inscription that develops and details this a little better, I need only produce the one found in Lower Germany, a short half-league from Andernach <note>A town in the Rhineland-Palatinate, Germany, known for its significant Roman history.</note>.

## TO THE JUNONES AND MATERNAL BROTHERS, THE SON OF INVINCIBLE FORTUNE.
<note>original: "JUNONIBUS. ET. MATERNIS FRATRIBUS. INVICTRICIS. FORTUNAE. FILIUS." In Roman religion, the "Junones" were the female counterparts to the "Genii," acting as guardian spirits for women; here, the author links them to the "Mothers" or "Matronae" of Gaulish and Germanic tradition.</note>

In addition to the consecration to the *Junones*—that is to say, to the Mothers, Matrons, Fates, etc., about whom I have already elaborated—this monument clearly contains the proof of everything I have just said; first, we see uterine brothers, <note>original: *maternis fratribus* — brothers born of the same mother.</note> who share the honor of the consecration. These uterine brothers are placed in parallel with the *Junones*: they were, consequently, of the same nature as the *Junones*. 2ndly. The person making the consecration was indeed the brother, by his mother, of those to whose glory he erected the monument; however, this religious act performed by this brother for his brothers attests that he regarded them as being not only of a rank, order, and nature above his own, but also that he himself was merely an ordinary man. 3rdly. The one who erects this monument identifies himself as the "son of Invincible Fortune." This "Invincible Fortune" can be nothing other than one of the Fates represented on the gold medal of Diocletian with the inscription *To the Victorious Fates*. <note>original: "Fatis Victricibus."</note> The Fates were themselves Destiny and Fortune, as I proved in the preceding chapter; it is therefore only in this sense that Fortune can be described as invincible and all-powerful, according to Virgil. Father Menetrier <note>Claude-François Ménestrier (1631–1705), a French Jesuit historian and expert in inscriptions.</note> reads the first line as *Silvano* instead of *Syleiano*, and the last line as *D.S.P.P.* <note>Abbreviation for the Latin "De Sua Pecunia Posuit," meaning "placed at his own expense."</note>; to tell the truth, this reading is good, but it does not appear to be the best, and nothing compels one to prefer it. One might even suspect that a lack of familiarity with the God Syleianus led people to mistake him for Silvanus, or the God Silvanus <note>The Roman god of forests and fields.</note>, whose name was on everyone’s lips. On the contrary, *the Sulfes and the Suleves* <note>Gallic female deities or nymphs, often associated with water or protection.</note> authorize the reading of Syleianus; the "Y" of this word is visibly the "U" of similar words, which all derive from the Greek <term>hyle <note>original: ὕλη</note></term>, which means wood. This has a true connection with the Carpenters of the Inscription, who worked almost exclusively with wood; whereas the God Silvanus is always written with an "I," and appears to have been merely a god transplanted into the Gallic lands.

Whatever the case may be, Silvanus was finally admitted among the number of Gallic Deities: the example of the Romans, and the frequent commerce the Gauls were obliged to have with them, made this matter succeed, where a multitude of other similar Gods should have caused it to fail. The resemblance of his name to that of Syleianus smoothed over the difficulties; not to mention that he was perhaps, in truth, really Syleianus, being by nature the God of the Woods and Gardens, and carrying a cypress as his symbol. (a)

One finds several Inscriptions in France in honor of Silvanus; I have even already given one: as his worship has nothing singular about it, nor anything pure—

## CHAPTER XXVI.

->*Continuation of the same subject. Explanation of the word Comedoves. Antiquity of the cult of the Maires, Mothers, Matrons, etc.*<-

I have perhaps expanded a bit too much in the explanation of the first inscription: but I should be pardoned in favor of the insights I have shed on a subject that had not yet received any. One should even be grateful to me for having spared the reader the boredom of a longer reading by suppressing many other proofs I could have added. Moreover, it is certain that I would never have thought to enter into the details of all the fantasies of the Gauls without the desire expressed to be informed about the nature, quality, and purpose of the deities who are the object of research by scholars.

> "...a new superstition, and imagined that there were certain Nymphs, who generally watched over the conduct of Provinces, and others who applied themselves to the salvation of Emperors, and even of private individuals, to whom they gave indifferently the name of *Matres* and *Matræ* <note>original: "Mothers." But these Divinities having first been worshiped in the countryside, they were received into the Cities with the same names that the Villagers had given them. Thus one reads in various Inscriptions, *Matribus Gallaicis* <note>To the Gallaic Mothers, referring to the region of Gallaecia in modern-day Spain and Portugal.</note>, *Dis Matrabus* <note>To the Mother Goddesses.</note>, and *Matris Augustis* <note>To the August Mothers.</note>, etc. Those who were imagined to be more closely attached to the preservation of the Emperors and their House had the title of *Matres Augustæ*, Mothers of the Augusts <note>The title "Augustus" was used by Roman Emperors; these "Mothers" were seen as divine protectors of the imperial line.</note>."

A large part of what Chorier <note>Nicolas Chorier (1612–1692) was a lawyer and historian known for his works on the history of the Dauphiné region.</note> says is based only on chimeras <term>chimeras: unfounded fantasies or myths created without evidence</term> created for his own pleasure: to refute them would be a waste of time, or involve tedious repetitions. Until now, scholars have been divided concerning that famous city of the Aedui <note>The Aedui were a powerful Gallic tribe allied with Rome.</note> that Caesar and Strabo call *Bibracte*. Samson, Monsieur d’Ablancourt, and several others believed that this city is today's Autun: but Monsieur Valois maintained with such authority that *Bibracte* was a place entirely different from Autun, that he has won over all opinions. He relied primarily on a passage from Eumenius: but I doubt that he understood his author. Here are the words of this Panegyrist <note>A "Panegyrist" is an orator who delivers a speech in praise of someone, in this case, a Roman Emperor.</note>;

# ON THE GAULS. Book IV. #

To do this well, one must remember that the city of Autun, near the end of the third century of the Church, suffered several times and at different periods everything that the fury of war can inflict upon an important and exposed place—one that received no aid from the Emperors, nor the Republic <note>Meaning the Roman State</note>, nor finally from any ally. Constantius and Constantine, moved by the pitiful state to which it was reduced, restored it, had superb public buildings constructed there, and established colleges and academies; above all, they relieved a large portion of the taxes it was obliged to pay every year, and remitted the taxes for five entire years that it owed. So many benefits from these Princes gave rise to the name *Flavia*, with which Autun was then honored; this name was that of the family of Constantius and Constantine <note>The Constantinian dynasty belonged to the Flavian clan (*gens Flavia*)</note>. It is unknown whether Autun itself took this name to show its gratitude to its benefactors, or if its benefactors added this grace to so many others they had granted it. The latter sentiment seems more probable, and there is ground to suppose it.

In any case, it is upon all of this that the panegyric of Eumenius turns, which ends with the words cited by Mr. Valois <note>Hadrianus Valesius, a prominent 17th-century historian and geographer</note>: but far from the orator's terms suggesting in the slightest that the city of *Bibracte* was a place distinct from the city of *Flavia*, I maintain that they formally signify that the same city, which was then called *Flavia*, was called *Julia Bibracte* in Caesar's time.

Indeed, Eumenius, after having said to Constantine that if he ever came to Autun, the citizens would not be able to...

Regarding the Apotheosis <note>The act of elevating a place or person to the status of a god.</note> of Cities, which these Inscriptions also bring into full light, it must be remembered that the intention of the Ancients was to dedicate, by this means, each City to a certain Divinity, whose name was sometimes the same as that of the City, and sometimes different. # RELIGION

<meta>catchword: Genius</meta>

<margin>
In the work of Cyril of Alexandria, *Against Julian*, Oration.
</margin>

Julian the Apostate <note>The Roman Emperor Julian (reigned 361–363 AD), who attempted to revive traditional polytheism after the empire had begun converting to Christianity.</note>, speaking of Mars, Minerva, and Mercury, maintained that these Divinities were the Ministers of a universal Creator who, possessing all perfections in a sovereign manner, communicated them diversely—and with measure and proportion—to each of them, by establishing them to watch over the protection of Nations. He argued that these Divinities, by virtue of their administration, cultivated the spirit of the peoples committed to their care, and influenced their morals and their temperament more or less, according to how much they participated in the perfections of the Sovereign Being. This was why, he said, that the:
» Gauls and the Germans were enterprising. <note>original Greek: "(a) Κελτοὺς μὲν καὶ Γερμανοὺς εἶναι θρασεῖς" – "The Celts and Germans are bold."</note>
» The Greeks and the Romans, civilized and sociable,
» although otherwise brave and warlike; the Egyptians
» so industrious and intelligent; and the Syrians at once
» cowardly, voluptuous, clever, fiery, and vain; but
» fit to learn all things. Now, it is visible
» that Julian clearly says here that Mars was the Patron,
» so to speak, and the Tutelary God of the Gauls and the
» Germans, just as Minerva was for the Greeks and the
» Romans, and Mercury for the Egyptians and the Syrians.

All this refinement of spirit <note>original: "rafinement d'esprit"</note> teaches us that, in effect, the character <note>original: "génie," referring to the *Genius Loci* or the inherent nature of a people.</note> of the Pagans was entirely in conformity with that of their National, Provincial, and Municipal Gods; they studied to form and raise their children based on the vices, excesses, or moral virtues of these deities.

The Gauls were not content with merely deifying their cities; they also celebrated their Dedication <note>The anniversary of a city's founding or the consecration of its walls.</note> every year. This custom had not yet been abolished toward the end of the seventh century, as it prompted the charity of Saint Eligius <note>Saint Eloy (c. 588–660 AD), a goldsmith and bishop known for his piety and missionary work in Gaul.</note> to speak out against this detestable abuse. (a)

Moreover, one must take care not to confuse the divinities we have just discussed with the Gods who, being the object of a singular cult in some city, made it famous—and from which these Gods often took their names. The Gods I am dealing with here were quite different. Every place and, so to speak, every bush had its God, and its particular God. Whereas the other Gods, whom I call Municipal <term>Municipal Gods: From the Latin *municipium*; deities specifically associated with a particular town or administrative district.</term> (b) according to an 
<margin>Minucius Felix, chapter 6.</margin>
ancient author, were mostly known everywhere; and were distinguished in certain places only by a flight of blindness and an excess of sacrilegious devotion, founded upon chance or the trickery of the Priests. One Author has happily gathered in this Epigram those famous cities with the Divinities revered there.

duties, as misunderstood as they were pushed too far, <margin>Wisdom 14:15 etc. <note>original: "Sap. 14. v. 15. &c." refers to the Book of Wisdom in the Vulgate Bible, which discusses the origins of idolatry through the mourning of the dead.</note></margin> were the source of false religions, according to the testimony of Scripture.

These duties could not fail to be strongly linked to Religion, since they were a consequence of it, or had served as its pretext and foundation. Also, one can be certain that whatever idea one held about the fate of the soul after this life—that is to say, whether one believed it followed the destruction of the body, or estimated that it survived it—one would have believed they were wounding Religion in one of its essential points by refusing the dead those marks of piety which nature inspired, and from which no one was exempt.

The care taken to perform these duties testified in favor of the <term>dogma</term> <note>In this context, a "dogma" refers to a settled point of belief or a fundamental principle of a faith system.</note> of the immortality of the soul; thus, one found few nations that were not persuaded of it. There were some, however, that were not; but they were few in number, and this small number must be counted as nothing. Thus, generally speaking, everyone agreed on the belief that souls did not die with the body; but people were divided on their fate, on the place where they passed to, and on the commerce they might maintain with the living.

Some placed souls, at least those of good people, in the sphere of the Moon; others in the <term>Poetic Hell</term> <note>The "Poetic Hell" refers to the classical underworld (Hades or Tartarus) as described by ancient Greek and Roman poets, rather than the theological concept of Hell in Christianity.</note>, and still others elsewhere. The Britons and the Gauls believed that death was but a passage to a life that had no end, and they sometimes made Heroes or demi-gods of the souls of their dead, especially those who had

<summary>The author argues that funerary rites are a universal religious impulse rooted in the belief in the soul's immortality. He notes that while different cultures, including the Gauls and Britons, disagreed on where the soul went, nearly all agreed that it survived the body.</summary>

<page-num>213</page-num>
<header>OF THE GAULS. Book V.</header>

...had the misfortune of being slaughtered in sacrifice. The Romans gave the name <term>Lemures</term> <note>In Roman mythology, the Lemures were the wandering and vengeful spirits of those who died a restless or untimely death, though the author notes the term was sometimes used more broadly.</note> to all the souls of the dead; but they distinguished two kinds of them: some were benevolent and peaceful, the others malevolent and restless. This distinction, however, was not so unique to the Romans that it was not common to almost all nations, especially the Gauls. But what deserves particular attention is that this distinction was the foundation and the motive for the marks of piety shown at funerals, on anniversaries, and at other times consecrated to honoring the memory of the dead.

Everything practiced on these various occasions was reduced to sacrifices of chosen animals, which had to be black; <note>In ancient rites, black animals were traditionally offered to deities of the underworld or the dead, symbolizing the darkness of the earth and the afterlife.</note> to libations, to perfumes, to funeral meals, and finally to mausoleums or tombs, some of which took the form of Altars. All these expenses sometimes had as their object the <term>Inferior Gods</term> <note>These are the "chthonic" deities who ruled the underworld, such as Pluto or Proserpina.</note> or those of the Underworld, but more often the <term>Shadows</term> <note>The "Shadows" (or *Manes*) refers to the spirits of the deceased, imagined as shade-like versions of their living selves.</note> of the dead themselves. The inferior gods were honored so that they might be propitious and favorable to the souls of the relatives or friends of those making the offerings. The Shadows themselves were honored either as a testimony to their virtue, so that they might act as benevolent gods always ready to hear prayers, or finally to appease them; for they were regarded not only as the authors of almost all the evils of life, but also as having a strong inclination to harm mortals.

The ceremonies that the Gauls observed in their funerals were pompous and magnificent. They had the body of the deceased burned, along with everything he had most cherished during his life; slaves, <term>clients</term> <note>In Gaulish society, these were free men who had pledged their loyalty and service to a powerful lord in exchange for protection.</note>, animals, precious furniture—nothing was spared. They no doubt used this language to dazzle those unfortunate souls destined to serve as victims to their bloodthirsty Gods, so that they might take comfort in their fate; and that instead of the mortal blow they expected, they might envision the deification with which they were being fed.

I have said that the Gauls threw into the pyre what the deceased had most cherished: this is justified by some tombs discovered recently. Before proceeding further, it must be noted that the custom of burning living men with the body of the deceased had come to an end before Caesar's arrival in the Gauls. However, as for the practice of burning the dead, it was perhaps the only one that prevailed among the Gauls while they were buried in the errors of Paganism. Indeed, Sidonius Apollinaris <note>Gaius Sollius Apollinaris Sidonius (c. 430 – 489 AD) was a poet, diplomat, and bishop, and is one of the most important authors of 5th-century Gaul.</note>, speaking of the field where his grandfather had been buried, says that even in his time it was covered with so much ash and bone escaping from the pyres erected there every day, that there was no longer any room to dig the foundations for another sepulcher. It was for this reason that St. Eloi fought with all his might against this impious and superstitious cult, saying: *let no one believe in funeral pyres.* <note>original: "nullus in pyras credat"</note>

supposing further either that this Philosopher had never existed, or at least that he had never lent credit to this sentiment—of which he is made the author against all reason—I ask, with what eye would Valerius Maximus then have regarded the Gauls? A fine question: as fools. Indeed, can a sentiment held by those **trouser-wearers** <note>A derogatory Roman reference to the Gauls, based on their "braccae" (trousers), which the Romans considered a mark of the uncivilized compared to the toga.</note> who dared to take Rome, besiege the Capitol, and so often bring the Republic to the brink of ruin, be anything but the sentiment of fools? But because Pythagoras adopted <term>Metempsychosis</term> <note>The philosophical concept of the soul migrating into a new body after death; reincarnation.</note> and had his entire School receive it, it is no longer the same thing; it has lost all that was dishonorable about it, it has changed its nature, and has fortunately saved the trouser-wearers from the odious epithets that Valerius Maximus would have given them.

But it is far from the case that the Gauls ever invented, followed, or received the system of Metempsychosis. Here are proofs stronger than everything that could be said by Authors who spoke only through false inferences.

,, Does this other life in the other world have anything in common with **Metempsychosis** <note>The philosophical belief in the transmigration of the soul into a new body after death.</note>? Could these **ledgers**, these **obligations**, these **receipts**, serve souls who were passing into other bodies, whether of men or of beasts? Even if one stubbornly persisted in claiming so, does one consider that these souls, as soon as they had passed into whatever other body you please, were no longer the same persons whom these **ledgers** and **receipts** concerned? Furthermore, would those who carried their devotion so far as to wish to die with those they loved, in order to live with them, ( *a* ) have committed such a folly if they had the slightest inkling of **Metempsychosis**? How could they flatter themselves with the hope of going to live with those into whose funeral pyres they threw themselves, if they believed that both parties, upon leaving this life, were to take on other bodies—whether of beasts, or men, or women, or plants; some in one corner of the world, others in another? Indeed, what likelihood is there that the Gauls, a people so jealous of their liberty, would have braved death only to risk receiving as their lot the body—I do not say of plants or beasts—but merely of slaves, or even of women, over whom they held the **power of life and death** <note>The author refers to the ancient legal right (*jus vitae necisque*) held by the head of a household over his dependents.</note>.

A fairly common custom established in the Gauls, and reported by **Valerius Maximus** <note>A Roman writer of the 1st century AD famous for collecting historical anecdotes.</note>, contradicts Metempsychosis no less; and I cannot understand, given this, how that author could have attributed such a chimerical belief to our ancestors. (b) This philosophy, I admit, was somewhat peculiar; but it was far less greedy and usurious than that of the peoples who never deferred the payment deadline to the next world, and who demanded it in this one with the utmost rigor. The Gauls, therefore, did not hold to **Metempsychosis** <note>reincarnation</note> at all, but only the immortality of the soul; some authors have only claimed that they admitted to **Metempsychosis** because they viewed this life as a necessary consequence of the other—an absurd supposition, the falsehood of which I have just uncovered. Furthermore, the **Druids** <note>The high-ranking priestly and intellectual class of ancient Celtic societies.</note>, who were the teachers of the nation, followed the common notions of right reason and the traces of a tradition that went back to the most remote ages. Now, these notions, this tradition—everything decided in favor of the **Dogma** of immortality and contained no idea of **Metempsychosis**.

In confirmation of all this, one may add what the Gauls thought of those who had served in this world as victims to their Gods; they maintained that their souls were **deified**, that is to say, raised into Heaven to be happy there. The Gauls did not know what it was to admit souls of a different nature; the only difference they admitted consisted in the state of one or the other. According to this doctrine, the souls that were not deified (to use their language) enjoyed a more or less comfortable life in a place destined for them, in proportion to the care they had taken in this life to provide against the needs to which they might be exposed: whereas the others lived in Heaven, in the very life of the Gods.

### CHAPTER IV.
#### *The infernal Gods of the Gauls were Venus, Mars & Mercury. Reasons for this choice.*

An Inscription found in the forest of Belême teaches us that the Gauls, just like the Greeks and the Romans, had **infernal gods** <note>Deities associated with the underworld or the realm of the dead.</note>, and who they were;

->SACRED<- <note>original: "SACRVM"</note>
->TO THE INFERNAL GODS<- <note>original: "DIIS INFERIS"</note>
->TO VENUS<- <note>original: "VENERI"</note>
->TO MARS AND<- <note>original: "MARTI ET"</note>
->TO MERCURY<- <note>original: "MERCVRIO"</note>

Nothing proves better the difference, and if I dare say, the independence of the Religion of the Gauls from all others, than this Monument. For although one notices a fair amount of variety in **Paganism** <note>A term used here to describe the various polytheistic religions of antiquity.</note> regarding the different classes of Gods—some counting four; **Plato** <note>The Greek philosopher (c. 428–348 BC) whose works influenced later Roman and European thought.</note> and the Romans three, and others only two—nevertheless, all agreed never to place **Mars** <note>The god of war, usually associated with the upper world and physical conflict.</note> in the rank of the infernal deities. It is only the Gauls alone who did so; and at that time they gave him the surname **Olloudius**, as stated in an Inscription found at Aix-en-Provence.

### WILLINGLY AND DESERVEDLY FULFILLED HER VOW <note>Latin: "V. S. L. M." stands for *Votum Solvit Libens Merito*, a standard formula on Roman-era altars.</note>

That is to say, Vigilia Metia, Daughter of Massa, has heartily fulfilled the vow she had made to Mars Olloudius. This is the only monument that speaks of Mars Olloudius.

Olloudius means murderer, and comes ( *a* ) from the Greek *olluo* or *ollumi* <note>original: ὀλλύω or ὀλλυμι</note>, to kill, to put to death, or to ruin. Homer, instead of Olloudius, uses the word *oulos* <note>original: οὖλος</note> in the same sense; and calls Mars "baleful and murderous Mars" <note>original Greek: Ἄρης οὖλος</note>. Indeed, that was his character; and his sole occupation consisted only in unceasingly repopulating the Underworld with new inhabitants.

But of all the reasons they had to regard Mars as an infernal Divinity, the primary one was that in the heat of combat, and in all the perils where their lives were threatened, they vowed to Mars a sacrifice of slaves, which they offered on the spot, or which they never failed to fulfill; in the belief they held that the life of one man can be neither redeemed nor paid for except by that of another man.

This last reflection perfectly develops the true meaning of the Inscription of Vigilia Metia: she had perhaps run some great peril where her life had been in danger; she wished to escape it; she vowed slaves or clients. Having escaped death, she fulfilled her vow. In this sense, the four initial letters **V. S. L. From all this, it is easy to infer the reasons the Gauls had for counting Mars among the gods of the underworld, and the interest they had in making him favorable to them in the next life. We can also see the basis they had for hoping that this God would be favorable to them after their death, since they were so prodigal with their lives and held them so cheaply in order to do him honor.

It is not so difficult to explain why the Gauls placed Mercury in the class of the underworld Gods: we have already gone into such great detail in demonstrating that **Teutates** <note>A major Celtic deity, often identified by Roman writers as Mercury, though sometimes as Mars or, as here, Pluto.</note> was the true **Pluto** <note>The Roman god of the underworld and the dead.</note>, from whom the Gauls claimed their origin, that one could not recall the proofs we have used without immediately grasping the motives and views our Ancestors had in placing Mercury among the infernal Divinities.

So as not to retrace our steps or use repetitions, we shall employ only a few descriptions that perfectly mark the authority Mercury held in the Underworld. The first concerns all Nations and is taken from **Apuleius** <note>A 2nd-century Roman philosopher and writer known for "The Golden Ass."</note>, who testifies that it was customary to represent this God with one side of his face white and the other black, governing the heads of the dog **Cerberus** <note>The multi-headed dog that guarded the entrance to the underworld.</note> at his will, and holding in his right hand a green palm branch, which he used as a rod to lead souls to the Underworld. (*a*)

<margin>Justus Lipsius <note>Justus Lipsius (1547–1606) was a renowned Flemish humanist and scholar of Roman history.</note>, Vol. 1, *Select Works* <note>original: "Electorum," referring to his *Electorum Libri Duo*</note>, chapter 11.</margin>
Beyond that, there was an ancient Decree of the Senate, which required that public Games be consecrated and united with Acts of Religion. Also, Ausonius <note>Decimus Magnus Ausonius (c. 310–395 AD) was a Roman poet and teacher from Gaul.</note> observed that of the four famous Games of Greece, two were dedicated to the Gods, and two to Heroes or demi-gods.

If from these principles we come to our Inscription, one will find that it contains four truths important and necessary to History: the first, the Dedication of a place sacred in itself, the *proscenium* <term>proscenium: the stage area of an ancient theater, located in front of the scenery</term>; the second, the consecration of the *proscenium* to the God Mercury, which rendered it even more sacred; the third, the purpose of the consecration, which was the glory of the House of the Emperor; *in honor of the Divine House* <note>original: "in honorem Domus divinæ," a standard Roman formula of loyalty to the Imperial family</note>: which added a degree of inviolability to the *proscenium*, undoubtedly much greater than that which came to it from the nature of the place, or from the majesty of Mercury; finally, the last was the destination of the *proscenium*, which was the burial place of some person of note, perhaps from the family of the Emperor; *To the divine spirits of the dead in honor of the Divine House* <note>original: "Diis manibus in honorem Domus divinæ." The phrase "Diis manibus" (To the Manes) indicates a funerary monument</note>. This was another degree of sanctity and inviolability of a different nature, which adds value, so to speak, to all the others.

Between all the consequences that I can draw from all these different principles, I insist only on the one which relates solely to the subject I am treating; namely, that Mercury was one of the infernal gods <note>In this context, "infernal" refers to the "underworld" (chthonic) deities who watched over the dead</note> of the Gauls, whether one considers the care they took to consecrate to him all the ground where they wished to be buried, or whether one pays attention to the faith and confidence they had in his help.

## CHAPTER V.

### *On Tombs consecrated "under the adze" <note>original: "sub Ascia"</note>. Different opinions on the meaning of this formula.*

Nothing is more common in some provinces of France, primarily those that formerly composed Gaul, than inscriptions on tombs consecrated **UNDER THE ADZE** <note>original: "SUB ASCIA"</note>. These terms and the figure of the *Adze* <note>original: "Ascia"</note>, which is very often found engraved with the inscription on the tomb, have occupied most of our best antiquarians <note>Historical scholars who study ancient artifacts and inscriptions.</note>; and I do not know if everything they have provided on the subject is enough to satisfy a solid and discerning mind.

<margin>This is not the true meaning of the Law.</margin>
What creates the difficulty is the meaning usually given to the word *Ascia*, which is rendered as an adze <note>original: "doloire," a tool similar to a broad-axe or hatchet used for smoothing wood or stone.</note>: and indeed it looks much like one, as proven by most of the *Adzes* <note>original: "Ascias"</note> we have had engraved. From this, it is inferred that the use of the adze in tombs had established a custom contrary to one of the Laws of the Twelve Tables <note>The earliest code of Roman law, dating to the 5th century BCE, which formed the foundation of Roman jurisprudence.</note>, which forbids, it is said, polishing a funeral pyre with an adze (*a*).

Those who wished to save the honor of the Law have forged a meaning foreign to the word *Ascia*, and have claimed that it was composed of a negative alpha and *shadow* <note>original: "σκιά" (skia), a Greek word.</note>; as if to say, "uncovered and without shadow." Thus, "to dedicate under the Adze" <note>original: "sub Ascia dedicare"</note> was to build a tomb or sepulcher exposed to the air, *under the open sky* <note>original: "sub dio"</note>, and which would have no shadow.

(*a*) Thou shalt not polish the funeral pyre with an adze. <note>original: "Rogum Ascia ne poleito." This law was intended to limit the expense and luxury of funerals by preventing the wood of the pyre from being overly finished.</note>

This monument was found at Saint-Just in Lyon in the month of November, 1714. It was a marble block one foot square. This is how I read the inscription: <note>original: "DIIS MANIBVS ET MEMORIÆ ÆTERNAE HYLATIS DIMACHERO SIVE ASSIDARIO, PALMARVM SEPTEM, RVDE DONATO. ERMAIS CONJVX CONJVGI CARISSIMO PONENDVM CVRAVIT, ET SVB ASCIA DEDICAVIT"</note>

"This monument is consecrated to the **Spirits of the Dead** <note>original: "Dieux Manes"</note> and to the memory of Hylas. Having won victory seven times, either fighting with two swords or seated upon a chariot, he was honored with the **Rod of <term>Manumission</term>** <note>The formal act of releasing a slave from their master's control; for a gladiator, this meant receiving the "rudis" or wooden sword as a sign of their freedom and retirement from the arena.</note>. Hermais, his wife, saw to the placement of this tomb for her most dear husband, and dedicated it **under the <term>Ascia</term>** <note>The adze, a woodworking tool frequently depicted on Gallo-Roman tombs, the meaning of which remains a subject of historical debate.</note>."

To properly understand this inscription, one must observe:

1st. That Hylas must have been a gladiator.

2nd. That the word *Memoria* <note>Memory</note> can signify a sepulcher or tomb just as well as the French term *Memoire*.

3rd. That the letters **P. VII.** can equally signify *Palmæ septimæ* <note>The seventh palm/victory</note>, according to this passage from **Petronius**: *If the Green jacket won the first palm in the recent Circus games*; or else *Palmarum septem* <note>Of seven palms/victories</note> according to **Cicero**, **Lampridius**, **Apuleius**, and other authors whom it is unnecessary to cite.

4th. The **<term>Rudis</term>** was a rod or wooden sword given to gladiators to honor them and exempt them from practicing such a dangerous profession in the future.

Others have imagined that the *Ascia* in question was a specific adze <note>The French *doloire* refers to a long-handled adze or hatchet used for smoothing wood or stone.</note>, which persons of modest fortune used to make their sepulchers—which they constructed only of brick—smoother and more polished.

longer than the adze <term>ascia</term> <note>A tool similar to an axe but with the blade set at a right angle to the handle, used for smoothing wood.</note>, it is not found in any of the monuments that have appeared until now. Furthermore, one will never persuade anyone that it was possible in any country to use a scraper <term>rabot</term> or mixing tool <term>gâche</term> to take mortar and observe the ceremony mentioned by Father Menestrier; the length the handle of the adze <term>ascia</term> must have had, and the entire shape of the adze itself, did not allow it to be used for this purpose. 3°. Could the scraper or mixing tool of the Gallic masons have had the shape of the adze <term>ascia</term> found on tombs? As this is something eyes can judge better than anything one could say, let us examine and compare everything well together; and one will see that it was morally impossible for the adze <term>ascia</term> to serve for mixing <note>literally "thinning" or "tempering"</note> lime. 4°. Who told Father Menestrier that the scraper or mixing tool of the Gallic masons was made of iron and not of wood, as it is in most of our provinces? 5°. As for the authority of Vitruvius <note>A 1st-century BC Roman architect whose work "De Architectura" was the standard reference for classical building techniques.</note>, it counts for nothing here: this author is known for having created an infinite number of new words; and there is hardly anyone who would vouch for *ascia* being a proper Latin word in the sense used by Father Menestrier. 6°. Furthermore, Vitruvius never said that there was a mason's tool named *ascia*; and it is a strange abuse of this author’s text.

The <term>ascia</term> <note>A tool often depicted on ancient Gallic tombs, resembling a cross between a hatchet and a hoe.</note> which has been taken until now for a <term>doloire</term> <note>A large broad-axe or carpenter’s adze used for squaring timber.</note> and a tool for a carpenter or mason, is nothing of the sort; (a) it is, on the contrary, an instrument for moving the earth, which corresponds to the hoe and mattock of our vine-growers. Here at last is the meaning of the <term>ascia</term> <note>The "ascia" is a tool frequently depicted on Roman-era gravestones, often accompanied by the formula "sub ascia dedicavit" (dedicated under the ascia). Its exact purpose was a major subject of debate among 18th-century antiquarians.</note> found on sepulchral stones, clarified and fixed: but that is not all; the Gauls had two kinds of *ascia*, according to the difference or the quality of the terrain where they constructed their tombs: if it was in a field or a stony place, they used an *ascia* or sharp, pointed tool, like the pick used by masons, excavators, or pioneers today: if it was in good earth, they used an *ascia* or iron instrument to open it that was wide and flat, like an overturned spade, or like a curved hoe, which vineyard workers still use to work the vines. This latter form of *ascia* is very much in vogue in <term>Languedoc</term> <note>A historic province in Southern France known for its Roman heritage and viticulture.</note>, where it bears the name *assado*, as I have already mentioned.

Up to this point, I have only described the side of the *ascia* that served to move and dig the earth, which was indeed the most significant part; the other side, which corresponded to the first and crossed the handle like a hammer, also had the shape of a half-hammer, and it served to break off the points of living rock that protruded into the pit being dug, or to knock down and bring away the stones and pebbles that had the same effect and were only half-exposed.

These two types of *ascia* are often found engraved upon the tombs of the Gauls: we see the first not only on the stone and the Inscription of <term>St. Ferriol</term> <note>St. Ferréol; the author refers to a specific archaeological find previously discussed where the tool's shape led to its misidentification as a Christian cross.</note>, of which we have spoken, and which was mistaken for a Cross; but also above an Inscription found at <term>Lyon</term> <note>original: "Lion"</note>, which <term>Gruter</term> <note>Jan Gruter (1560–1627), a Renaissance scholar famous for his "Corpus Inscriptionum," a massive collection of ancient Roman inscriptions.</note> has given us.

...speaking according to Dom Montfaucon <note>Bernard de Montfaucon (1655–1741) was a Benedictine monk and a foundational figure in the field of archaeology, known for his multi-volume work "L'antiquité expliquée."</note>, the <term>Suovetaurilia</term> <note>original: "Suovetaurilia" — an ancient Roman purification sacrifice consisting of a pig (*sus*), a sheep (*ovis*), and a bull (*taurus*).</note> of these Nations was performed for the lustration <note>A ritual of purification involving a procession and sacrifices.</note>, or the expiation of fields, lands, armies, Cities, and several other things; to sanctify them, or to expiate them, or to purify them, and to attract the protection of the Gods.

It must nevertheless be admitted in good faith that, although the Gauls were themselves the authors and inventors of the consecration of sepulchers <term>under the adze</term> <note>original: "sub ascia" — a common Gallo-Roman funerary formula. The "ascia" was a mason's tool, and the phrase likely signified that the tomb was dedicated while still under construction, perhaps to claim legal or religious protections.</note>, they imitated almost all the ceremonies observed by the Romans, or more accurately the Etrurians <note>The Etruscans, a civilization of ancient Italy whose religious and architectural practices heavily influenced Rome.</note>, at the founding of Cities. One may judge this by what <margin>Plutarch, *Life of Romulus*. Ovid, *Fasti*, Book 4.</margin> Plutarch and Ovid have written of it; of which here is the summary.

A round pit was dug, into which were thrown the firstfruits of all things that men legitimately eat as good, and naturally as necessary; and each person added a handful of earth brought from the land from which he had come. After this, the perimeter was traced with a bronze plowshare, hitched to a white bull and a heifer of the same color. In the place where the gates were to be made, they suspended the plow and carried it across without continuing the furrow. As they traced the furrows, they threw flowers into them, and then earth to cover them. The entire ceremony concluded with the erection of an Altar, upon which the bull and the heifer were sacrificed. This ceremony was religiously observed by all Roman Colonies before laying the foundations of a City.

The partitioning of fields is quite curious and sheds light on the subject we are treating. Boundary markers were planted, at the foundations of which some placed nothing, while others threw in either ashes, coals, broken pots, shattered glass, burned bones, lime, or plaster: in certain places, it was a law to plant inverted bottles there. <margin>Father Menestrier, Dissertation 3. <note>Claude-François Menestrier (1631–1705) was a Jesuit historian and expert in heraldry and antiquities.</note></margin>
After this, oil was poured onto the <term>Termini</term> <note>original: "Termes" — boundary markers often personified by the god Terminus, who protected land divisions.</note>, they were covered with some veil, and decorated with garlands and crowns. This, however, was only done after a sacrifice, and after having poured the blood of the victim into the pit of the boundary stone. At this effusion or sprinkling, the Priest had to be veiled; besides this blood, incense, grain, honey, wine, and several other things were thrown into these hollows, to which they set fire; and while the fire consumed them, they placed, erected, and firmly secured these stones. (b)

I have said that some of the ceremonies I described were observed by the Greeks and the Romans in the construction of their sepulchers. The Gauls, on the contrary, when they consecrated a tomb <term>sub ascia</term> <note>original: "under the adze." This phrase is frequently found on Gallo-Roman funerary monuments, though its exact ritual meaning remains a subject of scholarly debate; it likely refers to a tomb being consecrated while still under construction or protected by a specific legal-religious status.</note>, observed all the ceremonies that the Etruscans or Tuscans practiced at the foundation of Cities; and it is this which constituted the distinction and the specific character of these sepulchers, as I shall demonstrate.

1. The first ceremony of the Etruscans, and of the Romans after them, when founding Cities, was to dig a circular pit. The sepulchers of the Gauls were, by their nature, nothing more than a very deep pit. All those unearthed until now justify this truth. The pit was sometimes adorned with circular masonry; even whole stones have been found in the pit, hollowed out in a circle, containing the ashes of the dead and other items unique to the Gallic Nation.

2. He who was charged with offering sacrifices, whether to consult the Gods or to win their favor in the construction of Cities, had to be veiled. Julius Marcianus, in the sepulcher consecrated **under the adze**, for which we have provided the illustration,

3. We have seen that the Romans threw flowers and the first fruits of all things that men legitimately eat, either into the furrows or into the round pit that they dug specifically for this purpose. But the Gauls observed all this, not only during the construction of the sepulchers, but also every year, on the day they celebrated the anniversary of someone's death, which they called the **birthday** <note>original: "jour natal." In Roman and Gallic tradition, the *dies natalis* or "birthday" often referred to the anniversary of a death or the dedication of a monument, celebrating the transition to the afterlife.</note>. An Inscription found in Nice contains a detail of these kinds of ceremonies, which is sure to pique the curiosity of the Reader. Laïs erects and consecrates a Statue to the memory of Publius Petreius, son of Publius, and gives a fund of twelve thousand <term>sesterces</term> <note>The sesterce was a standard unit of currency in the Roman Empire; twelve thousand represented a significant endowment for the perpetual maintenance of a ritual.</note> to the society of the <term>Centoniers</term> <note>original: "Centoniers." A guild or "college" of craftsmen, usually associated with making heavy cloth or acting as a fire brigade.</note>, (a) the income from which would be used for the expenses of the feast with which she wished to honor this dedication: on the other hand, the College of Centoniers binds itself to offer every year in perpetuity, a sacrifice of grains or flour and cakes, on the fifth of the Ides of April <note>April 9th.</note>, the birthday of Quadratus, when his ashes had been placed in the tomb: and to hold a feast in the Temple according to custom, during which they would be crowned with roses, as would the Statue of Publius Petreius.

It was the same for the consecration of tombs *under the adze* <term>sub ascia</term> <note>A common phrase found on Gallo-Roman tombs, often accompanied by a carving of an adze (a woodworking tool). That ceremony was not within their jurisdiction; their sex forbade it to them; it was necessary to have recourse to men, and to entrust to them a religious act that was forbidden to them by nature itself. This is why Catia, in the Inscription preceding this one, states clearly that she had herself erected a Monument to honor the memory of her daughter; however, she is careful not to continue in the same tone: for instead of saying that she also consecrated it *under the adze* <term>sub ascia</term> <note>A common Gallo-Roman funerary formula. Its exact meaning is debated, but it often refers to a tomb being dedicated while still under construction or under a specific legal protection ritual.</note>; she simply says that it was consecrated *under the adze*; "this Stone was dedicated under the adze." <note>original Latin: *hoc Saxum sub ascia dedicatum est.*</note>

We further gather from this Inscription, and from the low-relief of the Lion where Julius Marcianus himself consecrates a tomb *under the adze* for himself, for his wife, and all his posterity, that all men were, so to speak, born-priests to fulfill this function, and that there was no need to have recourse to the Druids <note>The high-ranking priestly class in ancient Celtic societies.</note> to perform it; nor was it necessary to be destined by choice or by status to the service of some Divinity, Temple, Oracle, or Altar.

This is all that a deep and serious attention has allowed me to notice regarding the similarities between the ceremonies of tombs dedicated *under the adze*, and the ceremonies observed by the Ancients at the founding of Cities. I have indeed found two other very similar traits: but the uprightness and good faith I profess oblige me to warn those who look upon this Work that these traits are not so unique to the tombs of the Gauls that they do not also apply to those of the Romans.

6°. The Etrurians <note>An ancient Italian civilization that heavily influenced Roman religious and legal customs.</note> and the Romans, who took pride in imitating them, always consecrated with ceremony a space of land which they called the *Pomerium* <term>Pomœrium</term> <note>A sacred, religious boundary around a city, distinct from its physical walls, within which certain activities were restricted.</note> or *Prosimurium*, which ran all around the walls and ramparts, where it was strictly forbidden to live or to farm.

IN 1710, as new foundations were being laid in the Abbey of St. Laumer of Blois <note>A Benedictine monastery in Blois, France, now known as the Church of Saint-Nicolas.</note>, there was discovered at a depth of ten or twelve feet a small brick vault in the shape of a furnace, one and a half feet high, with a circumference of only three feet on the interior. The body of the vault was round, formed into an arch, neatly coated on the inside with cement and on the outside with a kind of plaster, and set upon a square base; at the four corners of which some small ornament was observed. The vault, which was well-sealed on all sides except for a small opening that had been fashioned like a door through which a hand could easily pass; the vault, I say, contained three figures of Women cast in a mold, of a material similar to that from which tobacco pipes are made <note>This refers to white kaolin clay, commonly used for Gallo-Roman figurines discovered in Central France.</note>. The principal of these figures is a woman seated on a high-backed chair woven of rushes or wicker. The back of the chair wraps around the sides of this woman and rises to the base of her neck. This person’s hair is styled in well-arranged locks, twisted in coils and tiers that diminish in size, forming a kind of pyramid atop the head. She is dressed modestly and holds pressed against her

The crux of the difficulty is explaining what all this signifies. At first glance at these figures, one would say they represent Gaulish women who died in childbirth <note>original: "en couches". Archaeological theories of the 18th century often tried to find literal, biographical reasons for grave goods before broader symbolic interpretations became standard.</note>: but their great number and the various provinces where they are found do not allow us to rely on a conjecture that has only appearance as its guarantee; furthermore, the horse bones mixed with the bones of other animals suggest that these graves could just as well be the graves of men as the graves of women.

<margin>
Dom Montfaucon, *Antiquity [Explained]*, Supplement, Vol. 5, p. 142.

A learned antiquarian <note>Referring again to Bernard de Montfaucon (1655–1741), a Benedictine monk whose massive 15-volume work was the standard reference for ancient objects.</note>, speaking of these figures, offers a sentiment that deserves to be reported, although he does not dare to dwell on it; "Someone will perhaps say," he writes,
> "that this woman holding her little child is Mother Earth, who raises and nourishes us, and who receives us into her bosom after our death."
> "This appears plausible," adds the same author; "but to know if the ancient Gauls thought thus when they placed these figures in the tombs is a question difficult to decide."

It is true that it is a difficult question to decide, since we find no passage that clarifies it in either the authors or the monuments of antiquity. But could we not assume it, since it is so plausible? It remains certain that the Ancients represented the Earth in the form of a woman who held in each hand a small figure, also of a woman: these were, they said, Nature and Matter, which concurred with the Earth in the production of all [things].

(a) What prevents us after this from believing that the Woman whom the Gauls enclosed in their tombs was the Earth; and that the two children were the beings returning after death into the womb from which they had emerged? That this womb, which was the Earth, took back the *matter* and the *nature* that she had lent. That matter and nature were nothing other than the *body* and the *spirit* of those who died. Finally, that when this Woman held only one child, she was the Earth, who, after having absorbed and purified all that was material in men, preserved their *nature*—that is to say, their *spirit*; that she sustained it, and made it experience and taste the true state of immortality: a particular dogma of the Nation? <note>The Gauls were famous in antiquity for their belief in the "transmigration of souls" (reincarnation), believing that death was merely a transition to another life.</note>

<margin>Roman Questions 23.</margin>
The Romans, according to Plutarch, always observed the law established by Numa Pompilius <note>The legendary second king of Rome, credited with many of the city's religious institutions.</note>, of going to buy at the Temple of the Goddess Libitina—who was herself none other than Venus—all the things that were necessary for funerals. (a) Regarding which this Author says that Numa had perhaps made this law so that the Romans would familiarize themselves with funeral pomps, and would not regard the ceremonies as impure and defiled; or rather so that they would always remember that the same Divinity who presided over the conception of men also presided over their death, and that everything that comes by way of generation is subject to corruption. At Delphi, he adds, there is a Statue of Venus *Epithymbia* <note>original: "Epithymbia"; a Greek epithet meaning "upon the tombs" or "funerary."</note>, to which the <term>Manes: the ancestral spirits or souls of the deceased</term> are called to make libations to them. (b)

<margin>In *Life of Numa*.</margin>
This same Author also says elsewhere that *Libitina* presided over the last duties rendered to the dead; and that notwithstanding that some people took *Libitina* for Proserpina <note>The queen of the Underworld; the Roman equivalent of Persephone.</note>, the most Learned maintained that she was Venus.

If I had not already given proofs of this constant truth, these two inscriptions alone would suffice to bring it into full light; since the first is purely Greek; and *Tillu* is visibly the *telos* <note>original Greek: τέλος</note> of the Greeks; in place of which the Low Bretons say *Tellou*, from which we have formed the <term>Taille</term> <note>A significant land tax in pre-revolutionary France; the author is drawing a linguistic line from ancient Greek to modern French taxation.</note>, which has the same meaning.

One must not believe, for all that, that the difference between the words of these inscriptions implies a difference in their meaning: both contain the idea of *Tribute*—

(a) This is also the opinion of the Reverend Father de Montfaucon.

buried the dead, so that they might be admitted into 
Charon’s boat <note>the ferryman of the Greek underworld</note> and have the means to pay their fare: 
without which they were excluded and condemned to wander 
on the banks of the Styx <note>the principal river of the underworld</note> without ever being able 
to cross it. For this purpose, the Egyptians put 
a gold piece in the mouth of the deceased, 
which is still found in mummies today.

<margin>Dionysius of Halicarnassus, *Roman Antiquities*, book 4, page 220.</margin>
The Romans, besides perhaps a similar coin <note>referring to "Charon’s obol," a coin placed in the mouth of the dead to pay for passage to the afterlife</note>, were obliged to cast another into the treasury of the Temple of Venus *Libitina* <note>the Roman goddess of funerals and burials</note>, located in a sacred grove, in order to obey a law that Servius Tullius <note>the legendary sixth king of Rome</note> had enacted.

I am not quite sure if the Gauls observed either custom; it is nonetheless certain that in 1612, during the demolition of an ancient Palace of the Counts of Anjou, two bodies were found in the same tomb, each holding a medal in their right hand—one of Germanicus <note>a famous Roman general, 15 BC – 19 AD</note>, the other of the Tyrant Magnentius <note>a 4th-century usurper of the Roman Empire</note>; but nothing can be concluded from this discovery, because it does not appear that these skeletons were of any Gaulish origin. It is more probable that the tribute mentioned in our inscriptions—which are half Greek and half Gaulish—consisted of the expense the Celts incurred by having the figure of Venus enclosed with their ashes. They called her *Infera* <note>original Latin: "Infera," meaning "of the Underworld"</note>, while the Romans called her *Libitina*, and the Greeks *Ambologera* <note>original Greek: "Ἀμβολογήρα," meaning "she who postpones old age"</note>.

<margin>Aelian, *Varia Historia*, book 2, 35. Pitiscus, *Lexicon of Antiquities*, entry: Death.</margin>
All that has just been said proves unbeatably that the Gauls personified Sleep and Death, just as other nations did, and held them to be brothers; this was also the idea held by the Ancients. According to this view, Diogenes the Cynic <note>the famous Greek philosopher known for his asceticism and biting wit</note> gave a pleasant reply to his doctor a few days before his death. The doctor had come to visit him and, finding him sleeping, woke him to ask if he felt worse than usual. "No," he replied, "it is only Sleep who has come to prepare the way for *Thanatos* <note>original Greek: Θάνατος, meaning Death</note> his brother." Another Ancient, in the same circumstances, gave a similar response,

<margin>The same author, in the same place <note>referring to the citation of Aelian or Pitiscus from the previous page</note>.</margin>
...although the phrasing is a bit different, but no less ingenious; Sleep, he says, begins to place me into the hands of Death <note>original Greek: "Θάνατος" (Thanatos)</note>, his brother.

There is no doubt that the Gauls, by personifying Sleep and Death, made them male deities just as the Greeks did. The gender of the ancient deities depended on the grammatical gender that the concept they were deifying held in their language. A single example makes this truth apparent: the Romans believed that Death was a Goddess, because the word for death <note>original Latin: *Mors*</note> was feminine; the Greeks, on the contrary, maintained it was a God, because their word <note>original Greek: "Θάνατος" (Thanatos)</note> was masculine. Since the Celtic language was originally the same as that of the Greeks <note>The author is reflecting an 18th-century linguistic theory that incorrectly attempted to derive Celtic languages directly from Greek</note>, the Gauls undoubtedly used a masculine word to signify Death; and consequently, they considered Death to be a God who was the brother, and not the sister, of Sleep.

But when the Underworld Venus <note>original Latin: *Venus Infera*</note> of the Gauls was represented with a single child—which perhaps happened more often than representing her with two—which of her sons did she carry in her arms? Was it Death? Was it Sleep? I admit that it is difficult to put forward anything on this matter that is entirely certain. The records that the Ancients have left us concerning the funerals of the Gauls do not go into such great detail. Notwithstanding this silence, I would readily believe that the two figures of Venus I provide here represent Venus with Sleep rather than with Death. The reasons upon which I base this are:

I do not examine whether a Roman tomb included in *Antiquity Explained* <note>Referring to the monumental 1719 work by Bernard de Montfaucon, which documented the archaeological remains of the ancient world</note> was made on the model of Gaulish tombs. It remains certain that the Romans did, at least sometimes, have carved upon their sepulchers a Woman who held two children in her arms, in the midst of two other Women, who were indeed clothed, but lead a great mourning, and what is more, with their breasts all bared: which was always for women the sign of the most marked mourning.

I have gathered in this Chapter a wealth of Gaulish Monuments, which inform us not only of several important details regarding the funeral rites of our Ancestors; but which also place before our eyes the true appearance of their attire. Their tunic, their <term>saye</term> <note>From the Latin "sagum," a traditional Gaulish cloak made of coarse wool, often fastened at the shoulder with a brooch.</note>, their mantle, and the various fabrics with which they covered themselves, are so well represented there, that the eye immediately grasps the diversity of social statuses and genders. One can even go further; one can, I say, compare Gaulish clothing with the garments of the Greeks, the Romans, and other Nations—both barbarian and civilized—and note all their differences. But the greatest of all advantages is that while curiosity finds here plenty to satisfy itself, the desire that Scholars have to constantly make new progress in the knowledge of Antiquity also finds an inexhaustible source for research and reflections, as novel as they are important.

It is difficult to explain why the Gauls represented the dead with an urn in hand. It appears, however, that it was a fairly general custom in the Gauls; for historians note that Severus <note>Septimius Severus (reigned 193–211 AD), a Roman Emperor who died in York, Britain.</note>, who ended his days in England—that is to say, in a country where the same religion as in the Gauls was practiced—Severus, I say, had the little urn (*urnula*) in which his ashes were to be enclosed brought to him before he died; and that, holding it in his hands, he said: "You will soon contain a man whom the whole world could not contain." (*a*)

The words of this ambitious Emperor can lead us to the knowledge of the true motives that drove the Gauls. Severus, in speaking thus, made a public confession of his vanity; never was a nation more convinced of the vanity of this life than our ancestors. This conviction led them to brave the greatest perils, to despise death, to seek it out, and to fly toward it. Assured of another life, they were indifferent to this one, and they turned all their sights toward the one that was to succeed it.

This was done either to appease the **Manes** <note>The *Di Manes* were Roman spirits of the dead, often viewed as collective deities of the underworld.</note> and make them favorable to the dead in whom they were interested, or to provide the souls with the satisfaction they were said to take in smelling the food, or inhaling the smoke and scent that rose from it.

Its square shape is the standard form of the *acerra* seen on marble carvings; any other shape is rare or extraordinary. I noted in the description I gave above of these incense boxes that they were square in every direction; this is because, in fact, the *acerra* used at funerals were all made this way; they were made, according to **Festus** <note>Sextus Pompeius Festus, a Roman grammarian whose works provide vital information on ancient customs and language.</note>, on the mod- <note>The text cuts off here at the catchword "mon-", likely continuing "modèle" (model) or "monument" on the following page.</note>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Roman funerary laws and the practice of reserving a part of the deceased's body (like a finger or bone) before cremation. It transitions from the physical description of the "severed member" to the legal justifications found in the Twelve Tables.</meta>

<page-num>296</page-num>
<header>RELIGION</header>

One is not mistaken: for a law of the <term>Twelve Tables<note>The earliest code of Roman law, dating to approximately 450 BC, which formed the foundation of Roman constitution and legal thought.</note></term> in forbidding anything of the deceased to be reserved—in order to have an occasion to perform sacrifices once the funeral ceremonies were finished—makes an exception; unless, it is said, those from whom one wishes to reserve some bones died at war, or outside their country. (a)
Now, this exception, or if one prefers, permission to reserve some part of those who died either in the army or in a foreign land, was only because these reserved parts took the place of the whole body; and it was assumed that a death occurring either at war or far from one’s homeland, having been unable to be honored with the appropriate pomp and funeral; one could fulfill, in the person of these parts, so to speak, the same duties that would have been rendered to the whole body, if the deceased had died in his own home.

I reason the same regarding the intention of those who before the Law, or even against the Law, reserved either the finger, or a bone, or even the hair (b) of their dead; and I hold that they had no other view than to renew from time to time the funeral ceremonies of their relatives, or of their friends. I confirm this sentiment by the very spirit of the Law, which was to stop frequent expenses, and prevent the ruin of the greatest houses. But the Romans, having become masters of all the earth, and possessing riches in proportion to the extent of their Empire, could they believe themselves bound to a
