The handle of this urn is quite a singular thing; yet not so much that one cannot find examples among Roman monuments. It even appears that the Gauls ordinarily gave handles to the vessels consecrated to the <term>Mysteries<note>The secret religious rites of the ancient world.</note></term> of their religion; I have as my witnesses the *incense boxes* <note>original: "acerra," a small chest or casket used by the Romans for holding incense during sacrifices.</note>, and the other vessels or instruments of which I have had occasion to speak in different parts of this work. The urn held by <term>Casatus Caratius<note>A name appearing on Gallo-Roman funerary monuments, likely representing a specific deceased individual or a donor.</note></term> is another proof upon which I rely: for after all that I have just said, I do not think anyone would wish to call into doubt that it is a true urn. Thus, I shall be excused from speaking of it in particular, since it has nothing to distinguish it but its form: upon which it is sufficient to cast one's eyes to know all that it is permitted to know in this regard.

One might perhaps ask, on the occasion of so many Gaulish figures holding cinerary urns in their hands, if these urns were those of the very people these figures represent?

I reply that one finds nothing, either on monuments or in the writings of historians, that clarifies this question. Nevertheless, it seems one could initially say that these urns should not belong to those carrying them; because one cannot suppose that they survived themselves in order to take care of their own ashes; and thus it is likely that by representing them with an urn in hand, the intention was to pass down to posterity just to what extent—

...the extent to which they carried the heroism of devotion toward those to whom they were bound by the ties of blood or friendship.

It can also be said that they were depicted in this way through the care of their relatives and friends, who followed the taste and custom of the Country in doing so.

<margin>Lucan, *Pharsalia*, book 1. <note>Marcus Annaeus Lucanus (39–65 AD), a Roman poet. His epic poem *Pharsalia* is a primary source for the belief that Druids taught the immortality of the soul, which the author is referencing here.</note></margin>
But all these reasons are countered by the great number of Figures holding urns of so many different forms; indeed, this multitude of urns serves less to express the kind services that those depicted might have rendered to others after their death, or that others might have rendered to them, than to demonstrate the spirit of the Nation. This spirit consisted in envisioning, desiring, and confronting death as a passage to a life which, while being a continuation of this one, would nevertheless not be subject to the same hardships.

But this was not only the spirit of the Gauls; it was also the essence of the Religion they practiced. To prove this, it would suffice for me to recall either the two Monuments I mentioned at the beginning of this Chapter, or the Inscriptions with which I accompanied them, or finally everything I have said regarding the customs and way of life, both of the Nation in general and of the <term>Druids<note>The high-ranking priestly class in ancient Celtic societies, serving as judges, teachers, and religious leaders.</note></term> in particular. The ancient Britons had no other Religion than that of the Gauls; it is therefore certain that the similarity of the Gaulish and British graves, upon which the individuals of both Nations are represented with urns in their hands, serves to demonstrate that both were animated by the same spirit. The very terms of the Inscription certainly support this truth; for by reading as I do on the last line, *he erected this stone or tomb* <note>original: "hoc Saxum ou sepulcrum erexit". The author is interpreting the typical funerary shorthand to mean the deceased commissioned the work themselves while alive.</note>, one will recognize that the Gauls and the Britons viewed death with such indifference that they prepared their own tombs; and thus the Figures they had engraved on these tombs could only be their own likenesses.

Furthermore, when one knows that the ancient Britons had the same Religion as the Gauls, and that one finds similar images on the tombs of both, one is forced to agree that these Peoples had drawn these images from the very heart of their Religion; that Religion dictated this, and that it was its character and spirit. Now, let us compare the genius of the Gauls with that of their Religion...

# RELIGION

...and let it be seen if one can discover the slightest difference between the one and the other.

The sepulcher unearthed in England is therefore very interesting: it proves not only that the Religion of the Gauls was uniform everywhere, and that all the peoples who professed it were animated by the same spirit; but furthermore, it alone resolves the difficulty proposed; for as soon as the three letters of the last line signify *he erected this stone* or *tomb* <note>original: "hoc Saxum" or "sepulcrum erexit". These Latin phrases refer to the common funerary abbreviations (like H.S.E. or H.F.C.) found on Roman-era monuments, indicating the deceased commissioned the work themselves.</note>; one is no longer at a loss to know whose urns are seen on these types of tombs; since the Monuments bear witness that they were erected by those very people who were to be enclosed within them after their death; thus, one would not think to suggest that those who, during their lifetime, had work done on their tombs and prepared the urns meant to contain their ashes, would ever have thought to have any other urns or figures represented on their own tombs than their own. This does not, however, exclude certain figures that were sometimes engraved specifically to highlight the one that truly represented the person whose ashes and bones lay within the mausoleum <term>mausoleum: a magnificent tomb; the word originates from the tomb of King Mausolus, one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World</term>.

## CHAPTER IX.

Description of a <term>bas-relief<note>A type of sculpture where the figures are carved to stand out slightly from the flat background.</note></term> representing a young man on a sea-horse. An examination of whether this is an <term>apotheosis<note>The elevation of a human to the rank of a god.</note></term> or the abduction of Ganymede. It is neither. The Greeks represented Neptune in this manner. This monument represents what the Ancients called the Abduction of Day.

The following plate represents a beardless young man who has nothing to cover his nakedness but a large cloak, which hangs behind him from his shoulders to the bottom, without being brought forward. This young man has his arms outstretched; he has nothing in his left hand, but with his right hand he holds the edge of his cloak, either so that it cannot slip away from him, or so that it remains pressed to his body, and finally so that it does not flutter at the whim of the winds. He is shown from the front and standing upright on a sort of hippopotamus or sea-horse that is swimming. Behind his head rises an eagle, which flies and matches his movement.

The first explanation that presents itself upon glancing at this monument is that it is either the apotheosis of some Emperor, or the abduction of Ganymede <note>In Greek mythology, Ganymede was a beautiful youth snatched up by Zeus in the form of an eagle to serve as cupbearer to the gods.</note>. But when one comes to examine the matter closely, one finds that it is neither. Indeed, the sea-horse alone overturns all these ideas. Furthermore, the young man is not raised in the air, which would be necessary to support either of these explanations.

Here the term and the meaning of the "**Abduction** by the Day" <note>An ancient poetic concept where a person who dies young is said to have been stolen by the daylight or the gods.</note> are well-marked and were in use in Gaul. It would be useless quibbling to raise the slightest objection to a truth that is so evident. It only remains to be seen if the symbols that compose the monument can be related to this **Abduction**, and on this point, there is not the slightest difficulty. For first, the main character is young; he is naked like Europa, Ganymede, and the others whom Mythology represents as having been carried off by the gods. He makes a sign with one hand to indicate that one should be consoled by his loss, since it is less the effect of a scythe-stroke from Death than of the love the gods bear for him. The eagle behind him is engraved specifically to highlight this **Abduction** and to place it in parallel with that of Ganymede <note>In Greek myth, the beautiful youth Ganymede was abducted by Zeus in the form of an eagle to serve as cupbearer to the gods.</note>, suggesting perhaps that the boy could rival him in beauty. This young man stands upright upon a swimming sea-horse; everything is consistent and linked to the **Abduction** mentioned in the Inscription. Indeed, the young man’s posture clearly suggests that he is not dead, and the sea-horse cutting through the waves expressly marks that it is carrying away, by order of Neptune <note>The Roman god of the sea.</note>, the one it bears on its back.

These are the spiritual emblems under which the Gauls concealed the tragic death of a young man of noble birth who had drowned in the flower of his youth.

( a ) Abducted ones <note>original Greek/Latin: *Arpagi*. A term for those snatched away by premature death.</note>.

## CHAPTER X.

*A great number of bodies found in an ancient tomb in 1685. Burnt bones, ashes, urns, etc., found separately in the same place. Divided opinions regarding the nation of those buried there. It was a tomb of the ancient Franks or French. Description of the discovery of King Childeric’s tomb. Other tombs of the early Franks or French.*

THE King <note>Referring to Louis XIV, who reigned during the discovery in 1685.</note> having ordered several works to be carried out on the Eure River to make its navigation more convenient, Monsieur de Cocherel received orders to perform a task for which he required three to four hundred feet of dressed stone <term>dressed stone (*pierre de taille*): stone that has been precisely cut and finished for construction</term>. Because he could obtain no help from the neighboring quarries due to a lack of workers, he was obliged to search his own lands for anything that could provide him with stones suitable for the work. He cast his eyes especially upon two stones situated on a very high hill, exposed to the full midday sun and sloping toward the river. They stood upright and protruded from the ground by about a foot, like the markers <note>original: *bornes*</note> planted to separate private estates. These two stones had already been seen fifteen years earlier by three unknown men, who came to excavate this site on a day of

On the other hand, nothing is more certain than what is frequently written from Germany, and what is stated in the excerpt of the letter I used a little earlier: that across the Rhine, tombs similar to the one at Cocherel are often unearthed. These contain corpses placed indiscriminately alongside burned bones, urns, and mounds of stone and sand, some of which are sometimes up to a hundred paces in circumference, while others rise very high like small mountains. It is therefore to the Germans that we must turn, and we should seek only among them those whose bones and ashes were enclosed in this Monument. And since I have demonstrated as clearly as possible that the majority of the bodies occupying the tomb were certainly those Germans now known only by the name of Franks or French, it would be a true gamble to turn one’s gaze toward any of the other peoples who inhabited ancient Germany.

### RELIGION

I only ask those who make a study of the writings of the Ancients, and who find there nothing, or only a few things, of all that I say, to notice that Monuments <note>In this period, "Monuments" refers generally to any physical archaeological remains, such as ruins, statues, or unearthed artifacts, rather than just commemorative structures.</note> are often more reliable guides than Historians. Regardless of the accuracy they prided themselves on, not only did an infinite number of important things escape them, but they even fell into gross errors which would pass for constant truths were it not for the help of Monuments.

I will finish my reflections on the tomb of Cocherel by saying that it appears that those whose bodies were burned were persons of a lower social status than the others. I have as my warrant the Author of the letter I have cited several times, who says that in Germany the ordinary mark of the tombs of the common people are urns and burned bones. This fits very well with two other reasons that greatly strengthen this view. One is the kind of gradation noticed in the positioning of the bodies in the tomb of Cocherel; this consists in the fact that, taking these corpses one after another, one sees that the value of the axes <note>The "axes" mentioned here are polished stone celts. The Cocherel site is now known to be a Neolithic collective burial, though the author interprets it through the lens of ancient Germanic history.</note> belonging to each, beginning with those of the first, always decreases by degrees, so that the last are always of less value than the first. My final reason is that the burned bodies have no weapons like the others, nor any mark that distinguishes them.

Now, no one will dispute with me that the Cocherel tomb was truly a tomb of the ancient Franks, whether one considers the shape of this tomb or looks at the arrangement of those who were buried there. As for the stone weapons, they can be considered a casual and accidental circumstance, which depended on location, time, and the personal taste of the individuals; and all of that varied in the past just as it does today.

A more important matter arises, which deserves much more of our attention; it is that all these great tombs of Cocherel, Angers, and Childeric <note>Childeric I (died c. 481 AD) was a king of the Salian Franks and father of Clovis; his lavish tomb was discovered in 1653.</note>, which I shall soon discuss, and several other similar ones I could cite, although filled with the bodies and bones of several men; all these tombs, I say, were nevertheless, to tell the truth, the tomb of only a single person. This seems at first a paradox; nonetheless, nothing is more certain. Let us recall here what Caesar <note>Julius Caesar, in his "Commentaries on the Gallic War," recorded the customs of the Iron Age Gauls.</note> says of the funerals of the Gauls: that shortly before he came to the Gauls, the custom was to throw into the funeral pyre of a deceased person his slaves and his clients; even his closest kin often threw themselves in, to have the consolation of living with the dead. Let us reason in the same way regarding the tombs of the Franks: these peoples observed the customs and religion of the Gauls in almost everything, and they had no other theology than theirs. If it happened, then, that some high-ranking person of the nation came to pay their debt to nature <note>original: "payer le tribut à la nature" — a common historical idiom for dying</note>, a court was formed here below that they were to have in the other world: for this purpose, they slaughtered those who were to compose it: and in order to bind them further to the deceased, these wretched victims were buried with the one whose death was the cause of theirs. This is why in the tomb at Angers, there was only a single sepulchral stone, so small that only the name of Pattilius could be engraved upon it—in whose honor alone a sepulcher had been erected, which contained many other bodies than his own. Similarly, in the tomb of Childeric <note>Childeric I (d. 481 AD). His tomb was discovered in 1653 and contained spectacular gold and garnet treasures, as well as the remains of horses, which the author interprets as sacrificial companions</note>, besides the entire skeleton of this Prince, it still contained at least one other man, since a head was found there that had been placed there at the same time. ### OF THE GAULS. BOOK V.

Furthermore, all the precious monuments found in the tomb of King Childeric were removed and taken to Vienna, Austria, by Archduke Leopold William, who governed the Low Countries for the King of Spain. After the Archduke's death, they passed into the Emperor's Cabinet. Philip of Schönborn, Elector and Archbishop of Mainz, requested them from the Emperor, who granted them to him. As this Prelate had only taken this step to offer the true successor of Childeric a gift worthy of the antiquity of his throne, in recognition of the great assistance he had received from him against his rebellious subjects; as soon as he had this treasure in his power, he sent it to Louis the Great <note>original: "Loüis le Grand" — King Louis XIV of France</note>.

It would be a shortcoming in the description of Childeric's tomb to finish without noting that in the tombs of the Kings of France, which are numerous in the Church of Saint-Germain-des-Prés in Paris, many things similar to those I have just mentioned have been found. Above all, in the coffin of another Childeric <note>Childeric II, a later Merovingian king buried in Paris</note>, there were silver amphisbaenae <note>original: "amphisbénes" — mythical serpents with a head at each end</note>, a baldric <term>baldric: a belt worn over one shoulder to carry a sword</term>, swords, daggers, a clasp <note>original: "agraphe"</note> of very fine gold weighing more than eight ounces, part of a diadem, and a glass or crystal vial that still contained some balm—dried, to be sure, but which still gave off a faint scent—and many other things that are rightly suspected to have been stolen by the maneuvers of the workers who labored on these tombs, and who had opened them before calling the Monks <note>original: "Religieux"</note>.

## CHAPTER XI.

### *Discovery of a Tomb in the Environs of Angoulême.*

In the year 1541, there was found in Vars, a large town <note>original: "gros Bourg"</note> located three or four leagues <term>league: an old unit of distance, roughly 3 miles or 4.8 kilometers</term> from Angoulême, an ancient sepulcher of oblong shape, surrounded on all sides by a wall built of large and massive stones. This wall was, however, at an equal distance from the monument; the space separating the one from the other was one foot. The stone that covered the sepulcher was carved in the shape of a vault or a hoop: the edge of this stone descended by a third of a foot, so that the stone underneath recessed slightly, thus keeping the sepulcher perfectly sealed. 

When this stone was lifted, there was seen in the center a lead coffin, which did not touch the stone on any of its sides, except from below. This coffin was sealed with four iron hoops, each three inches wide and one inch thick. The lead was intact; but the iron was so eaten away by rust that at the slightest strike of a spade, it fell into pieces. Inside was found a human body covered with a skin so delicate that as soon as it felt the air, it disappeared, leaving the bones of a man visible, each in its place. A search was conducted to see if anything was hidden; the entire find consisted of a sheet of very fine gold, which was discovered at the very spot where the heart of the deceased must have been. This sheet weighed only half a ducat <term>ducat: a gold coin used as a standard of weight and currency across Europe; here used as a unit of weight</term>; it was longer than it was wide; although one of its

This puts us in possession of some of their jewelry, which has, so to speak, triumphed over time. These items compensate for the silence of historians and seem to have been preserved only to teach us many details of Antiquity that would never have reached us without their help. These are precious remains, of which even the smallest traces must be preserved, since the mere sight of them is a fertile source of knowledge. They serve at times to correct the writings of Authors, at times to resolve our most well-founded doubts, and finally to shed light on other antiquities upon which no one previously dared to give an opinion.

His plan required him to take land from an opposite field that the road itself could not provide.

I admit that I do not know what to think of these bones enclosed in urns and arranged in layers. It does not appear that these were the bones of Gauls who died of natural causes, because they were whole, they bore no marks of fire, and there was neither ash nor charcoal in the urns. Such remains are never missing from the bones of those whose bodies were burned after death, as was the custom of the Gauls of whom I speak. I am strongly inclined to believe that these bones belonged to those whom the Druids sacrificed to their Gods. The care they took to arrange them in layers with such art, and to spread over the top and bottom of the urns—as well as on each layer—this substance which served to nourish them, to preserve them, and to prevent them from turning to dust, is proof that they held a particular veneration for these bones. Now, the veneration they had for the relics of those they had offered in sacrifice could not be greater, since they held that this ceremony had the power to deify them <note>The author is interpreting these archaeological finds through the 18th-century fascination with Druidic human sacrifice, a common theme in the scholarship of that era.</note>.

I even believe, and Mr. le Haribel is of this opinion, that these bones had been stripped of their flesh and fat, and that the flesh and fat were included in the composition of that matter which served to embalm them. This was done so that no part of the body of those who, in their minds, had become Gods, would be lost. The last type of bracelet was found on the very arms of several skeletons unearthed in the city of Angers, while digging in a house that had formerly been part of the Palace of the ancient Counts of Anjou. All these bracelets were made of bronze; which may cast doubt on what Strabo <note>A Greek geographer and historian who lived during the transition from the Roman Republic to the Roman Empire.</note> says, that the bracelets of the Gauls were of gold, as were their collars.

The rings of the Ancients were of the same kind as bracelets; that is to say, they were to the fingers what bracelets were to the arms: they were also made of the same metal and the same shape; thus, it was only the difference in size that distinguished them. Furthermore, even this size was considered of no account when there were persons who had fingers as thick as the arms of others; for then they used bracelets in place of rings; as witnessed by the Emperor Maximinus <note>Gaius Julius Verus Maximinus, known as Maximinus Thrax, was Roman Emperor from 235 to 238 AD and was legendary for his massive size.</note>, who had a thumb so thick that his wife's bracelet served him as a ring. (a) <note>original: "Pollice ita vasto ut uxoris Dextrocherio uteretur pro Annulo." — With a thumb so vast that he used his wife's bracelet [dextrocherium] as a ring [annulus].</note>

This ring was found at Arles; it is enriched with a precious stone cut into an octagon, with these words engraved <gloss>in abbreviation</gloss> ARRA GENIALIS <note>original: "ARRA GENIALIS," meaning a "Nuptial Pledge" or "Marriage Earnest"</note>: terms that are quite rare, but whose meaning is drawn from this passage by Festus <note>Sextus Pompeius Festus, a 2nd-century Roman grammarian</note>; *The Nuptial Bed, which is spread for the newlywed in honor of the Genius <note>a protective spirit in Roman religion</note>, from which it also takes its name.* It was therefore the nuptial ring that the Latins usually called the *Annulus Pronubus* <note>the bridal ring or betrothal ring</note>. Two passages from Arnobius <note>an Early Christian apologist of the 4th century</note> taken from the fourth book of the *Apology* which he wrote in favor of the Christian Religion against the Pagans, confirm the definition of Festus; but they also prove that the term *Genialis* was not so restricted to the meaning of the nuptial bed that it did not also generally designate the beds of persons truly united by the bonds of marriage, as well as the beds upon which lovers obtained from their mistresses the favors they ought not to have granted them.

From this one can infer that our *Arra Genialis* could just as well be a testimony of some engagement made against the Law, as one made according to the Law. It remains constant that the words engraved on this ring teach us two meanings of the term *Genialis*, of which ancient and modern Grammarians do not speak.

Marcel <note>likely an antiquarian or collector who documented the find</note>, who provides this ring, does not say of what metal it was; but it appears likely that it was of gold, contrary to the custom of the Romans, among whom the nuptial ring was not only round and plain, but also made of iron. I hesitated for a long time before providing the names of certain Gaulish Divinities who are absolutely unknown. Mere names without explanation, nor any legitimate basis to form conjectures, did not seem to me an object worthy of the attention of Scholars. Furthermore, these names were found in Gruter <note>Jan Gruter (1560–1627), a Dutch philologist and historian famous for his massive collection of ancient inscriptions.</note>, in Spon <note>Jacob Spon (1647–1685), a French physician and archaeologist who was a pioneer in the field of epigraphy.</note> and in other Antiquaries <note>In this period, "Antiquaries" refers to scholars who studied ancient artifacts and manuscripts.</note>, who made it a point of merit to collect them: one could consult them and have recourse to their compilations. This was enough to be excused from gratuitously overburdening the Readers, who seek only light, instruction, and truth, while one has only darkness to offer them. But finally, yielding to I know not what fear that bad-tempered Critics might come to charge me with a crime for having failed the commitments they would wish I had contracted by virtue of the title I gave to this Work, and might reproach me for having deprived the Public of the knowledge of some Gaulish Gods, I have decided to provide them, but detached—set apart and at the end of the entire Work. I am persuaded that their small number and the barbarian syllables, which com- <note>The text breaks here; "com-" likely begins the word "composed" or "comprise."</note>

record their names, did not allow them to be integrated with the others, nor to be ranked in any class. Indeed, was it just that Gods bristling, I dare say, with thorns, and buried in the deepest obscurity, should be placed in parallel with those who present ideas that charm not only by themselves, but also by the light they shed on past centuries?

It must be admitted, however, that in making this decision, I acted less out of fear than out of a desire to oblige the Public. I reflected on the advantage they might gain from having all these names collected here: elsewhere they are scattered throughout great Works, and so confused with many others that one risks, while searching for them, either losing them, passing them over, or failing to distinguish them. I saw, moreover, that the study of Antiquity pleasantly occupies people of refinement <note>The original term "honnêtes gens" refers to the 18th-century ideal of the "honest man"—a person of good breeding, social grace, and educated interests.</note>; everyone takes pride in it and wishes to make progress: this progress is the delight of people of good taste; and everywhere people take pride in carefully gathering the smallest Monuments <note>In this period, "Monuments" referred broadly to any physical remnants of the past, such as inscriptions, coins, or statues, rather than just large buildings.</note> that are unearthed: today these Monuments enhance the value of the Cabinets <note>A "Cabinet of Curiosities" was a private collection of artifacts, the precursor to modern museums.</note> of Kings, Princes, Prelates, Magistrates, Scholars, and Collectors: everyone seeks them out, wants to possess them; and neither care nor expense is spared. On this basis, people will not fail to compare the reflections I offer in this work with these Monuments. to make them known. For what is required for that? An inscription, a relief, a symbol, a word, a stroke, a letter; all these carry their own light. Often a single ray is enough; one suddenly sees what could not be seen before, and what so many others had not noticed. It is to contribute to such a happy outcome that I provide almost all the inscriptions that speak of our unknown deities: these various pieces help one another and work toward the same goal; and what they cannot achieve alone, they will perhaps accomplish either with other similar pieces or with the reliefs found in the Cabinets <note>Refers to "Cabinets of Curiosities," the private collections of 18th-century scholars and aristocrats.</note> of the Antiquarians <note>In this period, an "Antiquarian" was a scholar who studied history through physical artifacts, such as coins, statues, and inscriptions, rather than just written texts.</note>.

Finally, this is what determined me to place the unknown *Gaulish Gods* here. One should not infer from this that I intend to provide a list, or an exact catalog, of all the deities recognized by our ancestors; such an undertaking is impossible, and I have stated the reason for this in the *Preface*. Here, it is only a question of some less significant <note>The original "moins intéressans" suggests these gods were less prominent in the grand mythologies or historical records, appearing only in obscure locations.</note> gods, about whom authors have remained largely silent, and who are known to us only through a few inscriptions from relatively late periods <note>The author likely refers to "Late Antiquity" or the later centuries of the Roman Empire.</note>. I even acknowledge that among these latter ones, some may have escaped the care I took to collect and seek them out. It is in vain to search sometimes: too much precision can be harmful; it causes one to often overlook what should most strike the eye.

I have included among the unknown *Gaulish Gods* several deities whom I freely acknowledge to be either Roman in origin, or at least to have been equally common to both Romans and Gauls. I further admit that one can know the nature and the

<meta>This page continues the explanation of the "God Tutelle" (Tutela) mentioned on page 359, transitioning from the description of the ruined temple in Bordeaux to the maritime origins and broader application of tutelary deities.</meta>

<page-num>360</page-num>
<header>RELIGION</header>

Gods could be Tutelary Gods: the term is generic, and it signifies Protector, Patron, or Safeguard. The origin of this superstition came from sailors who never ventured out to sea without placing the vessel or ship they boarded under the protection and safeguard of a God, whose Figure or one of whose most significant symbols they had engraved on the Stern. At first, all the ships that composed a fleet or naval force had only one and the same Tutelary deity or God for a Protector; later on, each vessel wanted to have its own. These observations serve to reveal the true meaning of several Fables of the Ancients; for example, the abduction of Europa <note>The author is using a "Euhemerist" interpretation here—a method of interpretation which treats mythological accounts as derived from real historical events.</note>, carried off by Jupiter in the form of a Bull cleaving the waves: the historical basis was that Europa had been taken away in a ship which had Jupiter for its *Tutelle* <note>original: *Tutele*. In Roman maritime tradition, the *tutela* was the guardian spirit of the ship, usually represented by a statuette or relief on the stern.</note>, represented in the form of a Bull.

It is evident from all this that the God *Tutelle* was properly nothing more than a ship's Divinity: however, one finds many Inscriptions dedicated to this God in different Cities; which would lead one to believe that the worship of this Divinity would have been adopted indifferently by people of all sorts of arts and trades, or at least by Municipal bodies. But it seems more likely that this worship never underwent any alteration, and that it was always the lot of persons who either went to sea or who traded on the water; indeed, I notice that the Cities which honored the God *Tutelle* were famous either for their Port or for the Rivers that bathed their walls; the three

<summary>This page explains the maritime origins of "Tutelary" gods, arguing that myths like Europa's abduction were actually historical accounts of ships named after their guardian deities, and suggests that Tutela worship in cities was linked to river and sea trade.</summary>

<header>RELIGION</header>

<margin>See the notes of Father Sirmond on this Council. <note>Jacques Sirmond (1559–1651) was a prominent French Jesuit scholar and historian who published extensive works on the councils of the ancient church.</note></margin>
—cient city of France, known only by the Council that was assembled there in the time of Sigismund, King of Burgundy, in the year 517. But until now, no one has been able to agree on the location of this city. Some have placed it in the Dauphiné <note>A former province in southeastern France.</note>, others in Savoy, and others finally in Bavaria; where, according to the latter, it still exists under the name of Bibruc or Pinburg. Be that as it may, it remains certain that the Goddess Epona is not a deified city: 1st, Because the inscriptions dedicated to this Divinity have not been found in any of the places suspected to be the city where the Council in question was held. 2nd, Because the site of the Council was called, according to all the ancient manuscripts, *Epao*, and according to only a very small number of recent ones, *Epauna*; now, neither of these corresponds well with our *Epona*. 3rd, and finally, it is because independently of any city, there was a Goddess Epona.

Indeed, besides the inscription of Solothurn <note>original: *Soleure*, a city in modern-day Switzerland.</note> which I will report hereafter, several ancient authors teach us that horses and stables were under the protection of this Divinity; and that muleteers, carters, wagoners, and those who were charged with providing horses for the Games of the Circus—in a word, those who rode or drove beasts of burden—invoked Epona, swore by her, and recommended themselves to her along with the animals they wished to preserve. The most singular sepulchral inscription that has perhaps ever appeared is the one engraved on an urn or square tomb of white marble, which **Father de la Chaize** <note>François de la Chaize (1624–1709), the Jesuit confessor to King Louis XIV; the Père Lachaise Cemetery in Paris is named after him.</note> brought in June 1706 to the **Academy of Inscriptions** <note>The *Académie des Inscriptions et Belles-Lettres*, a French learned society devoted to the humanities.</note>.

<margin>*</margin>
The front face of the urn and those of the two sides are decorated with **bas-reliefs** <note>term: *bas-relief* — a type of sculpture where the figures project only slightly from the background.</note>: the reliefs on the two sides are similar and represent a swan swooping down upon a fleeing bird, which is only half-visible; above the fleeing bird is a ram's head, from one horn of which hangs a wavy ribbon.

In the center of the front face is represented **Sulpicius Notus**, in whose honor the monument was erected; he is shown lying naked and slightly facing forward, leaning his head on his left arm. At each of the upper corners is a ram’s head, from which hangs a cord attached to a festoon of oak leaves, forming a sort of **Civic Crown** <note>In ancient Rome, the *Corona Civica* was a wreath of oak leaves awarded to a citizen who had saved the life of a fellow citizen in battle.</note> at the bottom. The two lower corners are each occupied by an eagle with wings outstretched and in a startled posture, turned toward the body of Sulpicius Notus. At the top of this same face, one reads this inscription in beautiful Roman characters within a square **cartouche** <note>term: *cartouche* — an ornamental frame or tablet, often oval or rectangular, used to enclose text or a coat of arms.</note>:

<meta>This page continues the analysis of the funeral urn of Sulpicius Notus, moving from a description of its physical features to an interpretation of the inscription and its symbolic imagery.</meta>

<page-num>371</page-num>
<header>ON THE GAULS, BOOK V.</header>

->TO THE SPIRITS OF THE DEPARTED<-
<note>original: "D. M." — an abbreviation for *Dis Manibus*, a standard Roman invocation to the gods of the underworld.</note>
->TO SULPICIUS<-
->NOTUS. BE PRESENT<-
->O GODS ABOVE<-
<note>original: "SVLPICIO NOTO ADESTE SVPERI"</note>

The meaning of this inscription is a prayer made by the deceased to the living who pass near his tomb, asking them not to trample his bones, nor to violate the place where his ashes rest; to pour water or make some libation, to appease the gods of the underworld, to make vows in his favor from which he might derive some benefit, or finally to offer some sacrifice for him. This is especially what the ram heads decorated with ribbons seem to indicate; accordingly, it would be a <term>criobolium</term> <note>term: *criobolium* — the ritual sacrifice of a ram, often performed in mystery cults like those of Cybele and Attis to seek purification or divine favor.</note> that Sulpicius Notus requested. It is also true that these ram heads could be signs of a <term>criobolium</term> that had been offered at his funeral.

Regarding the formula "Be present, O gods above" <note>original: *adeſte ſuperi*</note>, which is not commonly used in inscriptions—and this is the only instance where these terms are employed—the gentlemen of the Academy of Inscriptions have observed that an expression which appears "new and singular does not always contain great mysteries, and it falls back into the common order when one has no interest in overvaluing it."

Regarding the explanation of the bas-reliefs: the swans on the two side faces, as birds of good omen which, according to myth, sing melodiously when they are about to die <note>The "swan song" was a common motif in classical antiquity, symbolizing a peaceful or meaningful transition to death.</note>, mark the glorious end of Sulpicius Notus.

<header>OF THE GAULS. BOOK V.</header>

the years. The revenues of two-thirds of a vineyard are assigned to provide for the costs of the Ceremony. The term vineyard is followed in the Inscription by these four letters AREP. Mr. Lancelot has shown in an Academic discourse that they are the abbreviation of the word *Arepennis*, from which the French have formed the word *arpent* <note>term: *arpent* — a traditional French unit of land area, roughly equivalent to an acre, which survived in parts of North America and Mauritius long after the metric system was adopted in France.</note>.
<margin>Book 5, ch. 1.</margin>
This term, according to Columella <note>term: *Columella* — Lucius Junius Moderatus Columella (4–70 AD), a prominent Roman writer whose work *De Re Rustica* is one of our primary sources on ancient agriculture.</note>, is certainly Gallic; and it signified a space of one hundred and fifty feet, which made up only half a Roman arpent <note>original: *semi-jugerum* — the *jugerum* was the standard Roman unit of area, approximately 0.6 acres.</note>. (a) However, several skilled Grammarians derive the word *Arepennis* from different sources: some from *arare*, to plow or work the land; others from *Arvipendium*, a surveyor's measure: all false origins that fall of their own weight. Others have recourse to the Danish Language, and they derive this term from *aërt* and *pand*, which signify
<margin>Acts of the Saints, April, vol. 3, col. 72.</margin>
bounded land; finally, the Bollandists <note>term: *Bollandists* — a group of Jesuit scholars named after Jean Bolland, dedicated to the critical study of the lives of the saints (*Acta Sanctorum*).</note> derive it from two words, half Gallic and half ancient French; namely, from *ard* or *erd* (land), and from *pand* or *pend* (square). This assumes that the space of land comprised in the *arepennis* of the ancient Franks and Gauls was originally square.

Although I am persuaded that the letters *Arep.* are the abbreviation of *Arepennis*; and that *Arepennis* here signifies a Roman half-arpent; it remains constant that this term in the Inscription could very well signify something else entirely than a land measure; namely an elevation, a hill, or a mountain; for the Gauls in their Language used the syllable *ar* as an article; and *pen* or *penn* among them signified a high place, a sum—

---

(a) <note>original: "Galli Candetum appellant in areis urbanis spatium centum pedum, in agrestibus autem pedum 150. quod aratores Candetum nominant; semi jugerum quoque arepennem vocant."</note> The Gauls call a space of one hundred feet in urban areas *Candetum*, but in rural areas one hundred and fifty feet, which plowmen call *Candetum*; they also call a half-acre an *arepennis*.

puts, a chief, etc. Thus *Arepennis* could indicate that the vineyard, whose revenues the Author of the Inscription consecrates to the expense of the Libation <note>term: libation — a ritual pouring of wine or other liquids as an offering to a deity or the spirits of the dead.</note>, was on high ground, on a hill, or on the slope of some mountain. But this does not deserve to detain the Reader any longer:

Here is how I read the entire Inscription: <note>original Latin: "DIIS MANIBVS LIBERORVM AC CONIVGIBVS PVBLICI CALISTI ET IPSIVS CONSECRATVM CVM BESE VINEAE AREPENNIS EX CVIVS REDITV OMNIBVS ANNIS PROLIBARI VOLO HEMINIS QVINDECIM QVINQVE SEMILIBRIS FARRIS HIC TVMVLVS HAEREDES NON SEQVITVR"</note> **To the Divine Spirits <note>term: Manes — the "Diis Manibus" were the souls of deceased loved ones, often addressed at the start of Roman tomb inscriptions.</note> of the Children and Wives of Publicus Calistus and of himself; consecrated with two-thirds <note>original: "bese" — two-thirds of a unit.</note> of a half-acre <note>term: arepennis — a Gallic unit of land area, roughly half of a Roman jugerum.</note> vineyard, from the revenue of which I desire that every year a libation be made of fifteen heminas <note>term: hemina — a liquid measure approximately equal to half a pint.</note> [of wine] and five half-pound loaves of spelt <note>original: "farris" — a type of hulled wheat used in sacred offerings.</note>; this tomb does not pass to the heirs**; *that is to say, to the Divine Spirits of the Children & the Wives of Publicus Calistus, who establishes every year in their honor Libations, consisting of fifteen heminas of wine, & five half-pound loaves, from the revenues of two-thirds of a half-acre Roman vineyard. This Tomb does not pass to the Heirs.*

## Errors to be corrected.

Page * 2. line 13. [they] present to the Scholars before their eyes; *read, they present to the eyes of the Scholars.*
Page * 4. l. 18. could <note>original: "povoit", an archaic spelling</note>; *read, could <note>original: "pouvoit"</note>.*
Page * 5. l. 14. inferior & decorated; *read, is decorated.*
Page * 26. l. 18. which have the whole face; *read, which have completely the face.*
Page * 31. l. 12. who would not have wanted to give to him; *read, who would not have wanted to give it to him.*
Page * 33. l. 23. they called themselves; *read, they were* <note>The correction simplifies the phrasing by removing the word "appeller" (to call/name)</note>
Page * 47. l. 12. & to multiply them; *read, & by multiplying.*
Page * 62. l. 14. the Gulois; *read, Gauls.* <note>The Gauls were the ancient Celtic inhabitants of the region that is now France</note>
Page * 72. l. 24. Chilperic; *read, Childeric.* <note>This corrects the name of a Merovingian king; Childeric I was the father of Clovis</note>
Page 16. l. 12. thought of taking them; *read, thought to take them.*
Ibid. <note>From the Latin "ibidem," meaning "in the same place" (referring to Page 16)</note> l. 27. where one sees a K formed; *read, where one had formed a K.*
Page 17. l. 10. or satisfied; *read, or little satisfied.*
Page 35. l. 17. in the second Chapter; *read, in the fourth Chapter.*
Page 38. l. 2. *Lavaerum* <note>original: "Lavaerum"</note>; *read, Lavacrum* <note>Latin for a bath or ritual basin</note>
Page 39. l. 4. Mydonians; *read, Mygdonians.* <note>An ancient people of Mesopotamia or Macedonia</note>
Page 112. last line, fires <note>original: "ignes"</note>; *read, snakes <note>original: "angues"</note>.*
Page 122. third to last line, Diana; *read, Dione.* <note>Dione was a Titaness in Greek mythology, often associated with the mother of Aphrodite</note>
Page 138. l. 13. sanctity of her bearing, the Goddess who was consecrated; *read, bearing, which was consecrated, etc.* <note>The correction shifts the focus of the consecration from the Goddess herself to her "port" (bearing or carriage)</note>
Page 145. l. 13. the long space of time; *read, the long space of time.* <note>This correction removes a redundant article from the original French phrasing</note>
Page 214. l. 3. which serve as victims; *read, which served as victims.*
Page 225. l. 9. to unite with them; *read, to unite to them.*
Page 249. l. 20. under the base; *read, on the base.*
Page 250. l. 7. it must however be admitted in good faith that although the Gauls; *read, it must however be admitted in good faith, that the Gauls.*
Page 295. at the first marginal citation; book 9. letter 31. <note>original: "lib. 9. epist. 31."</note>; *read, book 9. epigram 31. <note>original: "lib. 9. epig. 31."</note>*
Page 312. second to last line, of the Megares; *read, of the inhabitants of Megara.*
Page 317. l. 1. thirteenth century; *read, thirteenth.*
Page 329. l. 17. near the skeletons; *read, near to the skeletons.*
Page 338. l. 10. PEGIS; *read, REGIS <note>Latin: "of the King"</note>. And delete the marginal note.*
Page 343. l. 13. sometimes finally, *read, sometimes.*
Page 349. l. 5. these engraved words, ARRA; *read, these words engraved in abbreviation, ARRA.* <note>Likely referring to "arrhae," a term for a pledge or earnest money in ancient law</note>
